﴿When Joseph said to his father: "O my father, indeed I saw eleven stars, and the sun and the moon; I saw them prostrating to me."﴾

The word governing *idh* (إذْ, "when") is an implied verb whose estimated form is: "Recall when" (اذْكُرْ إذْ). It is also permissible for the governing element (*al-'amil*, the word that determines the case or action of another word) to be *naqussu* ("We relate"), so that the meaning is: "We relate to you the situation when." Makki reported that the governing element is ﴿among the heedless﴾ [Yusuf: 3], but this is weak.

Talha ibn Musarrif recited "yu'safu" (يُؤْسَفُ) with a hamza and a fatha on the sin. There are six dialectal forms of the name: "Yusufu" with a damma on the ya, a sukun on the waw, and a fatha, damma or kasra on the sin; and likewise with a hamza. The majority recited "ya abati" (يا أبَتِ) with a kasra on the ta'. The ya of "abi" (أبِي, "my father") was dropped and the ta' was made a substitute for it, as stated by Sibawayh (the early grammarian). Ibn 'Amir alone, Abu Ja'far and al-A'raj recited "ya abata" (يا أبَتَ) with a fatha. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir would pause with a ha' (هاء). As for Ibn 'Amir's recitation with a fatha on the ta', it has two possible explanations: either the original was "ya abata" (يا أبَتا), then the alif was dropped for lightness while the fatha remained to indicate the alif; or it follows the pattern of the saying "ya Talhata aqbil" (يا طَلْحَةَ أقْبِلْ), where the word was shortened (*tarkhim*, apocope, the dropping of the end of a vocative) and the sign of the case was restored, without being counted after the shortening. This is like their saying "ijtama'at al-yamamatu" (اجْتَمَعَتِ اليَمامَةُ, "the dove gathered"), then they said "ijtama'at ahlu al-yamamati" (اجْتَمَعَتْ أهْلُ اليَمامَةِ, "the people of al-Yamama gathered"), restoring the word "ahl" and not treating it as counted.

Abu Ja'far, al-Hasan and Talha ibn Sulayman recited ﴿eleven stars﴾ (أحَدَ عَشَرَ كَوْكَبًا) with a sukun on the 'ayn, because of the succession of vowels, and so that it would be clear that the two words have been made one. It was said that he actually saw stars, and the sun and the moon, and Ya'qub interpreted them as his brothers and his parents. This is the view of the majority. It was said: they are the brothers, the father and the maternal aunt, because his mother had died. It was also said: he had only seen his brothers and parents, and he expressed them by the stars, the sun and the moon. This view is weak. al-Tabari gave it as a heading, then included, from Qatada, al-Dahhak and others, statements that could be understood as he headed them, or as being like the common speech of people. The exegetes said: the moon's interpretation is the father, and the sun's interpretation is the mother. Some people deduced from the mention of the mother first the obligation of honouring the mother and that it is greater than honouring the father.

al-Tabari reported from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah that a Jew named Bustana came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: "Tell me the names of the stars which Joseph (peace be upon him) saw." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was silent, and Jibril (peace be upon him) descended and informed him of their names. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) called the Jew and said: "Will you believe if I inform you of that?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Jaryan, al-Tariq, al-Dhayyal, Dhu al-Kaftayn, Qabis, Wathab, 'Amudan, al-Faylaq, al-Musbih, al-Daruh, Dhu al-Farigh, al-Diya', and al-Nur." The Jew said: "Yes, by God, these are indeed their names."

The repetition of "I saw them" (رَأيْتُهمْ) is due to the length of the speech. The application of the pronouns of these stars in this verse follows the pattern of the pronouns of rational beings, since they were described with actions that are specific to rational beings.

It is related that the dream of Joseph took place on the Night of Power, a Friday night, and that it came out after forty years. It was also said: after eighty years.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 12, verses 5–6:

The Exalted said:

﴿He said, "My son, do not relate your vision to your brothers, lest they plot a plot against you. Indeed, Satan is to man a clear enemy."﴾ ﴿And thus will your Lord choose you and teach you the interpretation of events (ta'wil al-ahadith) and complete His favor upon you and upon the family of Ya'qub, just as He completed it upon your two fathers before, Ibrahim and Ishaq. Indeed, your Lord is Knowing and Wise.﴾

This verse implies that Ya'qub (peace be upon him) sensed from his sons envy of Yusuf and hatred toward him. So he forbade him from relating the vision to them, fearing that it would kindle the rancor in their breasts, so that they would devise a scheme for his destruction. From this, and from their action toward Yusuf, which will be mentioned later, it becomes apparent that they were not prophets at that time. It occurs in al-Tabari's book, from Ibn Zayd, that they were prophets, but this is refuted by the certainty of the prophets' infallibility (ismah) from worldly envy, from disobedience to fathers, and from exposing a believer to destruction and conspiring to kill him. Then He informed him that Satan is to man a clear enemy, meaning: he leads them into that and urges them toward it.

Al-Kisa'i inclined (amala) the word "ru'yaka" and the word ru'ya wherever it occurs. It is narrated from him that he did not incline "ru'yaka" in this surah, but inclined ru'ya wherever it occurs. And he read "ruyaka" without hamza, which is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz. The rest did not incline it wherever it occurs. Ru'ya is a verbal noun (masdar) which came to be used frequently for this imagined thing seen in sleep, until it took the course of nouns (asma'), as they did with "al-durr" in their saying "li-Llahi darruka" (by God, your pearl). Thus they left the rule of verbal nouns' function, and pluralized it as ru'an, in the pattern of zulam, whereas verbal nouns for the most part are not pluralized.

(p. 43) And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And thus will He choose you﴾, the verse. "Yajtabika" means: He will select you and choose you. From it comes "jaba'tu al-ma'a fi al-hawd" (I gathered the water in the basin), and from it comes "jibayat al-mal" (the collection of wealth). And His saying: ﴿and teach you the interpretation of events﴾. Mujahid and al-Suddi said: it is the interpretation of dreams. Al-Hasan said: it is the outcomes of matters. It was said: it is general to that and to other unseen things. And His saying: ﴿and complete His favor﴾ means prophethood and what was added to it of the rest of the favors. And His saying: ﴿the family of Ya'qub﴾ means, in this place, the offspring and the kin who are of his lineage, meaning that He will place prophethood among them. It is narrated that Ya'qub only knew that from Ishaq's supplication for him when Esau (Ay'su, 'Isu) was made to resemble him. The full story is in the book of al-Naqqash, but I have abridged it because he did not refine its wording, and I do not think he took it except from the books of the Children of Israel (Isra'iliyyat), for it is a well-known story among them. The rest of this verse is clear.

The favor upon Yusuf was his release from prison, his preservation (from sin), and the kingship which he attained. Upon Ibrahim it was his being taken as a close friend (khalil). Upon Ishaq it was his ransom by the great sacrifice, all of this being attributed to prophethood. "Knowing" and "Wise" are two fitting descriptions for this promise.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 12, verses 7–10:**

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Indeed, in Joseph and his brothers are signs for those who ask.﴾ ﴿When they said: "Joseph and his brother are more beloved to our father than we, though we are a band. Indeed our father is in clear error."﴾ ﴿"Kill Joseph or cast him out to some land, that your father's face may be turned toward you, and you may be after him a righteous people."﴾ ﴿A speaker among them said: "Do not kill Joseph, but throw him into the bottom of the well; some of the travelers will pick him up, if you are going to act."﴾

[p-44] The majority read *āyātun* (signs) in the plural. Ibn Kathir alone read *āyatun* in the singular, and this is the recitation (qira'a) of Mujahid, Shibl, and the people of Mecca. The first reading means that every state of his is a sign, so the word is pluralized. The second means that he as a whole is a sign, even if it is detailed by meaning. The pattern of *āyah* is *fa'alah*, *fa'lah* or *fa'ilah*, and there is disagreement about this. Al-Zajjaj (al-Zajjaj, the grammarian) mentioned that in other than the Uthmanic codex the reading is *'ibratun lil-sa'ilin* (a lesson for those who ask). Abu Hatim said it is in the codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b.

His saying *lil-sa'ilin* (for those who ask) implies an exhortation to learn these reports, since what is meant is "a sign for people." He described them as askers because each person should seek to ask about such stories, for they are the seat of lessons and admonition. It is also valid to describe people as askers in that the cause of the revelation of the surah was the question of a questioner, as has been narrated.

Their saying *wa-akhūhu* (and his brother) means Benjamin, who was younger than Joseph. He is also called Yamin. It has been said that he was a full brother of Joseph, and their mother had died. That they were full brothers is indicated by the specification of the brotherhood to them with the phrase *akhūhu* (his brother), though this indication is not decisive. Jacob's love for Joseph and Benjamin was due to their youth and the death of their mother. This is from "the love of the young is the nature of humankind." It was said to the daughter of al-Hasan: "Which of your sons do you love most?" She said: "The young one until he grows up, the absent one until he returns, and the sick one until he recovers."

A group said it is an accusative of place (ẓarf), but that is an error, because a place adverb must be indefinite, and this is not so here; rather it is a land specified as being distant or remote and the like, so its indefiniteness is removed. It is known that Joseph was not without being in some land, so it made clear that it is a distant land, other than the one he was in, near his father.

His saying *yakhlu lakum wajhu abīkum* (that your father's face may be turned toward you) is a metaphor, meaning: if Joseph is lost, his love will return to you. Similar to this is the Arab saying when his mother loved him after his brothers were killed, though previously she did not love him: "Bereavement has softened her toward him," meaning her compassion for him. The pronoun in *ba'dihi* (after him) refers to Joseph, or to his killing, or to his casting out. As for *ṣāliḥīn* (righteous), al-Suddi and Muqatil ibn Sulayman said they meant the improvement of the state with their father. This resembles their intention in that state, and at that time they were not prophets. The majority said *ṣāliḥīn* means by repentance, and this is the more apparent from the wording, and their situation also indicates it, for they were believers who had committed a great sin and consoled themselves with repentance.

The speaker among them: it was said he was Ruwbil, the eldest, as said by Qatadah and Ibn Ishaq. It was said Yahudha, the wisest of them, and it was said Shim'un, the bravest of them, as said by Mujahid. This was an act of mercy from him toward his brother, without doubt, because of what God willed of the execution of His decree.

*Al-ghayabah* is what is hidden from you of places, or what hides something else from you. The majority read *ghayabati al-jubb* (the depths of the well). Nafi' alone read *ghayabāti al-jubb* (the depths of the wells). Al-A'raj read *ghayyābāti al-jubb* with a doubled ya'. Abu al-Fath said: "It is a noun that came on the pattern *fa''alah*. Abu 'Ali used to classify it with what Sibawayh mentioned, such as *al-fayyād* and the like. I found from this: *al-tayyār* for the wave, and *al-fakhkhār* for pottery."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

There is doubt about likening *ghayyābah* to these examples, because *ghayyābah* follows a verb pattern. Al-Hasan read *fī ghaybati al-jubb* on the pattern *fa'lah*, and likewise it is written in the codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b. From this word is the saying of the poet, who is al-Munakhkhal:

"If one day I am hidden by my hiding place,
then travel in my path among the tribe and the family."

*Al-jubb* is a well that has not been lined with stone, because it was dug out of the earth only.

The majority read *yaltaqiṭhu ba'ḍu* (some will pick him up) with a ya' below, according to the wording of *ba'ḍ* (some). Al-Hasan al-Basri, Mujahid, Qatadah and Abu Raja' read *taltaqiṭhu* with a ta', since *al-ba'ḍ* was made to refer to *al-sayyārah* (the caravan), and so it took from it the feminine marking of the verb. From this is the poet's saying:

"I see the passing of years has taken from me
as the crescent takes from the moon."

And from it is the saying of another:

"When a chief among them dies, another chief rises,
and the people of the towns and churches are humbled before him."

And the saying of Ka'b:

"... ... ..."
"All of Nizar was humbled by its blow."

Here he meant by *Nizār* the tribe. Examples of this are many. It is narrated that a group of Bedouins picked up Joseph, peace be upon him. *Al-sayyārah* is the plural of *sayyār*, which is a pattern of intensification.

It has been said about this well: it is the well of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), and it has been said it is other than that. It has been said there was no water in the place where they cast him; rather God brought it forth in it until people came to it for drawing water. It has also been said that in fact there was much water in it which would drown Joseph, so a rock jutted from the bottom of the well until Joseph stood upon it. It is narrated that they lowered him into the well with a rope, and he held on with his hands until they tied his hands, and they took off his shirt and threw him then. They intended to crush him with stones, but their brother who advised casting him out prevented them from that.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 12, verses 11–15:

God, the Mighty and Majestic, says:

﴿They said: "O our father, why do you not entrust us with Yusuf, when we are indeed his sincere well-wishers?"﴾ ﴿"Send him with us tomorrow, that he may enjoy himself and play, and indeed we will be his guardians."﴾ ﴿He said: "It grieves me that you should take him away, and I fear that the wolf may devour him while you are heedless of him."﴾ ﴿They said: "If the wolf devours him while we are a band, then we would indeed be losers."﴾ ﴿So when they took him away and agreed to put him in the depths of the well, We revealed to him: "You will surely inform them of this affair of theirs, while they do not perceive."﴾

The first verse indicates that their father had known from them their evil intention concerning Yusuf, and this indicates that they knew that he knew of it.

Al-Zuhri and Abu Ja'far read "لا تأمنا" with idgham (assimilation of the two identical consonants) without ishmam (a partial rounding of the vowel). Al-Hulwani transmitted it from Qalun. The Seven (readers) read it with ishmam towards the damma. Talha ibn Musarrif read "لا تأمننا", and Ibn Wathhab and al-A'mash read "لا تيمنا" with a kasra on the taa' of the 'alama (the grammatical ending marker).

"Ghadan" is a adverb of time (zarf). Its original form is "ghadwun", but it became fixed to the whole day, and "al-ghuduww" and "al-ghudwa" remained as nouns for the first part of the day. Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: "What lies between dawn and the brightening (of the day) is called ghudwa and bukra."

Abu 'Amr and Abu 'Amir read "نرتع ونلعب" with nun in both and with sukun on the 'ayn and the ba'. In this reading, "narta'" is from al-rutu', which means staying in abundance and pasture, eating and drinking. From this is the saying of al-Ghadban ibn al-Qaba'thari: "The shackle, the abundance of pasture, and the scarcity of stammering." From it is also the saying of the poet:

.................... 
"And after your gift, the hundred plentiful (camels)?"

Their play was of the permissible kind of play, like playing with horses, shooting, and the like. So there is no blame upon them for it, and it is not the play that is the opposite of truth and the companion of frivolity. It was said to Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala': "How can they say 'we play' when they are prophets?" He replied: "At that time they were not prophets."

Ibn Kathir read "نرتع ونلعب" with nun in both, with kasra on the 'ayn and jazm (sukun) on the ba'. It has also been transmitted from him "ويلعب" with ya'. This is the reading of Ja'far ibn Muhammad. In this reading, "narta'" is from the tending of camels. Mujahid said it is from al-murra'a (watching over), meaning that some of us watch over and guard one another. 'Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "يرتع ويلعب" with all of this attributed to Yusuf. Nafi' read "يرتع ويلعب" with ya' in both, with kasra on the 'ayn and sukun on the ba'. In this reading, "yarta'" is from the grazing of camels. Ibn Zayd said the meaning is: he trains himself in herding and guarding property. From al-irtila' (grazing) is the saying of al-A'sha:

"You graze the slope, then the sand dune, then Dhaqa (?), 
Then the meadow of the sandgrouse, then Dhat al-Ri'al."

Abu 'Ali said: The reading of Ibn Kathir, "narta'" with nun and "yal'ab" with ya', has a good approach, because the consideration of guarding the property and watching over it is attributed to them, and the play is attributed to Yusuf because of his youth. Al-'Ala' ibn Sayyaba read "يرتع ويلعبُ" with damma on the ba', as an interruption (qat', i.e., breaking the clause into a nominative sentence). Mujahid and Qatada read "نرتعِ" with damma on the nun and kasra on the ta', and "نلعبْ" with nun and jazm. Ibn Kathir, in some transmissions from him, read "نرتعي" with the ya' retained; this is weak and is not permitted except in poetry, as the poet said:

"Has the news not reached you, while the reports spread, 
Of what the she-camel of the Banu Ziyad suffered?"

Abu Raja' read "يُرتع" with damma on the ya' and jazm on the 'ayn, and "يلعب" with ya' and jazm.

They justified their request and their taking him out by what might attract Yusuf because of his youth: grazing, play and liveliness.

God, the Exalted, says: ﴿Indeed it grieves me﴾, the verse. 'Asim, Ibn Kathir, al-Hasan, al-A'raj, 'Isa, Abu 'Amr and Ibn Muhaysin read "ليحزنني" with fath on the ya' and damma on the za'. Abu Hatim said: Nafi' read with damma on the ya', kasra on the za' and idgham. The transmission of Warsh from Nafi' is to make both nuns clear, with damma on the ya' and kasra on the za' throughout the Qur'an. The first "an" is the subject (fa'il), and the second is the object (maf'ul) of "akhafu" (I fear).

Al-Kisa'i alone read "al-Dib" without hamza, while the rest read it with hamza, which is the original form. From it comes their plural "dhu'ban", and from it the saying: "The wind and the wolves ran back and forth (tadha'abat)" when they came from here and there. Warsh transmitted from Nafi' "al-Dib" without hamza. Nasr said: I heard Abu 'Amr not pronounce the hamza. He said: The people of the Hijaz pronounce it with hamza.

Ya'qub feared the wolf specifically, and singled it out, because it was the common wild animal spread throughout the region. It is narrated that Ya'qub had seen in his dream a wolf attacking Yusuf.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This, in my view, is weak, because if Ya'qub had seen that, it would have been a revelation. Either it would have come true in the way he saw it, and that did not happen; or Ya'qub would recognise, through his knowledge of the interpretation of such a vision, the one seen, and he would have been warning him specifically. Unless his saying "and I fear that the wolf may devour him" means: I fear that he may be struck by something like what I saw of the matter of the wolf. This is far-fetched. Likewise al-Rabi' ibn Dab' said:

"And the wolf, I fear it..."

He singled it out only because it was the common animal of his region. It is also possible that Ya'qub, peace be upon him, singled it out because of Yusuf's young age: i.e., I fear for him this lowly creature, and what is above it. Likewise al-Rabi' singled it out for its lowliness and weakness among animals. The rest of the verse is clear.

God, the Exalted, says: ﴿So when they took him away﴾, the verse. Al-Tabari transmitted through al-Suddi who said: They took Yusuf away with him (Ya'qub) showing him honour. When they emerged into the desert, they showed him enmity. His brother began to strike him, and he sought help from the other, who struck him as well. He saw no mercy from any of them. They beat him until they nearly killed him. He began to cry out and say: "O my father, O Ya'qub, if only you knew what the sons of the slave-women have done to your son!" Yahuda (Judah) said to them: "Did you not give me a covenant that you would not kill him?" So they took him to the well. They began lowering him, and he clung to the edge. They tied his hands and stripped off his shirt. He said: "O my brothers, return my shirt to me, that I may cover myself with it in the well." They said: "Call upon the sun, the moon and the stars, they will comfort you." They lowered him until he reached the middle of the well, and then let him fall, intending that he should die. There was water in the well, so he fell into it, then stood upon a rock weeping. They called out to him, and he thought they had shown mercy, so he answered them. Then they wanted to crush him with a rock, but Yahuda prevented them, and he (Yahuda) used to bring him food.

The answer (jawab) of "lamma" is omitted; its estimated meaning is: "So when they took him away and agreed (to do it), they agreed." This is the view of al-Khalil and Sibawayh, and it is explicitly their statement. Of this is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"So when we passed the courtyard of the tribe and it turned aside..."

..............

A similar example is God's saying: ﴿So when they both submitted and he laid him down upon his forehead﴾ [al-Saffat: 103]. Some grammarians said that in such cases the waw is extra (za'ida), but this view is rejected, because there is nothing superfluous in the Qur'an without a meaning.

"Wa-ajma'u" means: they resolved, and their opinion agreed upon it. From it is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning the traveller: "As long as he has not resolved to stay (in one place)." Yet the agreement of one person may be singular in the sense of resolving and beginning, and this can be imagined in the agreement of Yusuf's brothers and in all other groups. Also, the agreement of a group may occur in matters where there is no resolve or beginning, and this cannot be imagined in the agreement of one person.

The pronoun in "ilayhi" refers to Yusuf. It was said to refer to Ya'qub, but the first is more correct and more common. It is possible that the revelation at that time was to Yusuf through a messenger, or through inspiration, or through sleep, and all of this has been said. Al-Hasan said: God gave him prophethood while he was in the well.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This is far-fetched.

The majority read "لتنبئنهم" with ta', while in some Basran codices it is with ya'. Salam read it with nun. All of this concerns the 'alama (the ending sign) that follows the lam.

God, the Exalted, says: ﴿while they do not perceive﴾. Ibn Juraij said: "At the time of the warning that you are Yusuf." Qatada said: "They will not perceive our revelation to him."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

According to the first interpretation, God's saying "and they do not perceive" is part of what was revealed to him; and according to the second interpretation, it is a report addressed to Muhammad (ﷺ).

This, in my view, is weak, because if Ya'qub had seen that, it would have been a revelation. ﴿And they came to their father in the evening, weeping.﴾ ﴿They said, "O our father, we went racing one another and left Joseph by our belongings, and the wolf devoured him. But you will not believe us, even though we are truthful."﴾ ﴿And they came with his shirt stained with false blood. He said, "Rather, your souls have enticed you to something. So patience is beautiful, and Allah is the One whose help is sought against what you describe."﴾

A group read "ʿishāʾan" (in the evening), meaning at the time of ʿishāʾ (the night prayer/evening time). Al-Hasan read "ʿushan" (ʿushan), on the pattern of "dujan," meaning the plural of "ʿāshin" (one who has poor night-vision or weeps). Abu al-Fath said: "ʿushāh" is like "mashin" and "mushāh," but the hāʾ was dropped for lightness, just as it was dropped from "maʾlukah." ʿAdiyy said:

"Convey to al-Nuʿman from me, the ma'lak (messenger),
that my imprisonment has been long and my waiting."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The meaning is that they were struck with a "ʿashā" (a dimness of sight) from weeping, or something resembling dimness of sight, since that is the appearance of the eyes of one who weeps, for he becomes dim-sighted. Shurayh gave the example of a woman who wept while being in the wrong, comparing her weeping to the weeping of these men, and he recited the verse. It is narrated that when Jacob heard their weeping he said, "What is the matter with you? Has something happened to the sheep?" They said, "No." He said, "Where is Joseph?" They said, "We went racing one another..." Then he wept and cried out and said, "Where is his shirt?" The account of this will come.

"Nastabiq" means: on foot, that is, we run competitively. It was also said: by shooting arrows, that is, we race at archery, which is a kind of contest; this was said by al-Zajjaj.

Their saying, "But you will not believe us" means: you will not affirm us as truthful. The meaning of the sentence is: even if we were described as truthful. It was also said the meaning is: even if you believed this about us in all our past statements, you would not have believed us in this particular matter, because of the grief that befell you in it, the hardship that reached you, and the accusation you had earlier made against us.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a view mentioned by al-Zajjaj and others. It is possible that their saying, "even though we are truthful," means "even if we are truthful," as al-Mubarrad said. As if they were informing about themselves that they were truthful in this matter, and this is a continuation of their lying. It would be like the words of the Exalted: ﴿Even though we were unwilling?﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 88], meaning: even if we were unwilling.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In this example, in my view, there is an issue. al-Rummani went astray at this point and said, "They obliged their father with stubbornness," and similar things that do not follow. For they did not say, "You will not affirm us for your belief, even though we are truthful." Rather they said, "You will not affirm us, even though we are truthful in what we believe, but as for you, ill opinion of us has overcome you." It is not denied that prophets, peace be upon them, may believe a liar to be truthful and a truthful person to be a liar, as long as it is not revealed to them; for they are but human, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "I am only a human, and you bring your disputes to me, and perhaps one of you is more eloquent in his argument than another, so I judge for him according to what I hear from him..." This hadith indicates that he allowed for himself that he might believe a liar. Likewise, he, peace be upon him, did accept the oath of ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy when he swore to the statement, and he disbelieved Zayd ibn Arqam, until revelation came down and the truth became manifest. So the speech of Joseph's brothers was merely deception and argument, not an obligation of stubbornness.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they came with his shirt stained with false blood.﴾ It is narrated that they took a young goat or a kid, slaughtered it, and smeared Joseph's shirt with its blood, and said to Jacob, "This is his shirt." He took it, smeared his face with it, and wept. Then he examined it and saw no tear and no trace of fangs. From this he inferred their lying, and said to them, "When did the wolf become gentle, devouring Joseph yet not tearing his shirt?" Ibn ʿAbbas and others related this account, and they agreed that he inferred their lie from the soundness of the shirt. The jurists relied on this in acting upon indicators (amarat) in matters such as the qasama (oath procedure in homicide) and others, according to the view of Malik, and beyond that. al-Shaʿbi said: "There were three signs in the shirt: its indication of their lie, its testimony by its tearing from behind, and the restoration of Jacob's sight through it." It is also narrated that they went and took a wolf, smeared its mouth with blood, drove it to him, and said to Jacob, "This is what ate Joseph." Jacob called the wolf, and it sat on its haunches and spoke, denying their claim.

The description of the blood as "false" (kadhib) is either in the sense of "blood possessing falsehood," or it may mean "falsely attributed," as the word "al-maʿqul" came in place of "al-ʿaql" in the verse of the poet:

"Until, when they left nothing of his bones of flesh, nor of his heart al-maʿqul (the intellect)..."

Likewise "al-takdhib" (the lying) may come in place of "al-makdhub" (the lied-about).

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is the speech of al-Tabari, and there is no evidence in it according to me, for the negation of "al-maʿqul" implies the negation of "al-ʿaql" and needs no substitute. Rather, in my view, "the false blood" is a description by the verbal noun in the manner of emphasis. al-Hasan read "bi-damin kadibin" with an unpointed dal, meaning fresh or the like, but this reading is not strong.

Then Jacob said to them when their lie became clear: ﴿Rather, your souls have enticed you to something.﴾ That is, they were pleased with it and made it their desire and aim. "Amran" means: an ugly act toward Joseph. As for his saying: ﴿So patience is beautiful﴾, it is in the nominative either by omitting the subject or by omitting the predicate: either as "my affair is beautiful patience," or as "so beautiful patience is better." It is mentioned that al-Ashhab and ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar read it in the accusative: "fa-sabran jamilan," with an implied verb, and it is so in the codex of Ubayy and the codex of Anas ibn Malik. This reading is weak according to Sibawayh, and the accusative in such a case is not suitable except with a command; hence the accusative is good in the poet's line:

"...patience, beautiful, for both of us are tested."

It is also recited with the nominative: "Sabrun jamilun, fa-kilana mubtala," and it is narrated as an address to the camel mentioned in the line:

"My camel complained to me of the length of the journey; O my camel, there is no complaint to me..."

"Sabrun jamilun, fa-kilana mubtala."

The reading in the accusative is valid only if it is assumed that Jacob, peace be upon him, turned to address himself in the midst of addressing his sons. The beauty of patience is that no complaint is made to any human. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever discloses [his grief] has not been patient with beautiful patience." His saying: ﴿And Allah is the One whose help is sought against what you describe﴾ is a submission to the command of Allah the Exalted and reliance upon Him; the meaning is: [He is the One sought for help] in bearing what you describe.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 12, verses 19–20:

The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿And a caravan came, and they sent their water-drawer, and he let down his bucket. He said, "Good news! This is a boy!" And they hid him as merchandise; but Allah was Knowing of what they did.﴾ ﴿And they sold him for a paltry price, a few dirhams counted out; and they were of those who had no desire for him.﴾

It is said that the caravan came on the second day after he was cast into the well. The word sayyara (caravan) is the plural of sayyar, as they say baghgal and baghgala (mule and mule-drivers/ mules), though this is the reverse of tamra and tamr (a date and dates). Sayyara is also a form of intensification (binā' mubālagha) for those who repeatedly travel the roads. It is related that this caravan were a people from the folk of Madyan; and it is said they were a people of Bedouin Arabs. The wārid (water-drawer) is the one who comes to the water to draw water for his group. It is related that the one who let down the bucket was called Mālik ibn Dhu'r. The wārid here may refer to one person or to a group. It is related that this well was in al-Urdunn, three farsakh from the dwelling of Ya'qub. It is said: adlā al-dalw means he cast the bucket into the well in order to draw water, and dallāhu yadlūhu means he drew water from the well with it. In the speech here there is an ellipsis, its estimated meaning being: Yusuf clung to the rope, and when the one who let down the bucket saw him, he said, "O my good news!" It is related that Yusuf was at that time seven years old. The word "ghulām" (boy) supports this, for it applies from two years of age until puberty. If it is said of what is beyond that, it is by way of retaining a previous state and by metaphorical usage. It is also said he was seventeen years old, but this is far-fetched.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir recited "yā bushrāya" with the word bushrā being attached to the first person and with the yā vowelled with fatha, as if he were saying: "Come, for this is your time," similar to His saying: ﴿Alas for the servants﴾ [Yasin: 30]. Warsh related from Nafi': "yā bushrāy" with the yā sukun. Abu 'Ali said: in this there is a combination of two sakin letters, on the pattern of dābba and shābba. The reasoning for this is that the alif may be particularly singled out with it, because of the extra prolongation in it over the prolongation in its two sisters, just as it is singled out in rhyme by ta'sis, and singled out in the easing of the hamza, as in habā'. None of that applies to yā and wāw. Abu al-Tufayl, al-Jahdari, Ibn Abi Ishaq and al-Hasan recited "yā bushrayya", where the alif is changed into yā and then merged into the yā of attribution. This is a widespread dialect, and from it is the verse of Abu Dhu'ayb:

"They outran my desire and let their desire run wild, so they were cut off, and for every side there is a place of fall."

Abu al-Fath and others recited in this regard:

"He makes me wander like a servant among Ma'add, and stabs me with the ṣumulla in my back (qafayya)."

"If you do not avenge me among Ma'add, then what you two have given drink to never again will quench my thirst (ṣadayya)."

He intended: hawāya, qafāya, and ṣadāya. Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited "yā bushrāy" with imāla, and they incline it and do not add a pronoun. 'Asim recited likewise, except that he opens the rā and does not incline. The interpretation of this recitation has been differed upon. Al-Suddi said: among the companions of this wārid there was a man named Bushrā, so he called out to him and informed him about the boy. It is said it is the calling of bushrā as we previously mentioned.

The pronoun in "wa-asarrūhu": the apparent sense of the verses is that it refers to the water-drawers. Mujahid said this, and said: they feared that the merchants of the caravan, if they said "we found him," would share with them in the boy found, (this if they were wicked), or would prevent them from owning him if they were believers. So they concealed among themselves that they would say: "A man of the city entrusted him to us as merchandise." "Bid'a" (merchandise) is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl); and bidā'a is a portion of wealth traded in without a share of profit, derived from their saying bada'at, meaning she cut off. It is also said: they concealed within themselves that they would take him as merchandise for themselves, meaning a source of trade, and they did not fear anything from the caravan folk. Then the pronoun in His saying "wa-sharawhu" would also refer to them, meaning they sold him for a small price, since they did not recognise his worth or value, rather they were indifferent to him. It is related on this view that they sold him to a merchant. Mujahid said: the pronoun in "asarrūhu" refers to the owners of the bucket, and in "sharawhu" refers to Yusuf's eleven brothers. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: rather the pronoun in "asarrūhu" and "sharawhu" refers to Yusuf's brothers.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is because it is related that when his brothers returned to their father and informed him, some of them returned to the well to verify the matter of Yusuf and to establish the truth of his disappearance. When they learned that the water-drawers had taken him, they came to them and said: "This is a runaway slave of our mother, and she gave him to us, and we sell him to you." Yusuf acquiesced to this statement out of fear of them, and so that Allah's command might be carried out. Then his brothers concealed him when they denied his brotherhood, so they concealed it and took him as merchandise, meaning a source of trade and gain for themselves. And they sold him as well for a paltry price, meaning they sold him.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And Allah was Knowing of what they did﴾: if the pronouns refer to Yusuf's brothers, then this is a warning; and if the pronouns refer to the water-drawers, then this is an alert to the will of Allah, blessed and exalted, for Yusuf, and the driving of destinies according to the shaping of his condition. In that case it carries the meaning of the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "The son of Adam plans, while the decree laughs." And in the verse there is also consolation for the Prophet ﷺ regarding what befalls him from the side of Quraysh, meaning: the end which belongs to the God-fearing is what is awaited and to be looked to.

"Sharawhu" here means "sold him," though it may be said that shara can mean "bought," and from the first meaning is the verse of Yazid ibn Mufarrigh al-Himyari:

"I sold a cloak, would that I had..., after the cloak I had been a fool (hāmah)."

"Burd" was the name of a slave-boy over whose sale he regretted, and the pronoun admits of both the two aspects previously mentioned.

"Bakhs" is a verbal noun described as the price, and it means deficiency; this is its most well-known meaning, so it is as if it were the small, deficient price. This is the saying of al-Sha'bi. Qatada said: bakhs here means injustice; al-Zajjaj preferred this on the ground that a free person may not lawfully be sold. Al-Dahhak said: it means the unlawful, and this too means that his sale is not lawful.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿dirhams counted out﴾ is an expression for the smallness of the price, because they were dirhams not weighed due to their small quantity; for they did not weigh anything less than an uqiyya, which is forty dirhams. There is disagreement over the amount of the price of Yusuf, peace be upon him. It is said they sold him for ten dirhams. Ibn Mas'ud said: for twenty. Mujahid said: for twenty-two, his brothers taking two dirhams. ['Ikrima said: for forty dirhams, paid short, and this was its paltriness.]

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and they were of those who had no desire for him﴾ is a description that applies to the water-drawers, meaning they did not know his worth, so their elation at him was slight. But it is more fitting for Yusuf's brothers, since the true meaning of indifference to a thing is removing love for it from the heart and rejecting it from the hand, and this was the state of Yusuf's brothers regarding Yusuf. As for the water-drawers, their clinging to him and their pulling him is contrary to indifference, except by way of figurative usage. Adverbial phrases permit fronting that is not permitted in other complements. The discussion of the plural pronoun in His saying "sharawhu" has already been given earlier.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 12, verses 19–20:

The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿And a caravan came, and they sent their water-drawer, and he let down his bucket. He said, "Good news! This is a boy!" And they hid him as merchandise; but Allah was Knowing of what they did.﴾ ﴿And they sold him for a paltry price, a few dirhams counted out; and they were of those who had no desire for him.﴾

It is said that the caravan came on the second day after he was cast into the well. The word sayyara (caravan) is the plural of sayyar, as they say baghgal and baghgala (mule and mule-drivers/ mules), though this is the reverse of tamra and tamr (a date and dates). Sayyara is also a form of intensification (binā' mubālagha) for those who repeatedly travel the roads. It is related that this caravan were a people from the folk of Madyan; and it is said they were a people of Bedouin Arabs. The wārid (water-drawer) is the one who comes to the water to draw water for his group. It is related that the one who let down the bucket was called Mālik ibn Dhu'r. The wārid here may refer to one person or to a group. It is related that this well was in al-Urdunn, three farsakh from the dwelling of Ya'qub. It is said: adlā al-dalw means he cast the bucket into the well in order to draw water, and dallāhu yadlūhu means he drew water from the well with it. In the speech here there is an ellipsis, its estimated meaning being: Yusuf clung to the rope, and when the one who let down the bucket saw him, he said, "O my good news!" It is related that Yusuf was at that time seven years old. The word "ghulām" (boy) supports this, for it applies from two years of age until puberty. If it is said of what is beyond that, it is by way of retaining a previous state and by metaphorical usage. It is also said he was seventeen years old, but this is far-fetched.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir recited "yā bushrāya" with the word bushrā being attached to the first person and with the yā vowelled with fatha, as if he were saying: "Come, for this is your time," similar to His saying: ﴿Alas for the servants﴾ [Yasin: 30]. Warsh related from Nafi': "yā bushrāy" with the yā sukun. Abu 'Ali said: in this there is a combination of two sakin letters, on the pattern of dābba and shābba. The reasoning for this is that the alif may be particularly singled out with it, because of the extra prolongation in it over the prolongation in its two sisters, just as it is singled out in rhyme by ta'sis, and singled out in the easing of the hamza, as in habā'. None of that applies to yā and wāw. Abu al-Tufayl, al-Jahdari, Ibn Abi Ishaq and al-Hasan recited "yā bushrayya", where the alif is changed into yā and then merged into the yā of attribution. This is a widespread dialect, and from it is the verse of Abu Dhu'ayb:

"They outran my desire and let their desire run wild, so they were cut off, and for every side there is a place of fall."

Abu al-Fath and others recited in this regard:

"He makes me wander like a servant among Ma'add, and stabs me with the ṣumulla in my back (qafayya)."

"If you do not avenge me among Ma'add, then what you two have given drink to never again will quench my thirst (ṣadayya)."

He intended: hawāya, qafāya, and ṣadāya. Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited "yā bushrāy" with imāla, and they incline it and do not add a pronoun. 'Asim recited likewise, except that he opens the rā and does not incline. The interpretation of this recitation has been differed upon. Al-Suddi said: among the companions of this wārid there was a man named Bushrā, so he called out to him and informed him about the boy. It is said it is the calling of bushrā as we previously mentioned.

The pronoun in "wa-asarrūhu": the apparent sense of the verses is that it refers to the water-drawers. Mujahid said this, and said: they feared that the merchants of the caravan, if they said "we found him," would share with them in the boy found, (this if they were wicked), or would prevent them from owning him if they were believers. So they concealed among themselves that they would say: "A man of the city entrusted him to us as merchandise." "Bid'a" (merchandise) is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl); and bidā'a is a portion of wealth traded in without a share of profit, derived from their saying bada'at, meaning she cut off. It is also said: they concealed within themselves that they would take him as merchandise for themselves, meaning a source of trade, and they did not fear anything from the caravan folk. Then the pronoun in His saying "wa-sharawhu" would also refer to them, meaning they sold him for a small price, since they did not recognise his worth or value, rather they were indifferent to him. It is related on this view that they sold him to a merchant. Mujahid said: the pronoun in "asarrūhu" refers to the owners of the bucket, and in "sharawhu" refers to Yusuf's eleven brothers. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: rather the pronoun in "asarrūhu" and "sharawhu" refers to Yusuf's brothers.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is because it is related that when his brothers returned to their father and informed him, some of them returned to the well to verify the matter of Yusuf and to establish the truth of his disappearance. When they learned that the water-drawers had taken him, they came to them and said: "This is a runaway slave of our mother, and she gave him to us, and we sell him to you." **Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah Yusuf, verses 21–22:**

His Exalted and Majestic words:

﴿The one who bought him from Egypt said to his wife, "Make his stay honorable; perhaps he will benefit us, or we may adopt him as a son." Thus We established Joseph in the land, and that We might teach him the interpretation of events. And Allah prevails in His command, but most people do not know.﴾ ﴿And when he reached his maturity, We gave him judgment and knowledge. Thus do We reward the good-doers.﴾

It is narrated that the buyer of Joseph, who was the one who came to him from his brothers or the merchant among the caravan-men, according to the disagreement mentioned earlier, brought him to Egypt, the well-known city, and for this reason it is not declined (it is treated as a diptote). He displayed him in the market, and he was the most beautiful of people. Bidding for him rose until it reached a great price. It was said: his weight in gold, silver and silk. The one who bought him was al-'Aziz, who was the king's chamberlain and treasurer. The name of the king was al-Rayyan ibn al-Walid, and it was said: Mus'ab ibn al-Rayyan, and he was one of the Pharaohs. It was also said that he was the Pharaoh of Moses, who lived long until his time.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is weak, because Joseph's rise to prominence did not occur during the reign of an unbeliever whom Joseph served. The name of the aforementioned al-'Aziz was Qatfir, as Ibn 'Abbas said; it was also said Atfir, and Qantur. The name of his wife was Ra'il, as Ibn Ishaq said; it was also said Rabiha, and Zulaykha. The apparent state of al-'Aziz is that he was an unbeliever, and what indicates this is the presence of the idol in his house, as we will mention in (the account of) the proof that Joseph saw. Mujahid said: al-'Aziz was a Muslim. The "mathwa" is the place of residence, and honoring applies only to the one who resides there, so there is a metaphor in the speech. His words, ﴿perhaps he will benefit us﴾, mean: by helping us in the affairs of our worldly life and in other respects of benefit. His words, ﴿or we may adopt him as a son﴾, mean: we would take him as an adopted son, and he had no child, as it is said.

Then the Exalted said, "Thus," meaning: as We have described, ﴿We established Joseph in the land, and that We might teach him﴾, We did that. The "ahadith" (events, sayings) here means dreams in sleep, as Mujahid said; it was also said: the accounts of the prophets and nations. The pronoun in "amrihi" (His command) may refer to Joseph, as al-Tabari said, and it may refer to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, as Ibn Jubayr said. In that case it is a notice drawing attention to the power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, not specifically regarding Joseph's affair but general in every matter. The same possibility applies to the words of the poet:

"I saw Abu Bakr, and your Lord is Dominant over His command, seeking the caliphate with dates."

Those people from whom knowledge is negated are the unbelievers, and among them are those who held Joseph in disregard and others who were ignorant of his affair. It is narrated from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: The three most perceptive (firasa) people are: al-'Aziz, when he said to his wife, ﴿Make his stay honorable﴾; the daughter of Shu'ayb, when she said, ﴿Hire him, for the best one you can hire is the strong, the trustworthy﴾ [al-Qasas: 26]; and Abu Bakr, when he appointed 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The perceptiveness (firasa) of al-'Aziz was only in his sense of Joseph's nobility, not that he discerned the matter as in the other two examples, for what the perceptive person discerned came out exactly as he perceived it.

(p. 63) "Al-ashudd" (full maturity): the completion of strength and the culmination of vigor. There are two stages of it: the first is puberty, which Malik and Rabi'a expressed as "ashudd," and Mundhir ibn Sa'id mentioned it; the second is the one the Arabs use. It was said: it runs from eighteen years to sixty years, but this is a weak view. It was said: al-ashudd is reaching forty; it was also said: thirty-six; it was said: thirty-three, and this is the most evident of the views in our estimation. It was said: twenty years, but this is weak. Al-Tabari said: al-ashudd has no singular from its own form. Sibawayh said: al-ashudd is the plural of shidda, like ni'ma and an'um. Al-Kisa'i said: ashudd is the plural of shadd, like qadd and aqudd. And shadd al-nahar means its greater part, when its daytime is completed.

His Exalted words, "hukman" (judgment), may mean wisdom and prophethood, and this would be at the highest level of maturity. It may also mean wisdom and knowledge without prophethood, and this is more fitting if the account of the seduction came after this. "Wa 'ilman" (and knowledge) means the interpretation of events and other things. It may also mean by "hukman" authority in this world and judgment among people with truth, and then prophethood, the interpretation of events and other things would be included in His words "and knowledge."

﴿Thus do We reward the good-doers﴾: these words contain a promise to the Prophet ﷺ, so let not the deeds of the unbelievers against you and their arrogance toward you alarm you, for Allah, the Exalted, arranges for the good-doers the most beautiful arrangement.

[p. 64]

The saying of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿She, in whose house he was, sought to seduce him from himself, and she closed the doors and said, "Come, you." He said, "I seek refuge in Allah. Indeed, he is my lord; he has made my residence excellent. Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed."﴾ ﴿And she certainly desired him, and he would have desired her had he not seen the proof of his Lord. Thus [it was], that We might avert from him evil and immorality. Indeed, he was of Our chosen servants.﴾ ﴿And they raced to the door, and she tore his shirt from behind, and they met her husband at the door. She said, "What is the penalty for one who intended harm to your wife except that he be imprisoned or [suffer] painful punishment?"﴾

Al-murawada (coaxing): gentle solicitation toward an aim. The word is used most often in this sense, which holds between men and women. It seems to derive from "rada yarudu," when someone goes ahead to test the land and pastures. Thus the one who seeks (al-murawid) is always testing, by his words and gentleness, the state of the one he courts, whether she will respond or refuse.

In Ibn Mas'ud's codex: "and she knocked on the doors" (wa qara'at al-abwab). It is also narrated from al-Hasan. "The one in whose house he was" is Zulaykha, the wife of the Aziz. His saying "from himself" (an nafsihi) is a metaphor for the aim of intercourse. His saying "and she closed" (wa ghallaqat) is an intensive form (ta'dif mubalagha), not a transitive one. The apparent sense of this incident is that it occurred before he was made a prophet.

Ibn Kathir and the people of Makka read "Hayta" (هَيْتُ) with a fatha on the ha', sukun on the ya', and damma on the ta'. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Ibn Muhaysin, Abu al-Aswad and 'Isa read "Hayta" (هَيْتَ) with a fatha on the ha' and a kasra on the ta'. Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan and the Basrans read "Hayta" (هَيْتَ) with a fatha on both the ha' and the ta', and sukun on the ya'. It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and Abu 'Amr. Abu Hatim said: "The people of Basra know no reading other than this, and they are the least excessive of people in recitation." Al-Tabari said: "It has also been narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read "Hiyta" (هِيتَ) with a kasra on the ha', sukun on the ya', and a fatha on the ta'. This is the reading of al-A'raj, Shayba and Abu Ja'far. All four readings have one meaning, though they differ according to the dialects in them.

[p. 65]

Its meaning is an invocation, i.e., "Come, and turn toward this matter." Al-Hasan said: its meaning is "hallum" (come here). It is good for "laka" (for you) to be joined to it, since it takes the place of her saying "approach" (iqbalan) or "nearness" (qurban). It thus functions like "saqyan laka wa ra'yan laka" (watering and pasturing for you). From this is the saying of the poet addressing 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him:

Convey to the Commander of the Faithful,
the brother of Iraq, when we come to him:
Indeed Iraq and its people
are a neck (bent) toward you, so come, come!

In the other dialect, from this is the saying of Tarafa:

My people are not the most distant
when a summoner from the clan calls "Hayt!"

From this also is the saying of another poet:

I have been troubled that sleep fell silent,
and if (someone) were to call us, it would have called out "Hayta!"

"Asqata" means he entered into silence. "Hayyata" means he said "Hayt," just as they say "uffafa" when he says "uff, uff," and from it "sabbaha" (he glorified), "kabbara" (he magnified), and "da'da'a" (he said "da', da'") when he says "da', da'."

The letter ta' in all these dialects is indeclinable (mabniyya). In the nominative it is like "qablu" and "ba'du." In the genitive it follows the pattern (of the other particles) because of the meeting of two sukuns. In the accusative it is like "kayfa" and similar words. Abu 'Ubayda said: [p. 66] "Hayta" is not dualized or pluralized. The Arabs say "hayta laka," "hayta lakuma," and "hayta lakum."

Hisham ibn 'Amir read "Hi'ita" (هِئِتُ) with a kasra on the ha', a hamza, and a damma on the ta'. This is the reading of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Abu Wa'il, Abu Raja', Yahya, and it is narrated from Abu 'Amr. This may derive from "ha'a al-rajulu yahi'u" when a man improves his appearance, on the pattern of "ja'a yaji'u." It may also mean "tahayya'tu" (I prepared myself), just as it is said "fi'tu" and "tafayya'tu" with one meaning. Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿whose shadows incline﴾ [al-Nahl: 48], and He said: ﴿until it returns to the command of Allah﴾ [al-Hujurat: 9].

Ibn Abi Ishaq also read it in this way, except that he eased the hamza. Ibn 'Abbas also read: "Hu'yi'tu laka" (I have been prepared for you). Al-Hulwani narrated from Hisham: "Hi'ita" with a kasra on the ha', a hamza, and a fatha on the ta'. It seems to derive from "rada yarudu," when someone goes ahead to test the land and pastures. the brother of Iraq, when we come to him:
Indeed Iraq and its people
are a neck (bent) toward you, so come, come!

In the other dialect, from this is the saying of Tarafa:

My people are not the most distant
when a summoner from the clan calls "Hayt!"

From this also is the saying of another poet:

I have been troubled that sleep fell silent,
and if (someone) were to call us, it would have called out "Hayta!"

"Asqata" means he entered into silence. "Hayyata" means he said "Hayt," just as they say "uffafa" when he says "uff, uff," and from it "sabbaha" (he glorified), "kabbara" (he magnified), and "da'da'a" (he said "da', da'") when he says "da', da'."

She said, "What is the penalty for one who intended harm to your wife except that he be imprisoned or [suffer] painful punishment?"﴾

Al-murawada (coaxing): gentle solicitation toward an aim. The word is used most often in this sense, which holds between men and women. It seems to derive from "rada yarudu," when someone goes ahead to test the land and pastures. Thus the one who seeks (al-murawid) is always testing, by his words and gentleness, the state of the one he courts, whether she will respond or refuse.

In Ibn Mas'ud's codex: "and she knocked on the doors" (wa qara'at al-abwab). It is also narrated from al-Hasan. "The one in whose house he was" is Zulaykha, the wife of the Aziz. His saying "from himself" (an nafsihi) is a metaphor for the aim of intercourse. His saying "and she closed" (wa ghallaqat) is an intensive form (ta'dif mubalagha), not a transitive one. The apparent sense of this incident is that it occurred before he was made a prophet.

Ibn Kathir and the people of Makka read "Hayta" (هَيْتُ) with a fatha on the ha', sukun on the ya', and damma on the ta'. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Ibn Muhaysin, Abu al-Aswad and 'Isa read "Hayta" (هَيْتَ) with a fatha on the ha' and a kasra on the ta'. Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan and the Basrans read "Hayta" (هَيْتَ) with a fatha on both the ha' and the ta', and sukun on the ya'. It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and Abu 'Amr. Abu Hatim said: "The people of Basra know no reading other than this, and they are the least excessive of people in recitation." Al-Tabari said: "It has also been narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read "Hiyta" (هِيتَ) with a kasra on the ha', sukun on the ya', and a fatha on the ta'. This is the reading of al-A'raj, Shayba and Abu Ja'far. All four readings have one meaning, though they differ according to the dialects in them.

[p. 65]

Its meaning is an invocation, i.e., "Come, and turn toward this matter." Al-Hasan said: its meaning is "hallum" (come here). It is good for "laka" (for you) to be joined to it, since it takes the place of her saying "approach" (iqbalan) or "nearness" (qurban). It thus functions like "saqyan laka wa ra'yan laka" (watering and pasturing for you). From this is the saying of the poet addressing 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him:

Convey to the Commander of the Faithful,
the brother of Iraq, when we come to him:
Indeed Iraq and its people
are a neck (bent) toward you, so come, come!

In the other dialect, from this is the saying of Tarafa:

My people are not the most distant
when a summoner from the clan calls "Hayt!"

From this also is the saying of another poet:

I have been troubled that sleep fell silent,
and if (someone) were to call us, it would have called out "Hayta!"

"Asqata" means he entered into silence. "Hayyata" means he said "Hayt," just as they say "uffafa" when he says "uff, uff," and from it "sabbaha" (he glorified), "kabbara" (he magnified), and "da'da'a" (he said "da', da'") when he says "da', da'."

The letter ta' in all these dialects is indeclinable (mabniyya). In the nominative it is like "qablu" and "ba'du." In the genitive it follows the pattern (of the other particles) because of the meeting of two sukuns. In the accusative it is like "kayfa" and similar words. Abu 'Ubayda said: [p. 66] "Hayta" is not dualized or pluralized. The Arabs say "hayta laka," "hayta lakuma," and "hayta lakum."

Hisham ibn 'Amir read "Hi'ita" (هِئِتُ) with a kasra on the ha', a hamza, and a damma on the ta'. This is the reading of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Abu Wa'il, Abu Raja', Yahya, and it is narrated from Abu 'Amr. This may derive from "ha'a al-rajulu yahi'u" when a man improves his appearance, on the pattern of "ja'a yaji'u." It may also mean "tahayya'tu" (I prepared myself), just as it is said "fi'tu" and "tafayya'tu" with one meaning. Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿whose shadows incline﴾ [al-Nahl: 48], and He said: ﴿until it returns to the command of Allah﴾ [al-Hujurat: 9].

Ibn Abi Ishaq also read it in this way, except that he eased the hamza. Ibn 'Abbas also read: "Hu'yi'tu laka" (I have been prepared for you). Al-Hulwani narrated from Hisham: "Hi'ita" with a kasra on the ha', a hamza, and a fatha on the ta'. Abu 'Ali said: "It is clear that this reading is an error, because it should have been 'hi'ita li'" (for me), and the context of the verses contradicts this." Al-Nahhas narrated that he read "Hiyti" with a kasra on the ha', sukun on the ya', and a kasra on the ta'.

"Ma'adha" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar). The meaning of the sentence is "I seek refuge in Allah." Then He said: ﴿Indeed, he is my lord﴾. The pronoun in "innahu" may refer to Allah the Mighty and Majestic, or it may mean the Aziz, his master, i.e., "it is not proper for me to betray him, since he has honored my residence and entrusted me." Mujahid, al-Suddi and Ibn Ishaq said: "rabbi" means "my master" (sayyidi).

The author, al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Whoever preserves a human's favor to him, that is a pure deed, and it is more fitting that he preserve (the favor of) his Lord.

[p. 67]

The pronoun may also refer to the matter and the affair, and then he begins: ﴿My lord has made my residence excellent﴾. The pronoun in His saying ﴿Indeed, he does not prosper﴾ refers only to the matter and the affair.

Some exegetes narrated that when Yusuf, peace be upon him, said: ﴿I seek refuge in Allah﴾, and then repelled the matter with argument and gentleness, Allah tested him with the desire for what she desired. Had he said, "There is no power nor strength except in Allah," and repelled her with violence, or with none of that, he would not have been afflicted with what he disliked.

Al-Ja'dari read "mathwayya" (مَثْوَيَّ), and Abu Tufayl read it likewise. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿Whoever follows My guidance﴾ [al-Baqara: 38].

As for His saying ﴿And she certainly desired him﴾, the verse. There is no doubt that Zulaykha's desire was that Yusuf should have intercourse with her. Scholars differed about Yusuf's desire, peace be upon him. Al-Tabari said: a group said it was like her desire. They differed about how such a thing could occur from someone like Yusuf, who is a prophet. It was said that this was so that Allah the Exalted might show him the place of pardon and sufficiency. It was also said that the wisdom in this is that he would serve as an example for sinners, so that they would see that their repentance returns them to the pardon of Allah, just as it returned one better than them, and his nearness to sin did not destroy him. All of this is based on the claim of this group that Yusuf's desire reached the point of sitting between Zulaykha's legs and beginning to untie his garments, his belt, and similar things, while she had lain down for him. This was narrated by Ibn 'Abbas and a group of the early Muslims (al-salaf). Another group said that his desire was only the passing thoughts of the heart, which no human can guard against. He withdrew at that point and did not go beyond it, so this is not far-fetched for someone like him, peace be upon him. In a hadith: "Indeed, whoever intends an evil deed but does not do it, will have ten good deeds recorded for him," and in another hadith: "one good deed." So Yusuf may enter into this category. Another group said Yusuf's desire was to strike her and similar things.

[p. 68]

The author, al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is absolutely weak.

What I say about this verse is: that Yusuf being a prophet at the time of this incident is not authentically established, nor is it supported by any consistent report. If that is so, then he was a believer who had been given judgment and knowledge. It is permissible for him to have the desire that is the intention of a thing without actually committing it, and to hold onto a bad thought, with the sin that this involves. If we assume he was a prophet at that time, then, in my view, what is permissible for him is only the desire that is a passing thought. None of what was mentioned about untying a belt and similar things can be attributed to him, because infallibility (ʿisma) goes with prophethood. As for what has been narrated, that he was told: "You will be in the register of the prophets and act like the foolish?!" its meaning is a promise of prophethood to come later. Desire for a thing has two levels. The first is permissible even with prophethood. The second, the major one, does not occur except from a non-prophet, because holding onto the thought of disobedience and enjoying it is itself a sin that is recorded. The saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed Allah has overlooked for my community what their souls whisper, as long as they do not speak it or act upon it," means: [what passes through] the thoughts. As for holding onto a thought, it is inconceivable that it be permissible. If it occurs, it is one of the sins, but it is not like committing the act of disobedience that the thought concerns. Something that supports the view that holding onto a thought is disobedience is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed he was eager to kill his companion," and the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, some suspicion is a sin﴾ [al-Hujurat: 12]. This is drawn from more than one place in the Law. The consensus (ijma') is established that desiring disobedience and holding onto enjoyment of it is impermissible and is not included in what is overlooked.

It has been disputed what the proof (burhan) was that Yusuf saw. It was said: he was called out. There is also disagreement about what he was called with. It was said: Jibril, peace be upon him, called to him: "O Yusuf, you will be in the register of the prophets and act like the foolish?!" It was said he was called: "O Yusuf, do not commit the disobedience, lest you be like the bird that disobeyed and whose feathers fell out so that it was left lying (on the ground)." Yaʿqub called him with this. It was said: other than this, or something of similar meaning. It was also said: the proof was a writing he saw, written on the wall of the room in which he was. It was said: between the eyes of Zulaykha. It was said: in a palm of the earth that came forth without a body. There is disagreement about what was written. It was said: the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Is He who stands over every soul in what it has earned [like any other]?﴾ [al-Ra'd: 33]. It was said: the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And do not approach unlawful sexual intercourse. Indeed, it is an immorality and an evil way﴾ [al-Isra: 32]. It was said: other than this. It was also said: the proof was that he saw Yaʿqub, peace be upon him, depicted with him in the house, biting on his thumb. It was said: on his lip. It was said: rather, the ceiling split open and he saw him thus. It was said: Jibril, peace be upon him, said to him: "If you commit the disobedience, I will erase you from the register of prophethood." It was said: Jibril struck him with his foot, and his desire came out onto his fingertips.

The author, al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is weak.

It was also said: rather, the proof was his reflection on the punishment of Allah and His threat for disobedience. It was also said: rather, the proof through which he took admonition was that Zulaykha said to him: "Stay where you are until I cover this idol" (for an idol that was with her in the house), "for I am shy before it that it should see me in this state." She got up to him and covered it with a garment. Yusuf took admonition and said: "Who will cover me from Allah, the Sustainer over everything?! If you do this for what does not understand, then I am more entitled to be shy before Allah."

In the language of the Arabs, "burhan" (proof) is a thing that gives certainty and conviction, because it is known either by necessity, or by a definitive report, or by theoretical analysis. So these things that were narrated about what Yusuf saw are proofs.

The "an" in His saying ﴿lawla an ra'a﴾ (had he not seen) is in the nominative position. The estimate is: "Had it not been his seeing the proof of his Lord." This is the "lawla" after which the predicate is omitted. Its estimate is: "he would have done it" or "he would have committed the disobedience." Some people held that the sentence was complete at His saying ﴿And she certainly desired him﴾, and that the response of "lawla" is in His saying ﴿and he would have desired her﴾, meaning: "Had he not seen the proof, he would have desired her," i.e., "he did not desire her, peace be upon him." This opinion is refuted by the language of the Arabs and the sayings of the early Muslims. Al-Zajjaj said: "Had the sentence been 'wa lahamma bi-ha lawla,' it would be remote. How much more so with the particle 'lam' dropped?"

The "ka" in His saying ﴿kadhalika﴾ (thus) is connected to an implied verb. Its estimate is: "Our acts and decrees proceeded thus, so that We might avert." It is also possible that the "ka" is in the nominative position, with the estimate: "Our protection of him is thus, so that We might avert." The majority read "linasrifa" with a nun. Al-A'mash read "liyasrifa" with a ya', as a report about an absent party.

[p. 71]

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and Abu Raja' read "al-mukhlisin" (المُخْلِصِينَ) with a kasra on the lam throughout the Qur'an. Likewise "mukhlisan" in Surat Maryam. Nafi' read "mukhlisan" likewise with a kasra on the lam. He read the rest of the Qur'an as "al-mukhlasin" (المُخَلَصِينَ) with a fatha on the lam. Hamza, al-Kisa'i and most of the reciters read "al-mukhlasin" (المُخْلَصِينَ) with a fatha on the lam, and "mukhlasan" likewise throughout the Qur'an.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they raced to the door﴾, the verse. "Wa-istabaqa" means each of them raced the other to the door. She wanted to draw him back to herself, and he wanted to flee from her. She grasped the upper part of his shirt from behind, so the shirt was torn at the collar, and the tearing went down to the bottom of the shirt. "Qadd" means cutting, and it is mostly used for what is lengthwise. "Qatt" is used for what is crosswise. This is likewise the wording in the saying of al-Nabigha:

She cuts the saluqi [...]

Ibn 'Atiyya's statement that her saying "she kindles [a fire] with the sheets" (تُوقِدُ بِالصُفّاحِ) requires that the cutting was lengthwise.

[p. 72]

The word "ألْفَيا" (alfayā) means "they found," and "والسَيِّدُ" (al-sayyid) means "the husband." This is said by Zayd ibn Thabit and Mujahid. It is related that they found al-Aziz and a man from Zulaykha's relatives at the door toward which they had raced. This is said by al-Suddi. When she saw the disgrace, she hurried to accuse Yusuf and to attack him, so she showed al-Aziz that Yusuf had wanted her. She said: ﴿What is the penalty for one who intended evil to your family, except that he be imprisoned or [suffer] a painful punishment?﴾ She spoke of the penalty as if the offence were established and certain.

This verse indicates the great weight that imprisonment carries in people's minds, especially for those of high station, since it is paired with painful punishment.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 12, verses 26–29:

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says:

﴿He said: "It was she who sought to seduce me," and a witness from her own household testified: "If his shirt is torn from the front, then she has spoken the truth and he is one of the liars. But if his shirt is torn from the back, then she has lied and he is one of the truthful."﴾ ﴿So when he saw that his shirt was torn from the back, he said: "Indeed, it is of your guile, women. Surely your guile is great."﴾ ﴿Joseph, turn away from this. And you, seek forgiveness for your sin, for you were certainly among the sinners.﴾

Nawf al-Shami said: Joseph (peace be upon him) did not clear himself, so when she accused him, he became angry and spoke the truth. He informed them that it was she who had sought to seduce him. It is related that the witness was a man, her paternal cousin, who said: "Look at the shirt. If its tear is from the back, then she has lied; if it is from the front, then she has spoken the truth." This was said by al-Suddi. Ibn 'Abbas said: he was a man from among the close associates of the king. This was said by Mujahid and others. It was also said that the witness was an infant in the cradle who spoke these words. This was also said by Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Hurayra, Ibn Jubayr, Hilal ibn Yasaf and al-Dahhak.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What weakens this view is that in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim there is: "No one spoke in the cradle except three: 'Isa ibn Maryam, the companion of Jurayj, and Ibn al-Sawda' who said of him that he would be like a wicked, tyrannical man." He said: "No one spoke," and he omitted the companion of Joseph from it. Another point is that if the infant had spoken, the proof would have been his own speech itself, rather than needing to infer from the shirt. Al-Tabari also transmitted through Ibn 'Abbas that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Four spoke in the cradle." He mentioned the three and added the companion of Joseph. Al-Tabari also mentioned from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the son of Pharaoh's hairdresser spoke in the cradle. Thus, according to this, they are five. Mujahid also said: the witness is the shirt.

(p-73) The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is weak, because the shirt cannot be described as being "from the household."

The majority of readers recited "min qubulin" and "min duburin" with a dammah on the ba' in both and with tanwin. Ibn Ya'mur, al-Jarud ibn Abi Sabra, Nuh and Ibn Abi Ishaq recited "min qubulu" and "min duburu" with three dammahs and without tanwin. Abu al-Fath said: these are two indeclinable forms (ghayatan), built like the Qur'anic verse ﴿from before and from after﴾ [al-Rum: 4]. Abu Hatim said: this is very poor in Arabic, and this form of construction occurs only in adverbs of time and place (zurūf). Al-Hasan recited "min qablin" and "min dabrin" with sukun on the ba' in both and with tanwin. It is also transmitted from Abu 'Amr. It is related from Nuh al-Qari that he made the ba' sakin in both and pronounced the final letters with a dammah without tanwin. He transmitted it from Ibn Abi Ishaq, from Yahya ibn Ya'mur.

The one who spoke these words was called a witness because his words pointed to a witness, and the witness itself is the tearing of the shirt.

One group recited: "fa-lamma ra'a qamisahu 'uththa min duburin" (when he saw his shirt, it was torn from the back). The pronoun in "ra'a" refers to the 'Aziz (the minister), and he is the one who said: ﴿Indeed, it is of your guile﴾. This was said by al-Tabari. It was also said: rather, the witness said that, and the pronoun in "innahu" refers to her earlier statement of complaint against Joseph.

Those who hold the view that judgment may be based on an indicator (amarah) among the scholars took this verse as evidence, for it is their basis. "Yusuf" in His words: ﴿Joseph, turn away from this﴾ is a vocative (munada), said Ibn 'Abbas. The witness called out to him, and he was the man who was with the 'Aziz. The meaning of ﴿turn away from this﴾ is: refrain from speaking about it, that is, conceal it and do not talk about it. Then he turned to her and said: ﴿And seek forgiveness for your sin﴾, meaning: seek forgiveness from your husband and your master. He said: ﴿for you were among the sinners﴾ and did not say "among the sinful women," because "al-khati'in" is more general. It derives from khati'a yakhta'u khat'an and khata'an. From this is the statement of the poet:

"By your life, my error and my correctness are upon me, and I have destroyed my wealth."

And he recites the verse of Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt:

"Your servants err, and You are the Lord, with Your two hands are the deaths and the destinies."

﴿He said: "It was she who sought to seduce me," and a witness from her own household testified: "If his shirt is torn from the front, then she has spoken the truth and he is one of the liars. But if his shirt is torn from the back, then she has lied and he is one of the truthful."﴾ ﴿So when he saw that his shirt was torn from the back, he said: "Indeed, it is of your guile, women. Surely your guile is great."﴾ ﴿Joseph, turn away from this. And you, seek forgiveness for your sin, for you were certainly among the sinners.﴾

Nawf al-Shami said: Joseph (peace be upon him) did not clear himself, so when she accused him, he became angry and spoke the truth. He informed them that it was she who had sought to seduce him. It is related that the witness was a man, her paternal cousin, who said: "Look at the shirt. If its tear is from the back, then she has lied; if it is from the front, then she has spoken the truth." This was said by al-Suddi. Ibn 'Abbas said: he was a man from among the close associates of the king. This was said by Mujahid and others. What weakens this view is that in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim there is: "No one spoke in the cradle except three: 'Isa ibn Maryam, the companion of Jurayj, and Ibn al-Sawda' who said of him that he would be like a wicked, tyrannical man."
