Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 12, verse 30–31:

His saying, exalted is He:

﴿And women in the city said, "The wife of the al-'Aziz is seeking to seduce her servant boy from himself; he has captivated her with love. Indeed, we see her in clear error."﴾ ﴿So when she heard of their scheming, she sent to them and prepared for them a banquet (muttaka'), and gave each one of them a knife, and said, "Come out before them." And when they saw him, they were struck with awe of him and cut their hands and said, "Glory to Allah! This is not a human; this is none but a noble angel."﴾

He mentioned the verb attributed to the women to take into account the collective noun. "Al-niswa" (the women) is a plural of paucity (jam' qilla), which has no singular from its own form, while the plural of abundance is "nisa'". "Niswa" is on the pattern fi'la, which is one of the four patterns that are used for the lowest number (adna al-'adad). A poet has versified them in a line of verse:

"With af'al, af'al, af'ila, and fi'la, the lowest of numbers is known."

It is related that these women were four: the wife of the king's baker, the wife of his cupbearer, the wife of his chamberlain, and the wife of his doorkeeper.

"Al-'Aziz" means the king, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"A pearl which a merchant dove for... was brought to an 'Aziz on the day of Tull."

"Al-fata" (the youth) means the boy; its usual usage is for a slave, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "None of you should say 'my slave' or 'my slave-girl'; let him say 'my young man' (fataya) and 'my young woman' (fatati)." However, it may also be said of someone other than a slave, as in: ﴿And when Musa said to his young man﴾ [al-Kahf: 60]. The original meaning of fata in the language is the young man, but since most servants were young, the name fata was borrowed for them. "Shaghafaha" means: it reached until it was at the place of the shaghaf in her heart. According to most opinions, the shaghaf is a membrane enclosing the heart; it was also said: the shaghaf is the black core of the heart; and it was said: the shaghaf is a disease that reaches the heart.

Abu Raja', al-A'raj, 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, al-Hasan (in one report), Yahya ibn Ya'mar, Qatada (in one report), Thabit, 'Awf, Mujahid and others read "qad sha'afaha" with an unpointed 'ayn. For this there are two meanings: first, that it rose with her to every degree of love and took her every way; so it is derived, on this view, from sha'af al-jibal, which are their peaks and summits. From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "It will soon be that the best property of a Muslim will be sheep which he takes to the peaks of the mountains and the places of rainfall, fleeing with his religion from the trials." The second meaning is that the sha'af is a pleasure with burning pain, which is found in wounds, mange and the like; from it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"Will he kill me, when I have made her heart burn (sha'aftu fu'adaha), as the man with the mange-stricken camel burns (sha'afa) the mahnu'a (the one smeared with tar)?"

In the language, mash'uf is one whose heart love has burnt; from it is the saying of al-A'sha:

"She disobeys the slanderers, though love at times makes what it adorns for the one burnt by it (mash'uf) look worse."

It is related from Thabit al-Bunani and Abu Raja' that they read "qad sha'iafaha" with a kasra on the 'ayn, unpointed. Abu Hatim said: the known reading is with a fatha on the 'ayn, and this has also been read. Ibn Muhaysin read "qad shshaghafaha," assimilating the dal into the shin.

It is related that the speech of these women was only meant as a ruse against the wife of the al-'Aziz, so as to anger her until she would show them Yusuf, so that their excuse would be evident or her blame would be justified. Ibn Zayd said: shaghaf is used for love and for hatred. Al-Sha'bi said: shaghaf and mashghuf with a ghayn dotted are used for love, while sha'af is madness and mash'uf is the madman. These two statements are weak.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when she heard of their scheming﴾ and the verse. Their speech was called scheming only because they showed denunciation of something reprehensible while intending to stir up her anger against them. It was also said: their scheming was that they divulged that matter to others, though she had informed them of it and made them keep it secret. This would not be scheming unless they showed her the opposite of that and intended harm to her by the divulging.

The meaning of "she sent to them" is: so that they would come. "And prepared" means: she readied and arranged. "Muttaka'": that on which one reclines, of couches and cushions; by this is expressed a gathering prepared for honour. It is known that this kind of honour does not lack food and drink, so Mujahid and 'Ikrima explained muttaka' as food. Ibn 'Abbas said: "muttaka'" means a gathering; this was mentioned by al-Zahrawi. Al-Qutabi said: it is said, "We reclined (ittaka'na) at So-and-so's," meaning, we ate.

His saying: ﴿and gave each one of them a knife﴾ implies that among the food there was something that is cut with knives. It was said: it was meat, and they did not tear meat but ate it by slicing it with knives. It was said: it was citron. It was said: it was zumaward (a kind of citron-like fruit found in those lands). It was said: it was made of sugar, almonds and mixtures. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Jahdari, Ibn 'Umar, Qatada, al-Dahhak, al-Kalbi and Aban ibn Taghlib read "mutkan" with a damma on the mim, sukun on the ta', and tanwin on the kaf. Its meaning was disputed: it was said it is citron; it was said it is a term that covers whatever is cut with a knife among fruits, such as citron, apple and others. Al-Tabari recited:

"We drink sin openly from the cups, and we see the mutk among us as a loan."

The majority read "muttaka'an" with a shadda on the ta' fatha, a hamza and a short vowel. Al-Zuhri read "muttakan" with a shadda on the ta' without hamza; this is the reading of Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' and Shayba ibn Nassah. al-Hasan read "muttaka'an" with a long vowel, by full pronunciation of the vowel. The sikkin (knife) is masculine and feminine, as said by al-Kisa'i and al-Farra'; al-Asma'i knew only the masculine.

His saying: "Come out" is a command to Yusuf, and he obeyed her according to the authority (of the king). Makki and al-Mahdawi said: it was said that in the verse there is a transposition in the narrative: the story of the women was before her exposure, in the shirt, to the master, and when the matter became known to the master, what was between her and Yusuf was cut off.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is possible, but it is not necessitated by the words of the verse. Rather, it is possible that the story of the women came after the story of the shirt, because the al-'Aziz had little jealousy, and so did all his people. Do you not see that the denunciation at the time of the shirt was only: ﴿Indeed it is of your scheming; surely your scheming is great﴾ [Yusuf: 28]? This indicates little jealousy. Then the matter calmed down with: ﴿Yusuf, turn away from this﴾ [Yusuf: 29] and "you, ask forgiveness (istaghfiri)." She at that time had remained only in her denial and showing of innocence, so she was therefore overlooked afterward, because the evidence of the shirt was not conclusive; it was only a sign of some kind, unless the speaker was a child.

His saying: "akbarnahu" means: they magnified him and were awed by his beauty. This is the statement of the majority. 'Abd al-Samad ibn 'Ali al-Hashimi said, from his father, from his grandfather: its meaning is "they menstruated" (hadna). Some people cited as evidence for this interpretation:

"He comes to women in their times of purity, and does not come to women when they menstruate with a great menstruation."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a weak statement, its meaning is unfamiliar, and the line is fabricated and invented; so said al-Tabari and other verifiers, and 'Abd al-Samad is not among the transmitters of knowledge, may Allah have mercy on him.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and cut their hands﴾ means: they made many cuts in them with the slicing of the knives. 'Ikrima said: "the hands" here means the sleeves. Mujahid said: it means the limbs, and they cut them until they threw them away.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The apparent meaning of this is that the hands were severed, and this is weak in its meaning, because cutting through bone happens only with force, and it is impossible that anyone would be unaware of it; and cutting at the joint cannot be done without gentleness that must be intended. What seems likely is that they put their hands onto the bread-like load they were carrying before the banquet, and this was a slicing; this is the statement of the community. The "t" in "qatta'na" is doubled because of their great number and the great amount of slicing; perhaps it was repeated many times.

Abu 'Amr alone read "hasha lillah," Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud read "hasha Allah," the rest of the Seven read "hasha lillah," and a group read "hashа lillah" (hashā, a dialectal form); al-Hasan read "hāsh lillah" with a sukun on the shin, which is weak, and al-Hasan also read "hasha al-Ilah" with the alif of "hasha" omitted. As for "hasha," when it governs in the genitive it is a particle meaning exception, so said Sibawayh, and it may govern the accusative; you say, "hasha Zaydin" and "hasha Zaydan." Al-Mubarrad said: the accusative is preferable, since it is established that it is a verb, by their saying "hasha li-Zayd," and a particle is not elided from.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It appears from the collected statements of Sibawayh and al-Mubarrad that the particle governs only in the genitive, and that the verb is what governs the accusative. So this word is used as both verb and particle. In some places it is a verb on the pattern fā'il, and this is in the reading of whoever reads "hāshā lillah"; its meaning is taken from the meaning of the particle, which is removing a thing from a meaning attached to it. This verb is derived from "al-hashā" (the side), meaning: this is in one side and that is in another side. From this is the saying of the poet:

"Whoever walks to the protected area, his family says: on which side has the separated companion gone?"

From it is "al-hashiya" (margin), as if it is separated from everything it belongs to. Among the places where "hasha" is a verb is this verse; this is indicated by its entry upon the genitive particle, and particles do not enter upon one another; and this is indicated by the deletion of the yā' from it in the reading of the rest: "hasha," in the manner of their deletion from "lā ubāli," "lā adri," and "law tara." Deletion from particles is not permitted except when there is doubling in them, like "la'alla," where one deletes and "'alla" remains. This condition is challenged by "mundhu" and "mudh," for it has been deleted without doubling; so reflect on it.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

From this is the hadith of Khalid on the day of Mu'ta: "fa-hasha bil-nas" (he removed the people from it). So the meaning of "hasha lillah" here: Yusuf is removed from such, because of his obedience to Allah, or because of his station with Allah, or because of Allah's elevation of him, that he should be accused of what you accuse him of or be invited to its like; for those are the actions of humans, and he is not one of them; rather he is an angel. This is how Abu 'Ali al-Farisi arranged the meaning of this statement according to these two readings among the Seven. As for the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Ibn Mas'ud, it is on the basis that "hasha" is a particle of exception, as the poet said:

"Except Abi Thawban, for in him is a restraint from abuse and insult."

The sukun on the shin in one of al-Hasan's readings is weak, for it joins two sukuns; and his second reading lacks the alif of "hasha."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The comparison with an angel is of the category of comparison with the greatly esteemed, even if they are not seen. Abu al-Huwayrith al-Hanafi and al-Hasan read: "ma hadha basharan in hadha illa malakun karim," with a kasra on the lam of "malakin." On this reading the speech is eloquent: when they magnified the beauty of his form, they said: it is not fitting that this be a human slave; it is only fitting that he be a noble king. The accusative of "basharan" is in the dialect of the Hijaz, where "ma" is made like "laysa"; but the Tamim raise it, and it was not read in that way.

It is related that Yusuf, peace be upon him, was given a third of beauty, and from the Prophet ﷺ: he was given half of beauty. In some chains it is he and his mother, and in others he and Sarah, the grandmother of his father.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is by way of illustration: that is, if beauty were divisible, Yusuf's beauty would fall into half of it. The purpose is that the greatness of his beauty should settle in the listener's mind, in the manner of the comparison with the heads of devils and the fangs of ghouls.

Then the matter calmed down with: ﴿Yusuf, turn away from this﴾ [Yusuf: 29] and "you, ask forgiveness (istaghfiri)." She at that time had remained only in her denial and showing of innocence, so she was therefore overlooked afterward, because the evidence of the shirt was not conclusive; it was only a sign of some kind, unless the speaker was a child.

His saying: "akbarnahu" means: they magnified him and were awed by his beauty. This is the statement of the majority. 'Abd al-Samad ibn 'Ali al-Hashimi said, from his father, from his grandfather: its meaning is "they menstruated" (hadna). Some people cited as evidence for this interpretation:

"He comes to women in their times of purity, and does not come to women when they menstruate with a great menstruation."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a weak statement, its meaning is unfamiliar, and the line is fabricated and invented; so said al-Tabari and other verifiers, and 'Abd al-Samad is not among the transmitters of knowledge, may Allah have mercy on him.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and cut their hands﴾ means: they made many cuts in them with the slicing of the knives. 'Ikrima said: "the hands" here means the sleeves. Mujahid said: it means the limbs, and they cut them until they threw them away.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The apparent meaning of this is that the hands were severed, and this is weak in its meaning, because cutting through bone happens only with force, and it is impossible that anyone would be unaware of it; and cutting at the joint cannot be done without gentleness that must be intended. What seems likely is that they put their hands onto the bread-like load they were carrying before the banquet, and this was a slicing; this is the statement of the community. The "t" in "qatta'na" is doubled because of their great number and the great amount of slicing; perhaps it was repeated many times.

Abu 'Amr alone read "hasha lillah," Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud read "hasha Allah," the rest of the Seven read "hasha lillah," and a group read "hashа lillah" (hashā, a dialectal form); al-Hasan read "hāsh lillah" with a sukun on the shin, which is weak, and al-Hasan also read "hasha al-Ilah" with the alif of "hasha" omitted. As for "hasha," when it governs in the genitive it is a particle meaning exception, so said Sibawayh, and it may govern the accusative; you say, "hasha Zaydin" and "hasha Zaydan." Al-Mubarrad said: the accusative is preferable, since it is established that it is a verb, by their saying "hasha li-Zayd," and a particle is not elided from.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It appears from the collected statements of Sibawayh and al-Mubarrad that the particle governs only in the genitive, and that the verb is what governs the accusative. So this word is used as both verb and particle. In some places it is a verb on the pattern fā'il, and this is in the reading of whoever reads "hāshā lillah"; its meaning is taken from the meaning of the particle, which is removing a thing from a meaning attached to it. This verb is derived from "al-hashā" (the side), meaning: this is in one side and that is in another side. From this is the saying of the poet:

"Whoever walks to the protected area, his family says: on which side has the separated companion gone?"

From it is "al-hashiya" (margin), as if it is separated from everything it belongs to. Among the places where "hasha" is a verb is this verse; this is indicated by its entry upon the genitive particle, and particles do not enter upon one another; and this is indicated by the deletion of the yā' from it in the reading of the rest: "hasha," in the manner of their deletion from "lā ubāli," "lā adri," and "law tara." Deletion from particles is not permitted except when there is doubling in them, like "la'alla," where one deletes and "'alla" remains. This condition is challenged by "mundhu" and "mudh," for it has been deleted without doubling; so reflect on it.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

From this is the hadith of Khalid on the day of Mu'ta: "fa-hasha bil-nas" (he removed the people from it). So the meaning of "hasha lillah" here: Yusuf is removed from such, because of his obedience to Allah, or because of his station with Allah, or because of Allah's elevation of him, that he should be accused of what you accuse him of or be invited to its like; for those are the actions of humans, and he is not one of them; rather he is an angel. This is how Abu 'Ali al-Farisi arranged the meaning of this statement according to these two readings among the Seven. As for the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Ibn Mas'ud, it is on the basis that "hasha" is a particle of exception, as the poet said:

"Except Abi Thawban, for in him is a restraint from abuse and insult."

The sukun on the shin in one of al-Hasan's readings is weak, for it joins two sukuns; and his second reading lacks the alif of "hasha."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The comparison with an angel is of the category of comparison with the greatly esteemed, even if they are not seen. Abu al-Huwayrith al-Hanafi and al-Hasan read: "ma hadha basharan in hadha illa malakun karim," with a kasra on the lam of "malakin." On this reading the speech is eloquent: when they magnified the beauty of his form, they said: it is not fitting that this be a human slave; it is only fitting that he be a noble king. The accusative of "basharan" is in the dialect of the Hijaz, where "ma" is made like "laysa"; but the Tamim raise it, and it was not read in that way.

It is related that Yusuf, peace be upon him, was given a third of beauty, and from the Prophet ﷺ: he was given half of beauty. In some chains it is he and his mother, and in others he and Sarah, the grandmother of his father.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is by way of illustration: that is, if beauty were divisible, Yusuf's beauty would fall into half of it. The purpose is that the greatness of his beauty should settle in the listener's mind, in the manner of the comparison with the heads of devils and the fangs of ghouls.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 12, verses 32–34:

His Exalted and Majestic Lord said:

﴿She said: "That is the one you blamed me for. I did indeed seek to seduce him, but he held himself chaste. And if he does not do what I command him, he will surely be imprisoned, and he will be among the humiliated."﴾ ﴿He said: "My Lord, prison is dearer to me than what they invite me to. And unless You turn their plot away from me, I shall incline towards them and be among the ignorant."﴾ ﴿So his Lord answered him and turned away from him their plot. Indeed He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾

Al-Tabari said: The meaning is: "This is the one you blamed me for," that is, the one because of whom you cut your hands is the one who made me lost in my passion for him. The pronoun in "fihi" ("for him") refers to Yusuf. It is also permissible that the reference is to the love of Yusuf, with the pronoun referring to that love, so that "dhalika" is a pointing to an absent thing in its usual use.

Then the wife of the Aziz admitted to the women that she had sought to seduce him, and she sought their protection in this matter, since she knew that they had excused her. "Fa-istaʿsama" means: he sought chastity, held fast to it, and refused her. Then (p. 83) she began to threaten him, while he was listening, with her words: ﴿And if he does not do it﴾, to the end of the verse.

The lam in her saying "la-yusjananna" is the lam of oath, and the first lam is the one that announces the coming of the oath. The nun is the heavy (emphatic) nun, and pausing on it is done with its doubling. In "la-yakūnan," its nun is the light nun (nun al-khafifa, the lightened energetic nun), and pausing on it is done with an alif. It is like His saying, blessed and exalted: "la-nasfaʿan" (We will certainly seize). Similar to it is the saying of al-A'sha:

Pray at the times of evening and forenoon, and do not worship Satan, but worship God.

He intended "fa-ʿbudan" (worship, with the energetic nun), with the alif in place of the nun at the pause. A group recited "wa-la-yakūnunna" with the heavy nun. "Al-sāghirūn" means the humbled, those upon whom abasement has come.

As for His saying, exalted be He: ﴿He said: "My Lord, prison is dearer to me"﴾. It is narrated that when the wife of the Aziz threatened him, the women said to him: "Obey your mistress and do what she commands you." Therefore he said: ﴿than what they invite me to﴾. Al-Hasan said something similar. The form of "yad'ūnanī" (they invite me) in this verse is "yafʿulna," unlike your saying "al-rijāl yadʿūna" (the men invite).

Al-Jumhur recited "al-sijn" with a kasra on the sin, and it is the noun. Al-Zuhri, Ibn Hurmuz, Ya'qub and Ibn Abi Ishaq recited "al-sajn" with a fatha on the sin, and this is the recitation of ʿUthman, may Allah be pleased with him, and of his client Tariq. It is the verbal noun, like your saying "al-jidʿ" and "al-jadʿ" (both meaning cutting/slitting).

As for His saying: ﴿And unless You turn away from me...﴾ to the end of the verse, it is submission to Allah, blessed and exalted, a longing towards Him, and reliance upon Him. The meaning is: "And if You do not save me, I am ruined." This is what the context of his speech and his situation require. The pronoun in "ilayhi" (towards it) refers to the indecency intended by "mā" in His saying "mimmā" (than what).

"Asbu" is derived from "al-sabwa," which is the acts of youth. From this is the saying of the poet, which al-Tabari recited:

My heart inclined to Hind, and Hind is one who causes inclination.

From this is the saying of Durayd ibn al-Simma:

He inclined until grey hair overtook his head, and when it overtook him he said to falsehood: "Be gone."

"Al-jāhilūn" (the ignorant) are those who do not observe the limits of Allah, the Exalted, and His prohibitions.

As for His saying, exalted be He: ﴿So his Lord answered him﴾, the verse. The saying of Yusuf, peace be upon him: ﴿My Lord, prison...﴾ up to His saying ﴿among the ignorant﴾ is speech that contains a complaint to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, about his situation with them, and a supplication to Him to remove his trial. Therefore, after the saying of Yusuf, He said: ﴿So his Lord answered him﴾, that is, He responded to him according to his wish, and turned away from him their plot, in that He placed between him and disobedience. His saying ﴿All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾ are two attributes fitting the phrase "fa-istajāba" (so He answered).

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 12, verse 35–36:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿Then it occurred to them, after they had seen the signs, that they should imprison him for a time.﴾ ﴿And there entered the prison with him two young men. One of them said: "Indeed, I see myself pressing wine." And the other said: "Indeed, I see myself carrying bread upon my head, of which the birds eat. Inform us of its interpretation. Indeed, we see you to be among the good-doers."﴾

When Yusuf refused the sin and the wife of al-'Aziz despaired of him, she pressed him by saying to her husband: "Indeed, this Hebrew youth has disgraced me among the people. He makes excuses to them and describes the matter according to his own choice, while I am confined and kept hidden. So either you permit me, and I go out to the people and make excuse (p-85) and deny his claim, or you imprison him just as I am confined." Then it occurred to them to imprison him. Ibn 'Abbas said: So he ordered that he be mounted on a donkey, the drum was beaten, and it was proclaimed in the markets of Egypt: "This Yusuf the Hebrew wanted to seduce his mistress, so this is his reward: that he be imprisoned." Abu Salih said: Ibn 'Abbas did not narrate this report except that he wept.

"Bada" means "appeared," and its subject (fa'il) is omitted, its estimated form being "a manifestation" (badw) or "an opinion" (ra'y). The pronoun in "lahum" is plural because the matter involved consultation, though the one who imprisons is the king alone. "Layasjununnahu" is a clause introduced by the lam of oath, and the subject of "bada" cannot be "layasjununnahu," because the subject is never a clause in any way; this is the clear position of Sibawayh. It was said that the subject is "layasjununnahu," but this is an error; rather, it is an explanation of the subject.

Regarding "al-ayat" (the signs), the scholars of tafsir mentioned that they were the tearing of the shirt (said by Mujahid and others), the scratching of the face that accompanied the tearing of the shirt (said by Ikrima), and the women cutting their hands (said by al-Suddi).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The purpose of the statement is only that they saw his imprisonment after the appearance of the signs that cleared him of the accusation. Thus it shows their injustice towards him. The scratching of the face and the women cutting their hands do not clear Yusuf, and clearing is conceivable only in the report of the shirt. If the speaker was a child, as has been related, then it is a great sign; and if he was a man, then it is a sign containing some inference. It is customary that "sign" is used only for what is extremely clear in its manifestation, though (the signs) may also be applied to "clear proofs" of whatever degree of clarity occurs. It is possible that the meaning of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿after they had seen the signs﴾ is: after there had become apparent to them, from the aspects of the matter and its indications, that Yusuf was innocent. Thus He did not intend to specify a single sign, but rather the indications of the whole story.

"Hin" (a period of time) in the speech of the Arabs and in this verse means a span of time not limited, applying to a little or much, and this is among its occurrences in the Qur'an. Ikrima said: "Hin" here is meant to be seven years. It was also said: rather, it is meant to be one year.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is according to what the Unseen revealed about Yusuf's imprisonment. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, heard a man reading "'attā ḥīn" with the letter ʿayn (ʿ), which is the dialect of Hudhayl, and said to him: "Who taught you?" He said: "Ibn Mas'ud." So 'Umar wrote to Ibn Mas'ud: "Indeed Allah revealed the Qur'an in clear Arabic in the dialect of Quraysh, so teach people in it, and do not teach them in the dialect of Hudhayl." It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Yusuf, peace be upon him, stumbled three stumbles: he intended (the sin) and was imprisoned; he said, 'Mention me to your lord,' so Satan made him forget the remembrance of his lord, and his imprisonment was prolonged; and he said, 'Indeed you are thieves,' so it was answered: 'If he steals, indeed a brother of his stole before.'"

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And there entered the prison with him two young men.﴾ The meaning: they imprisoned him, and there entered the prison with him two young men who were also imprisoned. This "ma'a" (with) may mean that they entered at the same time, or it may mean that they entered separately, one by one. It is related that they were both servants of the greatest king, al-Walid ibn al-Rayyan: one of them was his baker, and the other his cupbearer.

"Fata" means a young man, and the word may be applied to a slave and to a free servant; it is possible that both of these possessed all of that. The word is of the ya' type (its root has ya'), and their saying "al-futuwwa" (chivalry) is anomalous. It is related that the king accused them, saying that the baker among them had intended to poison him, and the cupbearer agreed with him on that, so he imprisoned them; this was said by al-Suddi. When Yusuf entered the prison, he won the people over by his good speech, his excellence, and his nobility; he would console their grieving, visit their sick, ask on behalf of their poor, and urge them toward good. The two young men loved him and kept close to him, and the keeper of the prison and the one in charge of it loved him too, and said to him: "Be in whichever of the houses you wish." Yusuf said to him: "Do not love me, may Allah have mercy on you, for love has brought me harms: my aunt loved me and I was tested for her love; my father loved me and I was tested for his love for me; and the wife of al-'Aziz loved me and I was tested for her love, as you see." Yusuf, peace be upon him, had said to the people of the prison: "Indeed, I interpret dreams, and I excel at it." It is related from Ibn Mas'ud that the two young men put these two dreams forward in order to test him. It is related from Mujahid that they saw these things in reality and wished to ask him. One of them, whose name (according to what was related) was (Nabu), said: "Indeed, I saw a vine with three fine branches, with fine clusters of grapes upon it; I was pressing them and giving the king to drink." The other, whose name was (Mujlith), said: "I used to see myself coming out of the king's kitchen with three baskets on my head containing bread, and the birds were eating from its top."

As for His saying: ﴿I see myself pressing wine﴾: it was said that he called grapes "wine" by its eventual outcome. It was also said that this is the dialect of the Azd of Oman, who call grapes "khamr." Al-Asma'i said: Al-Mu'tamir related to me, saying: "I met a Bedouin carrying grapes in a container, and I said: 'What are you carrying?' He said: 'Khamr,' meaning grapes." In the recitation of Ubayy ibn Ka'b and 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud it is "Indeed I see myself pressing grapes" (ʿinaban). It is also possible that describing the wine as "pressed" is meant, since pressing is for it and because of it.

As for His saying "khubzan" (bread): it is related that he saw a thareed (bread soaked in broth) upon his head. In the Mushaf of Ibn Mas'ud it reads: "upon my head thareedan of which the birds eat."

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed we see you to be among the good-doers﴾: the majority said they meant: in knowledge. Al-Dahhak and Qatada said the meaning is: among the good-doers in his companionship with the people of the prison and in his kindness toward them. It was also said that they meant to inform him that they saw in him a benefit toward them and a favor, so that if he interpreted for them what they had seen, (he would be doing good). Ibn Ishaq inclined to this view.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 12, verse 35–36:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿Then it occurred to them, after they had seen the signs, that they should imprison him for a time.﴾ ﴿And there entered the prison with him two young men. One of them said: "Indeed, I see myself pressing wine." And the other said: "Indeed, I see myself carrying bread upon my head, of which the birds eat. Inform us of its interpretation. Indeed, we see you to be among the good-doers."﴾

When Yusuf refused the sin and the wife of al-'Aziz despaired of him, she pressed him by saying to her husband: "Indeed, this Hebrew youth has disgraced me among the people. He makes excuses to them and describes the matter according to his own choice, while I am confined and kept hidden. So either you permit me, and I go out to the people and make excuse (p-85) and deny his claim, or you imprison him just as I am confined." Then it occurred to them to imprison him. Ibn 'Abbas said: So he ordered that he be mounted on a donkey, the drum was beaten, and it was proclaimed in the markets of Egypt: "This Yusuf the Hebrew wanted to seduce his mistress, so this is his reward: that he be imprisoned." Abu Salih said: Ibn 'Abbas did not narrate this report except that he wept.

"Bada" means "appeared," and its subject (fa'il) is omitted, its estimated form being "a manifestation" (badw) or "an opinion" (ra'y). The pronoun in "lahum" is plural because the matter involved consultation, though the one who imprisons is the king alone. "Layasjununnahu" is a clause introduced by the lam of oath, and the subject of "bada" cannot be "layasjununnahu," because the subject is never a clause in any way; this is the clear position of Sibawayh. It was said that the subject is "layasjununnahu," but this is an error; rather, it is an explanation of the subject.

Regarding "al-ayat" (the signs), the scholars of tafsir mentioned that they were the tearing of the shirt (said by Mujahid and others), the scratching of the face that accompanied the tearing of the shirt (said by Ikrima), and the women cutting their hands (said by al-Suddi).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The purpose of the statement is only that they saw his imprisonment after the appearance of the signs that cleared him of the accusation. Thus it shows their injustice towards him. The scratching of the face and the women cutting their hands do not clear Yusuf, and clearing is conceivable only in the report of the shirt. If the speaker was a child, as has been related, then it is a great sign; and if he was a man, then it is a sign containing some inference. It is customary that "sign" is used only for what is extremely clear in its manifestation, though (the signs) may also be applied to "clear proofs" of whatever degree of clarity occurs. It is possible that the meaning of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿after they had seen the signs﴾ is: after there had become apparent to them, from the aspects of the matter and its indications, that Yusuf was innocent. Thus He did not intend to specify a single sign, but rather the indications of the whole story.

"Hin" (a period of time) in the speech of the Arabs and in this verse means a span of time not limited, applying to a little or much, and this is among its occurrences in the Qur'an. Ikrima said: "Hin" here is meant to be seven years. It was also said: rather, it is meant to be one year.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is according to what the Unseen revealed about Yusuf's imprisonment. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, heard a man reading "'attā ḥīn" with the letter ʿayn (ʿ), which is the dialect of Hudhayl, and said to him: "Who taught you?" He said: "Ibn Mas'ud." So 'Umar wrote to Ibn Mas'ud: "Indeed Allah revealed the Qur'an in clear Arabic in the dialect of Quraysh, so teach people in it, and do not teach them in the dialect of Hudhayl." It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Yusuf, peace be upon him, stumbled three stumbles: he intended (the sin) and was imprisoned; he said, 'Mention me to your lord,' so Satan made him forget the remembrance of his lord, and his imprisonment was prolonged; and he said, 'Indeed you are thieves,' so it was answered: 'If he steals, indeed a brother of his stole before.'"

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And there entered the prison with him two young men.﴾ The meaning: they imprisoned him, and there entered the prison with him two young men who were also imprisoned. This "ma'a" (with) may mean that they entered at the same time, or it may mean that they entered separately, one by one. It is related that they were both servants of the greatest king, al-Walid ibn al-Rayyan: one of them was his baker, and the other his cupbearer.

"Fata" means a young man, and the word may be applied to a slave and to a free servant; it is possible that both of these possessed all of that. The word is of the ya' type (its root has ya'), and their saying "al-futuwwa" (chivalry) is anomalous. It is related that the king accused them, saying that the baker among them had intended to poison him, and the cupbearer agreed with him on that, so he imprisoned them; this was said by al-Suddi. When Yusuf entered the prison, he won the people over by his good speech, his excellence, and his nobility; he would console their grieving, visit their sick, ask on behalf of their poor, and urge them toward good. The two young men loved him and kept close to him, and the keeper of the prison and the one in charge of it loved him too, and said to him: "Be in whichever of the houses you wish." Yusuf said to him: "Do not love me, may Allah have mercy on you, for love has brought me harms: my aunt loved me and I was tested for her love; my father loved me and I was tested for his love for me; and the wife of al-'Aziz loved me and I was tested for her love, as you see." Yusuf, peace be upon him, had said to the people of the prison: "Indeed, I interpret dreams, and I excel at it." It is related from Ibn Mas'ud that the two young men put these two dreams forward in order to test him. It is related from Mujahid that they saw these things in reality and wished to ask him. One of them, whose name (according to what was related) was (Nabu), said: "Indeed, I saw a vine with three fine branches, with fine clusters of grapes upon it; I was pressing them and giving the king to drink." The other, whose name was (Mujlith), said: "I used to see myself coming out of the king's kitchen with three baskets on my head containing bread, and the birds were eating from its top."

As for His saying: ﴿I see myself pressing wine﴾: it was said that he called grapes "wine" by its eventual outcome. It was also said that this is the dialect of the Azd of Oman, who call grapes "khamr." Al-Asma'i said: Al-Mu'tamir related to me, saying: "I met a Bedouin carrying grapes in a container, and I said: 'What are you carrying?' He said: 'Khamr,' meaning grapes." In the recitation of Ubayy ibn Ka'b and 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud it is "Indeed I see myself pressing grapes" (ʿinaban). It is also possible that describing the wine as "pressed" is meant, since pressing is for it and because of it.

As for His saying "khubzan" (bread): it is related that he saw a thareed (bread soaked in broth) upon his head. In the Mushaf of Ibn Mas'ud it reads: "upon my head thareedan of which the birds eat."

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed we see you to be among the good-doers﴾: the majority said they meant: in knowledge. Al-Dahhak and Qatada said the meaning is: among the good-doers in his companionship with the people of the prison and in his kindness toward them. It was also said that they meant to inform him that they saw in him a benefit toward them and a favor, so that if he interpreted for them what they had seen, (he would be doing good). Ibn Ishaq inclined to this view.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 12, verses 37–38:

His the Mighty and Majestic's saying:

﴿He said: "No food will come to you as your provision but I will inform you of its interpretation before it comes to you. That is part of what my Lord has taught me. Indeed, I have left the religion of a people who do not believe in Allah and who are, in the Hereafter, disbelievers.﴾ ﴿And I follow the religion of my fathers: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. It was not for us to associate anything with Allah. That is from the bounty of Allah upon us and upon the people, but most of the people do not give thanks.﴾

It is narrated from al-Suddi and Ibn Ishaq that when Yusuf (peace be upon him) knew the severity of the interpretation of the dream of the one who saw the bread, and that it indicated his execution, he turned to other talk, perhaps they would not demand the interpretation from him. So he said to them, informing them of the greatness of his knowledge of interpretation: "No food will come to you in your sleep, which you think you are being provided with, but I will inform you of the interpretation of that food, that is, of what its matter will lead to while awake, before that interpretation which I inform you of becomes manifest." It is narrated that they said: "From where do you have what you claim of knowledge, while you are neither a soothsayer nor an astrologer?" So he said to them: ﴿That is part of what my Lord has taught me.﴾ Then he rose, calling them away from disbelief and beautifying belief in Allah for them. It is narrated that he intended by this two aspects: the first: making them forget the matter of the interpretation of what they had asked about, since in that there was a warning of the execution of one of them; and the second: hope for their faith, so that the one who would be executed would take his share of faith and his Hereafter would be safe for him. Ibn Jurayj said: Yusuf (peace be upon him) meant: No food will come to you while awake, which you are provided with, but I will inform you of it with knowledge, and of what your affair will lead to, before that outcome comes to you.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

According to this, he only informed them that he knows unseen matters that have no connection to the dream, and he intended by that one of the two aspects mentioned earlier. This is in accordance with what is narrated, that he was given prophetic knowledge in the prison, so his informing was like the informing of 'Isa (peace be upon him). Ibn Jurayj said: It was the custom of that king that when he wanted to execute someone from among those in his prison, he would send to him food, making it a sign of his execution.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

All of this is not required by the wording, nor does the chain of narration support it.

His saying "I have left" (tarakt), although he had not engaged in it, is permissible and correct. That is because he expressed his avoidance of it from the beginning with the word "leaving," and he brought the word "leaving" to attract them, perhaps they would be led to true leaving, which comes after taking up a matter. The people whose religion he left were: the king and his followers. He repeated his saying "and they" for emphasis, and that was good because of the separation between them.

His saying "And I follow" and the verse: it is a continuation by Yusuf (peace be upon him) in calling them to the upright religion, and a departure from confronting what his dream required. Al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli and Abu 'Amr read "ʾābāʾiyy" with sukun on the ya', and the majority read "ābāʾiya" with an open ya'. Abu Hatim said: "Both are good, so recite as you wish. As for dropping the hamza, it is not permitted, but easing it is good, so it becomes a kasra ya' after a sakin or open ya'."

His saying "That" refers to their religion and their law, and that this is clearly a favour upon them, since Allah the Exalted singled them out with it and made them prophets. And that it is a favour upon the people is because through it they are called to the religion and driven to salvation from the punishment of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. "Min shay'" is the superfluous "min" that emphasizes negation, which occurs with negation. His saying "they do not give thanks" means the complete thanks in which faith is found.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah Yusuf, verses 39–42**

The Almighty said:

﴿O my two fellow prisoners! Are scattered lords better, or Allah, the One, the Subduer?﴾ ﴿You worship besides Him only names that you and your fathers have named, for which Allah has sent down no authority. Judgment belongs only to Allah. He has commanded that you worship none but Him. That is the upright religion, but most people do not know.﴾ ﴿O my two fellow prisoners! As for one of you, he will pour wine for his lord. As for the other, he will be crucified, and birds will eat from his head. The matter about which you inquire has been decided.﴾ ﴿And he said to the one he thought would be saved of the two, "Mention me to your lord." But Satan made him forget to mention him to his lord, so he remained in prison for several years.﴾

His addressing them as ﴿O my two fellow prisoners!﴾ is either because their relationship to the prison is that of companions, by virtue of their dwelling in it, as the Exalted said, "companions of the Garden" and "companions of the Blaze," and similar expressions. Or he meant their companionship with him in the prison, and so he attributed them to the prison on that basis, as if he had said, "my two companions in the prison." This is like what is said about the disbelievers: that the idols are "their partners."

He presented his argument to them by addressing the long-standing matter of the idols, describing them as scattered (divided), and describing Allah, exalted is He, as One and as Subduer. This is a graceful gentleness and a taking up of the easy proof before the abundant one, which may repel the natural disposition of the ignorant person and cause him to resist. Likewise, the proper way in disputing with the ignorant is to take him by a small step of argument that he accepts. When he accepts it, a further step above it is binding on him, and so on continually until he reaches the truth. Confronting the ignorant person at once with the full doctrine toward which he is being led causes him to recoil and to resist. He has been afflicted with "scattered lords," those who serve the people of this world and hold out hopes to them.

As for His saying ﴿except names﴾: some of the theologians held that in this verse the names are used to refer to the named things, and that He expressed them by the names because they possess names.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The word "name" (ism), which consists of the letters alif, sin and mim, may in the language function in the sense of "self," "essence," or "very thing." If you read the verse in that sense, the meaning is sound. On this reading, "name" is not in the same position as a mere label, such as "man" or "stone." If, however, the names in the verse are taken to mean the names of the idols, such as al-Lat and al-'Uzza and similar things by which they were called gods, then it is possible that the intended meaning is "except possessors of names," with the genitive term omitted and the genitive complement put in its place. It is also possible, and this is the preferred view, God willing, that the intended meaning is: "What you worship besides Him is only deity in name, and you have no connection to a god except by the designation you gave your idols as gods. So your worship is not directed to a god except by name only, not in reality. As for the reality, it is the same as all stones and wood. Your worship attaches only to the name you have coined. That is your object of worship when your affair is settled." He expressed this meaning through the wording recited in the verse. Because of this verse, some who said, "In our saying 'man' and 'stone'," wrongly held that the name is in every case identical with the named thing. This question was already made clear at the beginning of this commentary.

The second object of "you named" is omitted; its estimated form is "gods." This applies if the names are meant to refer to the essences of the idols. But according to the preferred meaning, that their worship is directed only to meanings which the names convey and which do not exist in the idols, the phrase "you named them" is equivalent to "you coined them." The pronoun then refers to the namings, and the pronoun was emphasized so that the following word could be coordinated with it.

The "authority" (sultan) means proof. His saying ﴿Judgment belongs only to Allah﴾ means: your idols, which you have named gods, possess no share of judgment, decrees, or provisions. That is, then, what about them? It is also possible that the intended meaning is a refutation of their judgment in setting up gods besides Allah, exalted is He, and that they have no right to transgress the command of Allah that none other than Him be worshipped. The word "upright" (al-qayyim) means straight. And ﴿but most people do not know﴾ is because of their ignorance and the dominance of disbelief.

Then he called out ﴿O my two fellow prisoners!﴾ a second time, so that their minds would be gathered to hear the answer. It is related that he said to Nabw, "As for you, you will return to your position and to pouring drink for your lord." He said to Mijlath, "As for you, you will be crucified." All this was after three days. It is related that they both said to him, "We saw nothing; we were only playing at dreams to test you." It is also related that only the one who had been told about the crucifixion said that. It was also said that both had seen something and then denied it.

A group read ﴿he will pour wine for his lord﴾ from saqa (to give drink). Another group read ﴿he will be given drink﴾ from asqa (to cause to drink). Both are two dialects with one meaning. 'Ikrimah and al-Jahdari read ﴿he will be given drink﴾ with a damma on the ya' and a fatha on the qaf, meaning "that which quenches him." Yusuf, peace be upon him, informed them, by an unseen matter that he knew from Allah, exalted is He, that the affair had been decided and agreed with the divine decree (qadar).

His saying ﴿He said to the one he thought would be saved﴾ and the rest of the verse: here "thought" (zann) means certainty. This is required by what precedes it, His saying ﴿The matter has been decided﴾. It is certainty concerning what has not yet come into existence. Qatada said: "Here 'thought' retains its usual meaning, because the interpretation of dreams is a conjecture."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Yusuf's saying, peace be upon him, ﴿The matter has been decided﴾ indicates revelation (wahy). Qatada's view does not follow except if the meaning of His saying ﴿The matter has been decided﴾ is that "my speech has been completed, and I have said what I have, and Allah knows best what will occur afterward."

There is another interpretation of the verse: that "thought" (zann) refers to the one who was told that he would pour wine for his lord, because joy in what he had been given good news of had come over him. He had reached the rank of one who is hoped for. When he thought, and his conviction became dominated by the belief that he would be saved, this was in contrast to what befell the other, who was known for crucifixion.

The meaning of the verse: Yusuf said to the king's cupbearer, when he knew that he would return to his former state with the king, "Mention me to the king." It is possible that he meant that he should remind him of his knowledge and standing, and it is possible that he meant that he should remind him of his injustice and of the trial he had been subjected to without right, or of both.

As for the pronoun in ﴿but made him forget﴾, it was said that it refers to Yusuf, peace be upon him. That is, at that moment he forgot to complain to Allah, and he inclined to seek refuge in a created being. It is related that Jibril, peace be upon him, came to him and rebuked him on behalf of Allah, exalted and mighty is He, for that. His imprisonment was prolonged as a punishment for it. It was also said that it was revealed to him: "O Yusuf, you have taken another than Me as a guardian; I will certainly prolong your confinement." It was also said that the pronoun in ﴿made him forget﴾ refers to the cupbearer. This was said by Ibn Ishaq. That is, he forgot the mention of Yusuf before his lord. The "mention" is attributed to "his lord" because Yusuf was with him. On this interpretation, "lord" (rabb) means the king.

As for "bid'" (a few) in the speech of the Arabs, opinions differ about it. The majority view is that it is from three to ten. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, and on this basis is the jurisprudence of Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, regarding claims and oaths. Abu 'Ubayda said: "bid' does not reach a full decade, nor half a decade; it is from one to four." Al-Akhfash said: "bid' is from one to ten." Qatada said: "bid' is from three to nine." This is strengthened by what is related that the Prophet ﷺ said to Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, in the matter of his wager with the Quraysh regarding the victory of the Romans over the Persians: "Do you not know that bid' is from three to nine?!" Mujahid said: (p-93) "from three to seven." Al-Farra' said: "bid' is mentioned only with tens; it is not mentioned with a hundred or with a thousand." What is related concerning this verse is that Yusuf, peace be upon him, was imprisoned for five years, then the story of the two young men came to him, and he was punished for his saying ﴿Mention me to your lord﴾ by remaining in prison for seven years. So the total duration of his imprisonment was twelve years. It was also said that he was punished by staying two years. Al-Hasan said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Had it not been for his words, he would not have remained in prison as long as he did." Then al-Hasan wept and said: "We, when a matter befalls us, we flee to people."

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 12, verses 43–45:**

The Exalted said:

﴿And the king said, "Indeed, I saw seven fat cows being devoured by seven lean ones, and seven green ears of grain and others dry. O assembly, explain to me my vision, if you are able to interpret visions."﴾ ﴿They said, "Confused dreams, and we are not learned in the interpretation of dreams."﴾ ﴿And the one who had been saved from the two of them said, having remembered after a long time, "I will inform you of its interpretation, so send me forth."﴾

The meaning: The great king said, ﴿"Indeed, I see"﴾, meaning: in his sleep. This is made explicit in His saying, ﴿"Indeed, I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you"﴾ [al-Saffat: 102]. A past state is narrated with "see" in the present tense, because he is seeing the vision in the present act of looking at it.

﴿Seven fat cows﴾: It is narrated that he said, "I saw them coming out of a river, and after them came out seven lean ones. I saw the lean ones devour those fat ones until they entered their bellies." He also saw the ears of grain, as was mentioned. The lean (ʿijāf) are those who have reached the utmost emaciation. From this is the saying of the poet:

> "And the men of Mecca are famished, lean."

Then he said to his company and those present: ﴿"O assembly, explain to me"﴾. One group read the two hamzas with full articulation (tahqīq), while another group pronounced the alif of "aftūnī" as a waw.

His saying ﴿"lil-ru'yā"﴾ (for the vision): the lām entered for the sake of emphasis and connection. This is because when the object precedes the verb, it is good, with some verbs, for the preposition lām to be attached to it; when it comes after, the verb does not need that. The phrase ʿibārat al-ru'yā (interpreting the vision) is derived from ʿabara al-nahr (he crossed the river), meaning to pass from one bank to the other. So the interpreter of a vision reaches the end of its interpretation.

His saying ﴿"They said, 'Confused dreams'"﴾ and so on. In the language of the Arabs, a ḍigh (bundle) is smaller than a ḥuzma (sheaf) and larger than a qabḍa (handful) of plants, herbs, or the like. It may be of one kind, or it may be a mixture of plants. From this is His saying, ﴿"And take in your hand a bundle (ḍigh)"﴾ [Ṣād: 44]. It is narrated that he took a cluster (ʿithkāl) of palm dates. It is also narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) did something similar in a legal punishment he carried out upon a man who was disabled. From this is the saying of Ibn Muqbil:

> "A young woman whose bedding, as if it had been laid with
> bundles of basil on a northern morning."

(p-٩٥) From the mixtures is the proverb of the Arabs: "A bundle upon a bale," so the mixing of dreams is likened to the mixing of a bundle of plants. The meaning is: what you have seen, O king, is a confusion of dreams caused by sleep, and we are not among the people of knowledge concerning it, that is, concerning what is confused and worthless. They only denied for themselves the interpretation of dreams (aḥlām), not the interpretation of visions (ru'yā) absolutely. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The vision (ru'yā) is from Allah, and the dream (ḥulm) is from Satan."

He (ﷺ) also said to one who used to see his head being cut off and then returned, and then he would return: "When Satan plays with one of you in sleep, he should not speak of it."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Dreams (aḥlām) and the stirrings of the soul (ḥadathān al-nafs) are disregarded; the vision (ru'yā) is what is interpreted, and its knowledge is sought. The bāʾ in His saying "bi-ʿālimīn" (knowers) is for emphasis, and the bāʾ in "bi-ta'wīl" (interpretation) is for transitivity, and it is connected to "bi-ʿālimīn."

"Aḥlām" is the plural of ḥulm. It is said: "ḥalama al-rajulu" (with the fatḥa on the lām), meaning he yahlumu, when something was imagined to him in his sleep. Dreams (aḥlām) are among the things affirmed by the Shariah. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The vision is from Allah, and it is the good tidings-bearer, while the troubling dream is from Satan. So if one of you sees what he dislikes, let him spit three times to his left and say, 'I seek refuge with Allah from the evil of what I saw,' for it will not harm him." As for what arises from the soul's talk while awake, one should not pay attention to it.

When the cupbearer who was saved heard this statement from the king and the discussion of his companions, he remembered Yusuf (p-٩٦) and his knowledge of the interpretation of dreams and visions, so he spoke these words in this verse.

"Iddakara" originally was "idhtakara," from the form "ifta'ala" from "dhikr" (remembrance). The tā' was changed to dāl, and the first was assimilated into the second. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 12, verse 46–49:

(p-97) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Yusuf, O man of truth, give us your interpretation concerning seven fat cows that seven lean ones devour, and seven green ears of grain and others dry, that I may return to the people so that they may know.﴾ ﴿He said: "You will sow for seven consecutive years, and what you harvest leave in its ear, except for a little of what you eat. Then after that will come seven hard years which will consume what you have stored up for them, except for a little of what you preserve. Then after that will come a year in which the people will be given rain and in which they will press (juice)."﴾

The meaning: The messenger, who was the cupbearer, came to Yusuf and said to him: "O Yusuf, ﴿O man of truth (al-siddiq)﴾." He named him "siddiq" because he had tested his truthfulness in more than one matter. It is an intensive form (bina' mubalagha) from (sadaqa). Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, was also called "siddiq" from (saddaqa ghayrahu, he confirmed others), since with every act of confirmation there is truthfulness, so one who confirms the realities is also truthful. On this basis the believers were called siddiqin in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who believed in Allah and His messengers, they are the siddiqun﴾ [al-Hadid: 19].

Then he said: ﴿Give us your interpretation concerning seven cows,﴾ that is, concerning one who saw in a dream seven cows. Al-Naqqash related a narration in which Jibril, peace be upon him, entered upon Yusuf in the prison, gave him glad tidings of Allah's favour toward him, brought him out of the prison, and that He had caused the king to have a dream which became the means of Yusuf's relief. It is related that the king saw seven fat cows coming out of the river, and seven lean cows coming out after them, and the lean ones devoured the fat ones. He was amazed how they overcame them, and how the fat ones fit into the bellies of the lean ones. He also saw seven green ears of grain wrapped around by seven dry ones, until they covered their greenness, and he was amazed at that too.

His saying: ﴿so that they may know﴾ means: the interpretation of this vision, so that the king's concern and the people's concern over it would be removed. It was also said: ﴿so that they may know﴾ your standing in knowledge and the true extent of your virtue, which would be a means of your deliverance.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said: "You will sow"﴾, the verse. This speech of Yusuf, peace be upon him, contained three kinds of speech: The first: interpretation both in meaning and in wording. The second: offering an opinion and commanding it, which is his saying: ﴿leave it in its ear﴾. The third: informing of the unseen concerning the matter of the eighth year, as Qatada said.

(p-98) Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This may be understood not to be the unseen; rather, the knowledge of interpretation indicated the ending of the drought after seven years, and it is known that nothing will end it except abundant, sufficient rain, just as it indicated that the river is an image of time, since it is the most similar thing to it; so the cows came as an image of the years.

"Da'aban" means: continuously, in keeping with your custom in farming, and from it comes the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

﻿Like your custom with Umm al-Huwayrith before her
........... the verse

The majority of the Seven read "da'aban" with a sukun on the hamza; 'Asim alone read "da'aban" with a fatha on the hamza; Abu 'Amr softens the hamza when reading continuously, and both are like nahrun and nahar. The governing word for "da'aban" is "tazra'una" according to Abu al-'Abbas al-Mubarrad, since in "tazra'una" there is the sense of "tad'abuna"; and to him it is like (qa'ada al-qurfusa'a, "he sat in the crouching position") and (ishtamala al-samma', "he wrapped himself in the single garment"). Sibawayh holds that all of this is governed by a verb implied from the verbal noun indicated by this apparent form, as if he had said: "You will sow, you will persist in sowing a persistence."

His saying: ﴿what you harvest, leave it﴾ is an indication of a noble and beneficial opinion suited to the food of Egypt and its wheat, which cannot last two years in any way except by the stratagem of keeping it in the ear; for the grain, when it remains in its husk, is preserved. The meaning: leave the crop in the ear except what is indispensable for eating, so that the food accumulates in this way and is stored, and one eats the oldest first, then the next oldest. When the years of drought come, people eat from that stored supply, the oldest first, and they also store what is lost in years of drought despite its scarcity, and the years carry one another until people are delivered. The Prophet, peace be upon him, alluded to these years in his supplication against Quraysh: "O Allah, help me against them with seven (years) like the seven of Yusuf." (p-99) This befell them, and a year came that struck everything, until the Prophet, peace be upon him, prayed for them and it was lifted from them, and it did not persist for seven years. It is related that when Yusuf, peace be upon him, went out and described this arrangement to the king, and the king was pleased with his matter, the king said to him: "I have entrusted to you the management of this affair concerning food during these coming years." This was the first office Yusuf held.

He attributed the eating to the years in His saying "ya'kulna" (they devour) by way of extension (ittisa'), from the viewpoint that food is eaten in them, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and the day as one that makes things visible﴾ [Yunus: 67], and as one says: "your day is idle and your night is standing." This is frequent in the speech of the Arabs. It is also possible that the occurrence of drought and the drying of the green crops be called "eating." In a hadith: "a year came upon them that struck everything." A Bedouin described the year as: "it scraped the star, bared the flesh, and bent the bone."

"Tuhsinun" means: you guard and store, as said by Ibn 'Abbas, and it is derived from al-hisn, which is refuge and shelter, and from it comes the women's (tahassun), since it has the meaning of guarding.

His saying, exalted is He: "yughathu" may be from al-ghayth (rain), which is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and the majority of the exegetes, meaning: they will be rained upon. It may also be from (aghathahumu Allah), when Allah relieves them, and from it comes al-ghawth, which is relief.

(p-100) Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and 'Asim read "ya'sirun" with a fatha on the ya and a kasra on the sad; Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with the ta' in address. The majority of the exegetes said: it is from pressing plants such as olives, grapes, cane, sesame, radish, and everything that is pressed. Misr is a land of pressing for many things. It is related that they pressed nothing during the period of drought. Milking is included in this, since it is pressing the udder. Abu 'Ubayda and others said: this is derived from al-'usra and al-'usr, which is refuge, and from it is the verse of Abu Zubayd concerning 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him:

﻿Thirsting, he seeks relief, not to be relieved ∗∗∗ and indeed he had been the refuge of the one who was saved

And from it is the saying of 'Adi ibn Zayd:

﻿If, other than water, my throat were choked ∗∗∗ I would be like the one drowning, my pressing (i'tisari) by water

And from it is the saying of Ibn Muqbil:

﻿My companion is a desert-sinking, ill-favoured one ∗∗∗ who stands between the wild donkey and the 'asar

(p-101) And from it is the saying of Labid:

﻿So he spent the night, and the people travelled the last part of their night, and he was not one who halts without a refuge (mu'sar)

That is: without a place of refuge. So the verse means: they will be saved by the 'usra (refuge).

Al-A'raj, 'Isa, and Ja'far ibn Muhammad read "yu'sarun" with a damma on the ya and a fatha on the sad; this is derived from al-'usra, meaning: they will be brought refuge. It may also be from: the clouds pressed their water upon them. Ibn al-Mustanir said: its meaning is: they will be rained upon. Al-Naqqash related that it was read "yu'assirun" with a damma on the ya, a kasra on the sad with shadda, and taken from 'asr al-balal (wringing out moisture). Al-Tabari rejected at length, without proof, those who derived the word from al-'usra.
