Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 12, verse 50:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿And the king said, "Bring him to me." But when the messenger came to him, he said, "Return to your lord and ask him what happened to the women who cut their hands. Indeed, my Lord is Knowing of their plot."﴾

Within the folds of this verse are elided elements which the apparent sense of the speech indicates and which point to them. The meaning here is: the messenger returned to the chieftains and the king, and related to them the statement of Yusuf. The king and those present saw the nobility of his interpretation, the goodness of his opinion, and his containing of the unseen regarding the matter of the eighth year, together with what the messenger had described of his truthfulness in the earlier dream. So Yusuf became great in the soul of the king, and he said, "Bring him to me." When the messenger reached him with the order to bring him out and said that the king had commanded that he come out, he said to him, "﴿Return to your lord﴾," meaning the king, "and say to him, ﴿what happened to the women?﴾" The aim of Yusuf, peace be upon him, was only: say to him, investigate my offense and examine my matter, whether I was imprisoned justly or unjustly. So he sketched his story with a part of it, for when the gaze falls upon it, the whole matter becomes clear, and he avoided mentioning the wife of the Chief (al-'Aziz), out of good companionship and in consideration of the al-'Aziz's bond with him.

Abu Bakr, on the authority of 'Asim, and Abu Haywa read "al-nuswati" with a ḍamma on the nun, while the rest read "al-niswati" with a kasra on the nun. Both are dialectal forms in the plural of "nisa'" (women), which is a collective noun with no singular from its own form. A group read "al-layi" with a yā', and a group read "al-lati" with a tā', and both are plurals of "allati" (the one who).

This action from Yusuf, peace be upon him, was patience, forbearance, and a seeking of the clearing of his name. That is because he, as is related, feared that he would go out and gain a rank with the king while remaining silent about the matter of his offense, so that people would always see him in that light and say, "This is the one who sought to seduce his master's wife." So Yusuf, peace be upon him, wanted his innocence to become evident and his station of chastity and goodness to be established, and only then would he come out, both for his errors and his rank. It is related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "May Allah have mercy on my brother Yusuf. He was patient and forbearing. Had I remained in prison for as long as he did, I would have answered the summoner and would not have sought an excuse at that time." A similar hadith has been related through 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Qasim, the companion of Malik, in the Book of Tafsir of Sahih al-Bukhari, and Ibn al-Qasim has nothing in the Diwan other than this.

Here there is an objection which should be resolved. The Prophet ﷺ mentioned this statement in praise of Yusuf, so why does he himself depart from a condition for which he praised another? The answer is that the Prophet ﷺ adopted for himself another view of opinion which also has a aspect of excellence, meaning: had I been in his place, I would have hastened to go out and then tried to explain my excuse afterward. This is because these stories and events are presented so that people may take them as examples until the Day of Resurrection, so the Messenger of Allah ﷺ wished to lead people toward the more cautious of matters. The one who goes to extremes in such a situation, by leaving the opportunity to exit such a prison, may, perhaps, end up remaining in his prison, and the one who would have brought him out will have turned away from him. Although Yusuf, peace be upon him, was secure from that through his knowledge from Allah, others are not secure from it. So the condition to which the Prophet ﷺ turned himself is a condition of caution and praise, while what Yusuf, peace be upon him, did was great patience and endurance.

His saying, ﴿Indeed, my Lord is Knowing of their plot﴾, may mean by "Lord" Allah, Exalted and Majestic, and in the verse there is then a warning and a threat. It may also mean by "Lord" the al-'Aziz, his master, and in that there is an appeal to him as witness and a rebuke to him. The pronoun in "bi-kaydihinna" refers to the women mentioned and not to the category in general, because this is a situation of questioning about a specific offense.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 12, verse 51:

His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿He said: "What was your affair when you sought to seduce Yusuf from himself?" They said: "Far be Allah from imperfection! We know of him no evil." The wife of the ʿAzīz said: "Now the truth has become manifest. It was I who sought to seduce him from himself, and indeed he is of the truthful."﴾

The meaning: The king gathered the women, together with the wife of the ʿAzīz, and said to them, "What was your affair?" (The verse continues.) That is, what was your story? This is a request from him that they inform him of the matter. The women replied with a good answer, from which the innocence of themselves is clearly shown in its entirety, and they gave Yusuf some measure of innocence. This is because when the king established against them that they had sought to seduce him, they said in answer to that: "Far be Allah from imperfection!" It is possible, though remotely, that their saying "Far be Allah from imperfection!" was directed toward Yusuf, peace be upon him, and their saying "We know of him no evil" is not a complete exoneration. Complete exoneration would only be a description of the matter in its proper form, so that the wrong is established on both sides. Had they said, "We know of him nothing but good," it would have been more inclusive in exoneration. Al-Bukhari has placed these expressions under the heading of commendation (tazkiyah), and included the saying of Usama ibn Zayd in the hadith of the slander: "Your family; we know of them nothing but good." As for Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, he is not satisfied with this for the commendation of a witness, because it is not an affirmation of uprightness (ʿadalah).

Some exegetes said: When the wife of the ʿAzīz heard their statement and their hesitation to fall into disgrace (al-khizy), an intention and resolve came over her, and she said: ﴿Now the truth has become manifest.﴾ "Ḥaṣḥaṣa" means: it became clear after being hidden, as al-Khalil and others said. It was also said that it is derived from ḥiṣṣah (portion), meaning its portion became distinct from the portion of falsehood. Then she confessed on herself to the seduction, took the sin upon herself, and fully exonerated Yusuf.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 12, verse 52:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿That is so that he (al-'Aziz) may know that I did not betray him in his absence, and that Allah does not guide the plot of the betrayers.﴾

A group of the people of ta'wil (interpretation) said: this statement is from Yusuf, peace be upon him, meaning: "That is so that al-'Aziz, my master, may know that I did not betray him regarding his family while he was absent, and so that he may also know that Allah the Exalted does not guide the plot of a betrayer nor set his endeavour aright."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Guidance (hudan) applied to a plot (kayd) is used metaphorically, in the sense that it does not make it succeed, nor carry it through on a path of success. Yet many a plot is "guided" when it is undertaken by a pious person for a good purpose.

This group differed. Ibn Jurayj said: this statement from Yusuf, peace be upon him, is connected to his saying to the messenger: ﴿Indeed my Lord is Knower of their plot﴾ [Yusuf: 50]. In the speech there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir). On this interpretation, the reference in his saying "That" (dhalika) is to his remaining in prison and his seeking acquittal, meaning: "This is so that my master may know that I did not betray him." Others said: Yusuf only made this statement when the wife of al-'Aziz had finished her speech up to her saying: ﴿And indeed he is of the truthful﴾ [Yusuf: 51]. On this view the reference is to her confession and to what Allah did in it. This view is weak, because it requires his presence with the women before the king, and after this the king says: ﴿Bring him to me﴾ [Yusuf: 54].

A faction of the people of ta'wil said: this verse is from the speech of the wife of al-'Aziz, and her speech is connected, meaning: "My saying this and my confession is so that Yusuf may know that I did not betray him in his absence, by lying about him or accusing him of a sin of which he is innocent." The estimate on this interpretation is: "my repentance and my confession, so that he may know that I did not betray him, and that Allah does not guide..." And on the view that the speech is from Yusuf, the estimate is: "and so that he may know that Allah does not guide the plot of the betrayers."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 12, verse 53:

And the saying of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿And I do not absolve myself. Indeed, the soul is ever commanding of evil, except those upon which my Lord has mercy. Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

This too is a matter of disagreement: is it from the words of Yusuf or from the words of the woman, following on from what came before it?

As for those who say, "It is from the words of Yusuf," they narrate on the authority of Anas ibn Malik that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'When Yusuf said: ﴿I did not betray him in secret﴾ [Yusuf: 52], Jibril said to him: "Nor when you desired [her] and loosened your trousers?!"'" Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, 'Ikrimah and al-Dahhak said something similar. It is also narrated that the woman said it to him; this was said by al-Suddi. And it is narrated that Yusuf, of his own accord, recalled what he had intended, and so said: ﴿And I do not absolve myself. Indeed, the soul is ever commanding of evil﴾; this was also said by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.

As for those who say, "The woman said: ﴿And I do not absolve myself﴾," the meaning of her words is an excuse for her falling into what human beings fall into of desires, as if she said: "This is not something novel, nor is it a reproach to human beings. So I do not absolve myself of it, and souls are commanding of evil, inclining towards it."

"Ammarah" is an intensive form (binā' mubālagha). The "mā" in His saying ﴿except those upon which﴾ is a verbal-source particle (maṣdariyya); this is the view of the majority concerning it, and on this basis the exception is disjunct (istithnā' munqaṭi'), meaning: except the mercy of my Lord. It is also permissible for it to carry the meaning of "man" (who), on the basis that "the soul" is intended to refer to souls, since "nafs" is used as a descriptor for one who has intellect, like "'ayn" and "sam'" (eye and hearing); so said Abu 'Ali. The interpretation of the verse is then: except the souls upon which Allah has mercy.

The qāḍī Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

And since "nafs" is a collective noun (ism jins), it is valid for "mā" to occupy the place of "man," for it is so in the attributes of one who has intellect and in its kinds. This is explicit in the words of al-Mubarrad, and in my view it is the meaning of Sibawayh's words, and it is the position of Abu 'Ali, which he mentioned in al-Baghdadiyyat.

It is also permissible for "mā" to be temporal (ẓarfiyya), the meaning being: indeed the soul is commanding of evil except for the duration of the mercy of Allah upon the servant and his turning away from desiring sins.

Then he expressed hope at the end of the verse with His saying: ﴿Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 12, verses 54–57:**

The Exalted said:

﴿The king said, "Bring him to me; I will take him for myself." So when he spoke with him, he said, "Indeed, you are today firmly established and trusted before us."﴾ ﴿He said, "Appoint me over the storehouses of the land; indeed, I am a knowledgeable guardian."﴾ ﴿And thus We established Joseph in the land, to settle therein wherever he willed. We bestow Our mercy upon whom We will, and We do not waste the reward of the doers of good.﴾ ﴿And the reward of the Hereafter is better for those who believed and used to be mindful of God.﴾

The meaning: When the king became clear about Joseph's innocence of what had been attributed to him, and his trustworthiness was confirmed in the story, and he also understood his patience and steadfastness, his station with him grew great, and he became certain of his good qualities. So he said, ﴿Bring him to me; I will take him for myself.﴾ This is what Joseph, peace be upon him, had been brought to, through his steadfastness in prison, namely that he would rise to the highest ranks. Reflect that the king first said, when his knowledge was established, only ﴿Bring him to me,﴾ and when Joseph did what he did, his trustworthiness, his patience, his lofty resolve and the soundness of his judgment became manifest, he said, ﴿Bring him to me; I will take him for myself.﴾ Then when he came and spoke with him, he said, ﴿Indeed, you are today firmly established and trusted before us.﴾ This indicates that he saw in Joseph's speech and eloquence what confirmed the report or exceeded it, for a person is hidden beneath his tongue. Then, when he engaged in affairs, he advanced step by step until he attained the post of the Azīz.

"Amīn" (trusted) derives from amāna (trustworthiness). Some said it means āmin (secure). This is weak, because it departs from the style of the speech and greatly diminishes the honouring of Joseph.

It is related that when the king drew Joseph near, he said to him, "I shall share with you in everything, except that I would prefer that you not share with me in my family, and that you not eat in my presence." Joseph said to him, "Do you disdain that I should eat with you? I have more right to disdain, for I am the son of Abraham the Friend of God, the son of Isaac the Sacrifice, and the son of Jacob the Truthful." This report is remote and weak. Ibn Maysara said: "This happened only at the beginning of his affair. He used to eat with the Azīz. Then when the affair of the woman occurred, she said to the Azīz, 'Will you leave this one to eat with you?' So he said to him, 'Go and eat with the slaves.' So he took offence and said what has been mentioned." As for the apparent meaning of his story at the time of the king's conversation, it is that he was in servitude; otherwise it would have been fitting for him to withdraw from the works of the unbeliever, since the people were idolaters. Joseph's dialogue with his two fellow-prisoners also implies this.

God, exalted is He, called the Pharaoh of Egypt a "king," since it is the narration of a name whose rule has passed and whose time has ended. Were he alive, it would be a judgment for him to be called "king or amir" if said to an unbeliever. For this reason, "the Prophet (ﷺ) wrote to Heraclius, saying, 'The great one of the Romans,'" and he did not say "king" or "amir," because that would be a judgment, whereas the right thing is that he should submit and they should submit. As for his being their "great one," that is a quality that does not leave him whatever state he turns to. Had the Prophet (ﷺ) written to him, "Amir of the Romans," he would have clung to that as a proof, in the manner of Ziyad's clinging to his saying, "Abu al-Hasan testified for me, by God."

As for God's words, ﴿Appoint me over the storehouses of the land,﴾ and the rest of the verse: Joseph, peace be upon him, understood from the king that he was in control of the matter and sought his help through his judgment in the kingdom, so he took up the task in which he could bring about justice, and in which benefit could be properly directed toward those who deserved it, and in which right would be placed with its people and in their presence.

Some of the interpreters (ahl al-ta'wīl) said: In this verse there is what permits a virtuous man to work for a wicked man, on condition that it is known that he is entrusted with doing what does not contradict his principles, so that he may set right whatever he wishes. But if his work is according to the wicked man's choice, his desires and his immorality, then it is not permissible for him.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

Joseph's request for work was only a form of hisba (service undertaken for the sake of God) from him, peace be upon him, out of his desire that justice should prevail. Similar to this was the accession of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq to the caliphate, despite his forbidding the one who consulted him among the Ansar from appointing himself over two persons, the hadith in its entirety. So it is permissible for the virtuous person to work and to seek work when he sees that no reward is attached to it. It is also permissible for a person to praise himself justly when his affair is unknown.

"Khazā'in" (storehouses) is a general term for all that the kingdom stores of food, wealth and other things. ﴿Ḥafīẓ 'alīm﴾ (a guardian, knowing) are two attributes that encompass all aspects of careful management and vigilance, with which no defect remains for a worker. People have restricted these two attributes to particular things, such as their saying: "guardian with respect to accounting, knowing with respect to languages," and the saying of some of them: "guardian of what you have entrusted to me, knowing of the years of famine." All this is an unjustified restriction. He only intended by his description of himself that the king should know the aspect by which he deserves to be in charge of the storehouses of the land. So he described himself as one who guards the revenues from every direction that needs guarding, and who knows all the disbursements. It is related from Mālik ibn Anas that he said: "Egypt is the treasury of the earth," and he cited this verse as evidence. His saying ﴿storehouses of the land﴾ means the land of Egypt, since the Pharaoh's kingdom was only in it. It is confirmed that it is called the treasury of the earth by its renown in the lands of the earth and its central position, for people set out from it to the regions of the earth, and it is the place where every importer arrives.

God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And thus We established Joseph﴾ and the rest of the verse. The reference of "thus" is to the good dealing of God with him that preceded. That is, through these mentioned acts We raised him in rank and transferred him, and so We established him in the land.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

It is related that the Azīz died during those nights. Ibn Ishaq said: Rather, the king dismissed him, then Qitfīr died, and the king appointed Joseph in his place and married him to his wife. When she came to him as a bride, he said to her: "Is this not better than what you had wanted?" She said to him: "O truthful one, I was at the peak of beauty, I was a young virgin, and my husband did not consummate the marriage, so my soul overcame me in my love for you." So Joseph consummated the marriage with her and found her a virgin, and she bore him two sons. It is also related that the king dismissed the Azīz and appointed Joseph in his place; then Joseph's kingship grew great and he gained dominance over the entire condition of the king. Mujāhid said: The king became a Muslim at the end of his affair, the affair of the Azīz was effaced, his worldly fortune departed, he died, his wife became poor, lame and aged. Then one day she met Joseph on a road, with the soldiers around him and behind him, and on his head were banners on which was written: ﴿This is my way; I call to God with insight, I and whoever follows me. Glory be to God, and I am not of the polytheists.﴾ [Yusuf: 108]. She cried out to him and said: "Glory be to Him who honoured the slaves through obedience and humbled the masters through disobedience." He recognised her, and she said to him: "Show compassion to me and grant me something." He summoned her and spoke with her, had pity on her condition, and prayed to God, exalted is He; so He returned her beauty to her, and he married her.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

Much has been related of this kind of stories that cannot be verified as sound, and to recount it at length would be lengthy.

Al-Jumhūr (the majority of reciters) read ﴿where he wills﴾ (ḥaythu yashā') as a report about Joseph. Ibn Kathir alone read ﴿where We will﴾ (ḥaythu nashā') with the first-person plural pronoun, meaning: where God wills, of Joseph's disposition, according to the variations of his management. Abu Ḥātim transmitted this reading from al-Ḥasan, Shayba, Nāfi' and Abu Ja'far, with a difference of narration from the three Medinan reciters. Abu 'Alī (al-Fārisī) said: Either the sense of this reading is: "where He wills, from the prayer-niches and places of worship, and conditions of obedience, for these are acts of nearness that God, blessed and exalted is He, desires and wills," or its meaning is: "where Joseph wills," but God, mighty and majestic, attributes the will that belongs to Joseph to Himself, insofar as he is one of His servants, and his will was by the power and might of God, exalted is He, as He said: ﴿And you did not throw when you threw, but God threw﴾ [al-Anfal: 17].

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

All this from Abu 'Alī is a Mu'tazilite tendency and a caution lest the acts of servants be attributed to two agents. So reflect on it. The lām in His words ﴿We established for Joseph﴾ may be of the type found in His words, exalted is He, ﴿Some of what you hasten on may have followed you﴾ [al-Naml: 72] and ﴿You interpret dreams﴾ [Yusuf: 43]. His saying "yatabawwa'" (settle) is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and ﴿ḥaythu yashā'﴾ is in the accusative as an adverb of place, or as a direct object, as al-Shammākh said:

…………………

"Where the tribes are branded."

The rest of the verse is clear.

Since it has been stated in this verse that good conduct from the servant, and walking on the path of truth, are not lost before God, and there must be a good outcome for it in this world, He followed this with the statement that the state of the Hereafter is more praiseworthy and more worthy of being made the goal and aim. This is what is drawn from the verse according to the linkage between faith and piety among people. And in it, along with that, there is an indication that his state in the Hereafter is better than his great state in this world.

He said: "Then bring me this brother, so that I may know the truth of your words, and see why your father loved him more than you, if you are truthful."

It is narrated in the stories that they arrived in Egypt and asked permission to enter upon the 'Aziz, and in asking permission they mentioned their lineage. He recognized them and ordered that they be lodged. On the second day he admitted them in a magnificent form, befitting his kingship and a splendid majesty. It is also narrated that he always veiled his face, to conceal his beauty. He would take the drinking cup (sawa') and strike it, and from its ringing he would understand whether what was being told to him was true or false. When they were questioned about their news, whenever they told the truth Joseph said to them: "You have spoken truly." But when they said: "We had a brother whom the wolf devoured," Joseph struck the cup and said: "You have lied." Then his manner changed toward them, and he said: "I see you are spies," and he ordered them to bring the remaining brother so that their truthfulness might become evident. There is a long account concerning this, to which the Qur'an alludes briefly.

Al-jihaz (provisions): what the traveler needs of provisions and goods, and everything that is carried. Likewise, the bride's trousseau (jihaz al-'arus) and the dead person's effects (jihaz al-mayyit).

As for Joseph's words (peace be upon him): ﴿Do you not see that I give full measure﴾, and the rest of the verse, he was encouraging them toward himself at the end, making them comfortable and winning them over. Al-munzilin means: those who host, in his land and at his time. The provisions referred to are the food he had loaded for them. Then he threatened them that if they did not bring the brother, there would be no measure for them with him in the future, and he commanded them not to approach any land or obedience to him. The phrase ﴿and you shall not come near me﴾ is a prohibition in both wording and meaning. It is also possible that its wording is a statement while its meaning is a prohibition, with one of the two nuns dropped, as is read in ﴿So with what will you give me good news?﴾ (Q. 15:54), where the nun is read with a kasra, and this is purely a statement. Al-Nahhas erred regarding this point. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said: this verse and what follows it indicate that the measuring of food is the responsibility of the seller. The same applies, according to the narration, to tawliya (sale at cost price) and shirka (partnership sale), which are treated as sale. But according to the narration concerning a loan (qard), the measuring is the responsibility of the borrower (p-112).

It is narrated that he held back Simeon (Shim'un) from them as a hostage until they brought him Benjamin. This was reported by al-Suddi. It is also narrated that he did not detain any of them. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Joseph would drop a pebble into a silver vessel decorated with gold, and it would ring, and he would say to them: 'This vessel tells me that you have an elderly father.'"

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It seems to have been a trick and a deception toward them. It is also narrated that this vessel was what he used to measure out food, to show its value according to its scarcity during that period. It is also narrated that Joseph (peace be upon him) seized the wealth of the people during those years, then their properties and lands; hence, to this day, no one in the land of Egypt and its farmlands owns property. The apparent meaning of all that Joseph did with them is that it was by revelation and command. Otherwise, the piety of Jacob would have required that he hasten to him and summon him. But Allah, Blessed and Exalted, informed him of what he was doing, so that Jacob's reward and trial would be completed, and the first dream would be interpreted.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 12, verses 61–63:

His saying, exalted and majestic is He:

﴿They said, "We will seek from him [i.e., from his father] to let him go with us, and indeed we will do [that]."﴾ ﴿And he said to his servants (fityan), "Put their merchandise back into their saddlebags, so that they may recognize it when they return to their families; perhaps they will [then] come back."﴾ ﴿So when they returned to their father, they said, "O our father, measure has been withheld from us, so send with us our brother that we may get a measure, and indeed we will be its guardians."﴾

The meaning of "al-murawadah" (soliciting, persuading) has already been mentioned; that is, "We will ask our father to let him come with us to you." Then they reinforced this statement by committing themselves to it in their saying, "and indeed we will do [that]." Yusuf, peace be upon him, intended to go to great lengths in winning them over by returning the property of each one of them into his saddlebag among his provisions, and he commanded his attendants (fityan) to do so.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read "li-fityatihi" (to his attendant, singular), while Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "li-fityanihi" (to his attendants, plural). It is reported from 'Asim that both forms are transmitted. "Fityan" (plural) refers to the multiplicity of those commanded, while "fityah" (fewer) refers to those who handle the goods, namely the servants; this description applies to both free men and slaves. In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, the reading is: "And he said to his attendants while he was measuring for them."

His saying, ﴿that they may recognize it﴾, means: perhaps they will recognize that it is a favour or a kindness, and seeing its value they will be inclined toward us, so perhaps they will return at that time. As for the goods themselves, one does not say "perhaps" about them. It was also said: Yusuf intended by returning the merchandise that they would be reluctant to take food without payment and would therefore return to pay the price. This view is weak on several grounds, and their joy at the merchandise and their saying, ﴿This is our merchandise, returned to us﴾ [Yusuf: 65], reveals that Yusuf, peace be upon him, did not intend this. Rather, he intended to win their hearts, to bestow favour upon them, and to make them inclined toward himself as before. He singled out the merchandise rather than giving them other wealth because it would have a greater effect upon their souls, since they knew its lawfulness; whereas his own wealth was, with them, of unknown status, and at most it could be accepted in the same way they accepted the grain. It would also show that what Yusuf did, in joining them and comforting them in that hardship, was obligatory upon him, since he is a just king and they are people of faith and prophethood. It was also said: he knew that there was no merchandise or silver with his father, so he returned the merchandise to them lest their lack prevent them from going back to him. It was also said: he made it a preparation for placing the drinking-cup in his brother's saddlebag afterward, to show that he had not stolen, for whoever reflects on the story.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What is apparent from the story is that he only intended to win them over and to maintain the ties of kinship.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read "naktal" (we shall measure) with the nun, in keeping with "measure has been withheld from us," and it is strengthened by "and we shall bring provisions for our family" [Yusuf: 65] and "and we shall gain an additional camel-load." Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "yaktal" with the ya', meaning: Benjamin will measure just as we measured. The root of "naktal" is "naktayil," whose form is "naf'al." Their saying, ﴿measure has been withheld from us﴾, apparently means that they were referring to his saying, ﴿So there shall be no measure for you with me﴾ [Yusuf: 60], so it is a prohibition for the future. It was also said that they were referring to Benjamin's camel-load, which had not been measured out; but the first is more probable. Then they undertook to guard him and to protect him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 12, verse 64–65:

(p-114) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿He said, "Shall I trust you with him any more than I trusted you with his brother before? But God is the best guardian, and He is the Most Merciful of the merciful."﴾ ﴿And when they opened their goods, they found their merchandise had been returned to them. They said, "O our father, what more could we want? This is our merchandise, returned to us. We will bring provisions for our family, guard our brother, and gain an extra camel-load. That is an easy measure."﴾

His saying "hal" (Is it not...?) is a question of confirmation and affirmation. Ya'qub's (peace be upon him) distress over the separation from Benjamin is clear. He did not explicitly forbid them from taking him, because he saw in that a benefit, but he informed them of his little confidence in them and that he feared for him from their scheming. Yet the apparent state of their affairs was that they had turned penitently to God and their condition had changed, so he did not fear for him as he had feared for Yusuf before. However, he made known that there was something in his soul, then he surrendered to God, Exalted, unlike his expression in the story of Yusuf.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim, in the narration of Abu Bakr, read "khayrun hifzan" (better in guarding). Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Hafsa, on the authority of 'Asim, read "khayrun hafizan" (better as a guardian). The accusative of that in both readings is as a tamyiz (specification). Al-Zajjaj said: it is permissible that "hafizan" be in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). Abu 'Ali al-Farisi rejected this, because it is a state that the sentence and meaning cannot do without, unlike the condition of a state. The meaning is only that the guardianship of God is better than your guardianship. Whoever reads "hifzan" it accords with their saying: "and we will guard our brother." Whoever reads "hafizan" it accords with their saying: "And indeed We are its guardians" [Yusuf: 63]. So Ya'qub (peace be upon him) surrendered to God and put his trust in Him. Abu 'Amr al-Dani said: Ibn Mas'ud read: "fa-Allahu khayru hafizin wa huwa khayru al-hafizin" (God is the best of guardians, and He is the best of guardians).

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

And in this there is remoteness.

His saying: ﴿they opened their goods﴾: he called the bound and tied bundle, in its entirety, "mata'" (goods), and therefore opening it was apt. The majority of people read "ruddat" with a dammah on the ra', according to the prevalent dialect of the Arabs; next is the dialect of those who use ishmam (a faint rounding), and next the dialect of those who use kasrah. 'Alqama and Yahya ibn Waththab read "ridda" (p-115) with a kasrah on the ra', according to the dialect of those who use kasrah, which is found among the Banu Dabba. Abu al-Fath said: As for the defective verbs like "qila" and "biya'", the prevalent form is with kasrah, then ishmam, then dammah, so they say "quwila" and "buwi'a". Tha'lab recited:

..................

"And it was said, having neither family nor wealth."

Al-Zajjaj said: whoever reads "ridda" with a kasrah on the ra' has made it transferred from the dal, as was done in "qila" and "biya'", to show that the original vowel of the dal is kasrah.

His saying: ﴿ma nabghi﴾ may be interrogative, as said by Qatada, and "nabghi" is from "al-bughya" (seeking), meaning: what do we seek beyond this honour? This is our property, returned to us along with our provisions. Al-Zajjaj said: it may also be negating, meaning: nothing remains for us that we seek. It may also be negating with "nabghi" from "al-baghy" (transgression), meaning: we have not transgressed, so as to lie against this king, nor in describing his generosity and honour; this merchandise is returned. Abu Haywa read "ma tabghi" with the ta', addressing Ya'qub, meaning: what do you desire? What do you seek? al-Mahdawi said: 'A'isha related it from the Prophet (ﷺ).

A group read "wa-namir" with a fatha on the nun, from "mara yamiru" meaning to bring in goods, and from this is the poet's saying:

"I sent you as a provider, and you stayed a year...
When will your aid come, O you who give aid?"

'A'isha, may God be pleased with her, read "wa-numir" with a dammah on the nun, and it is from the reading of Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami; according to this, "mara" and "amara" have the same meaning.

His saying: ﴿wa-nazdadu kayla ba'ir﴾ they mean the camel of their brother, since Yusuf had only given them ten camel-loads and had not given the eleventh because its owner was absent. Mujahid said: "kayla ba'ir" means the measure of a donkey, and he said: some Arabs call the donkey "ba'ir." This is anomalous.

(p-116) His saying: ﴿dhalika kayl yasir﴾ is a confirmation without an alif (interrogative), meaning: "Is that a small measure in a year like this, so that its matter is neglected?" It was also said: its meaning is: it is easy for Yusuf to give him. Al-Hasan al-Basri said: Yusuf had promised them that he would add the load of one camel without payment. al-Suddi said: the meaning of that is: a light measure, i.e., quick, in which we will not be detained or delayed.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

So, on this view, they were comforting him with the nearness of their return.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 12, verses 66–67:**

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿He said: "I will never send him with you until you give me a solemn covenant in the name of Allah that you will surely bring him back to me, unless you are surrounded." And when they had given him their covenant, he said: "Allah is Guardian over what we say."﴾

﴿And he said: "O my sons, do not enter by one gate, but enter by different gates. I cannot avail you anything against Allah. Judgment belongs only to Allah. In Him I have put my trust, and in Him let all who trust put their trust."﴾

Ya'qub (peace be upon him) wanted to obtain a covenant from them. *Al-mawthiq* (الموثق) is on the pattern *maf'il* from *al-wathaqah* (firmness, reliability). When they pledged to him, he called Allah as a witness between himself and them, saying: ﴿Allah is Guardian over what we say﴾. *Al-wakil* (الوكيل) means the one who takes charge and protects.

Ibn Kathir read *"tu'tunni"* (تُؤْتُونِي) with a *ya'* (ياء) both in *al-wasl* (continuing recitation without pause) and in *al-waqf* (pausing). It is narrated from Nafi' that he connected with the *ya'* and stopped without it. The rest omitted the *ya'* in both cases.

As for His saying: ﴿Do not enter by one gate﴾, it was said: he feared for them the evil eye (*al-'ayn*), because they were eleven men of one man, and they were people of beauty and stature. Qatadah said: unless you are unable to do that.

This is supported by the wording of the verse.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿He said: "I will never send him with you until you give me a solemn covenant in the name of Allah that you will surely bring him back to me, unless you are surrounded." And when they had given him their covenant, he said: "Allah is Guardian over what we say."﴾

﴿And he said: "O my sons, do not enter by one gate, but enter by different gates. I cannot avail you anything against Allah. Judgment belongs only to Allah. In Him I have put my trust, and in Him let all who trust put their trust."﴾

Ya'qub (peace be upon him) wanted to obtain a covenant from them. *Al-mawthiq* (الموثق) is on the pattern *maf'il* from *al-wathaqah* (firmness, reliability). "And when they entered from the gate their father had commanded them, it did not avail them against Allah at all; it was only a need within the soul of Ya'qub, which he fulfilled. And indeed, he was a possessor of knowledge because of what We had taught him, but most of the people do not know." ﴿And when they entered upon Yusuf, he drew his brother to himself and said, "Indeed, I am your brother, so do not be distressed by what they used to do."﴾

It has been narrated that when they bade farewell to their father, he said to them: "Convey my greetings to the king of Egypt, and say to him: Indeed our father sends blessings upon you, and prays for you, and thanks you for your kindness towards us." In the book of Abu Mansur al-Mihrani: that he addressed him with a letter which was read to Yusuf, and he wept.

As for His saying: ﴿it did not avail them against Allah at all; it was only a need within the soul of Ya'qub, which he fulfilled﴾, it is equivalent to saying: there was in that no repelling of the decree of Allah, but it was a desire for Ya'qub which he fulfilled, and a comfort to his soul, for he held fast to it and commanded its implementation. So the answer of "lamma" carries the meaning of His saying: ﴿it did not avail them against Allah at all﴾, and ﴿except a need﴾ is an exception that is not from the first. The need was that he would be content in his soul with their entering from separate gates out of fear of the evil eye. Mujahid said: "The need: the fear of the evil eye," and Ibn Ishaq said the same, though in their wording there is some figurative usage. A parallel to this act is that the Prophet (ﷺ) blocked a niche in a grave with a stone and said: "Indeed this does not avail anything, but it is a comfort to the soul of the living."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In my view, His saying: ﴿it did not avail them against Allah at all﴾ means: it did not turn away a decree from them, for if it had been decreed that the evil eye would strike them, it would have struck them whether scattered or gathered. Ya'qub only hoped that his instruction would coincide with the measure of safety, so he instructed, and by that fulfilled the need of his soul, in delighting in his hope that his instruction would coincide with the decree concerning their safety.

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, praised Ya'qub for being taught what Allah had taught him of this meaning, and other things fall under the general sense, and He said: indeed most people are not like that. It has been said that its meaning is: indeed he is one who acts upon what We have taught him; this is the view of Qatadah. Sufyan said: whoever does not act is not a person of knowledge.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The wording does not indicate this, but it is correct in itself, and the meaning and the station of Ya'qub, peace be upon him, favour it. Abu Hatim said: al-A'mash recited: "la-dhu 'ilmin li-ma 'allamnahu" (indeed he is a possessor of knowledge of what We taught him). It is possible that the answer of "lamma" in this verse is omitted and implied, and then He informs of their entering, that ﴿it did not avail﴾ and the rest of the verse.

As for His exalted saying: ﴿And when they entered upon Yusuf﴾ the verse. The meaning is that when Yusuf's brothers entered upon him and he saw his brother, he showed them gratitude for that, according to what has been narrated, and drew his brother to himself and sheltered him within himself. From this word comes "al-ma'wa" (shelter), and Benjamin was Yusuf's full brother, so he sheltered him. The description of that, as narrated from Ibn Ishaq and others, is that Yusuf, peace be upon him, instructed the steward of his hospitality to lodge them two by two, so Benjamin was left alone, and Yusuf said: "I will lodge this one with myself," and he did so, and he stayed with him, and said to him: ﴿Indeed I am your brother﴾. The interpreters differed over this expression. Ibn Ishaq (p-119) and others said: he informed him that he was truly his brother and asked him to keep it secret, and told him: do not mind whatever disagreeable things you see in my scheming to take you from them. According to this interpretation, His saying ﴿for what they used to do﴾ may refer to what the servants of Yusuf were doing regarding the drinking-cup and the like, and it may refer to what the brothers had done in the past. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: he only informed him that he was his brother in affection, in place of his brother who had gone, and did not reveal the matter to him, but left him to be subject to the scheme as the rest of his brothers were.

And "tabtais" is of the form "tafta'il", from al-bu's (distress), meaning: do not grieve and do not be concerned; and thus the commentators have explained it.

**The Commentary of Ibn ʿAṭiyya (al-Muḥarrar al-Wajīz) on Sūrah Yūsuf, verses 70–75**

The Exalted said:

﴿So when he had furnished them with their provisions, he placed the drinking-cup in his brother's bag. Then a crier called out: "O caravan, you are surely thieves!"﴾

﴿They turned towards them and said: "What is it that you are missing?"﴾

﴿They said: "We are missing the king's goblet, and for whoever brings it is a camel-load, and I stand surety for it."﴾

﴿They said: "By God, you know that we did not come to cause corruption in the land, and we were not thieves."﴾

﴿They said: "What then shall be its penalty, if you are lying?"﴾

﴿They said: "Its penalty is that he in whose bag it is found shall himself be its penalty. Thus do We requite the wrongdoers."﴾

This was part of the scheme which God facilitated for Yūsuf, peace be upon him. In the religion of Yaʿqūb, the thief was to be enslaved, while in the religion of Egypt, he was to be beaten and the fine doubled for him. Yūsuf knew that his brothers, relying on the innocence of their own position, would appeal to their own judgement regarding the theft. So he devised a stratagem for this, and made light of the matter, despite what it involved of casting innocent people under the charge of theft and bringing grief upon Yaʿqūb, peace be upon him, and upon them, because of the good he knew in that for the appointed time, and by revelation which was inescapable, and by the will of God, to test them through it. This is the interpretation of a group, and it is strengthened by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Thus did We contrive for Joseph﴾ (Yūsuf 76).

It has also been said: what was revealed to Yūsuf was only that he should place the drinking-cup, and then, if it was kept safe, it was lost, so he proclaimed on his own opinion what appeared to him. This was preferred by al-Ṭabarī, but the searching of the bags refutes it.

It has also been said: since they had sold Yūsuf, he deemed it permissible for them to be told this, and he was punished for it by their saying: ﴿Indeed, a brother of his has stolen before﴾ (Yūsuf 77).

His saying "jaʿala" (he placed) means, by his command, through his servants and attendants. Ibn Masʿūd recited "wa-jaʿala" with an added waw.

The *siqāya* (drinking-cup) is the vessel from which the king drinks, and with which he used to measure out food for the people. This is the explicit statement of the majority of the exegetes (*mufassirūn*, i.e. specialists in tafsīr): Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Ibn Zayd. In the books of those who have investigated its nature, it is a shape with two heads, joined by a handle which is gripped by the hands, so that food is measured with one head and drunk from the other, or from both. It is likely that it was for the drink of the king's guests and for his fine foods, for which large vessels are needed.

Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: the *ṣuwāʿ* is like the Persian *makkūk*, and it was Yūsuf's vessel from which he drank, and it was of the size it was. He said: Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with them both, related to me that al-ʿAbbās had one like it which he drank from in the Jāhiliyya.

Ibn Jubayr also said: the *ṣuwāʿ* is the Persian *makkūk* whose two ends meet, from which the non-Arabs used to drink. It is related that it was of silver, and this is the view of the majority. It is also related that it was of gold. al-Zajjāj said: it has also been said that it was of musk.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This has also been related with a fatḥa on the mīm (i.e. *makk*ūk pronounced with a fatḥa).

It has also been said that it resembled a basin (*ṭās*), and it has been said that it was of copper, as Ibn ʿAbbās also said. Because food was scarce in those years, its measure was restricted to that vessel. This placing was done without the knowledge of Yāmīn. So said al-Suddī, and this is the apparent meaning.

When the caravan departed with its loads, and went out from Egypt, according to what is related (and a group said: rather, before leaving Egypt), a command was given concerning them and they were detained. And ﴿a crier called out﴾. Addressing the caravan (*ʿīr*) is a figure of speech (*tajawwuz*), and what is meant is its owners. What is really meant is: "O company or party." Mujāhid said: their animals were donkeys. He described them as thieves because, apparently, one of them had stolen. This is like your saying: "The sons of so-and-so killed so-and-so," when in fact only one of them killed him.

When the brothers of Yūsuf heard this statement, they turned towards them, and it grieved them to be accused of this disgrace, and they said: ﴿What is it that you are missing?﴾ so that a search would take place and their innocence would become evident. They did not take refuge in denial from the start, but rather asked for the claim to be completed, perhaps there would be in it something by which it would be refuted, so that no dispute would be needed. Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān recited "tufqidūna" with a ḍamma on the tā', and Abū Ḥātim criticised this reading as weak.

﴿They said: "We are missing the king's goblet"﴾. It is *al-mikyāl* (the measure), and it is the *siqāya*. Its form is first made with one of its two sides, and last with the second. Most of the readers recited *ṣuwāʿ* with a ḍamma on the ṣād and an alif. Abū Ḥaywa recited *ṣiwāʿ* with a kasra on the ṣād and an alif. Abū Hurayra and Mujāhid recited *ṣāʿ al-malik* with a fatḥa on the ṣād and no waw. ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAwf recited *ṣūʿ* with a ḍamma on the ṣād. Abū Rajāʾ recited *ṣawʿ*.

These are dialectal forms (*lughāt*) for the measure, as said by Abū al-Fatḥ and others. These nouns are used both as feminine and as masculine. Abū ʿUbayd said: *al-ṣāʿ* is made feminine insofar as it is named a *siqāya*, and made masculine insofar as it is a *ṣāʿ*. Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmur recited *ṣawgh* with a dotted ghayn, and this is on the basis that it is the thing fashioned (*maṣūgh*) for the king, according to what is related, that it was of gold or of silver. So it is a verbal noun used as a name. This reading was related from Abū Rajāʾ. Abū Ḥātim said: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and al-Ḥasan recited *ṣuwāgh* with a ḍamma on the ṣād, an alif, and a dotted ghayn.

His saying: ﴿and for whoever brings it is a camel-load﴾ means: for whoever points out its thief, exposes him, and restores the *ṣuwāʿ* to the king. This is a reward (*juʿl*). His saying: ﴿and I stand surety for it﴾ is a guarantee (*ḥamāla*). This is because food was obtainable only from the king, so it was understood from the crier that he had made the reward on behalf of someone else. Fearing that this reward would not be trusted, since it came from another, he undertook it himself. Mujāhid said: the *zaʿīm* is the crier who said: ﴿O caravan﴾. *Zaʿīm* in the speech of the Arabs means guarantor, and the chief is called *zaʿīm* because he takes on the needs of the people.

His saying: ﴿They said: "By God"﴾, the verse. It is related that the brothers of Yūsuf had returned the merchandise which was found in their bags, and they were scrupulous about taking food without payment. Therefore they said: ﴿you know﴾, meaning: you know from us our scrupulousness. It is also related that they had become well known in Egypt for righteousness and abstention, and they used to put a muzzle (*akimma*) in the mouths of their camels so that they would not eat people's crops. Therefore they said: you know that we did not come for corruption, and we are not people of theft.

The *tā'* in *Tallāhi* is a substitute for a waw, as it is substituted in *turāth*, in *al-tawrāh* (the Torah), and in *tukhma* (indigestion). The *tā'* does not enter into the oath except with the written names of God Exalted, and not in anything else. You do not say *tarraḥmān* or *tarraḥīm*.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They said: "What then shall be its penalty"﴾, the verse. The servants of Yūsuf said: what is the penalty of the thief, if you are lying in your statement: ﴿and we were not thieves﴾? The brothers of Yūsuf said: the penalty of the thief is the ruling contained in these words: ﴿he in whose bag it is found shall himself be its penalty﴾. So the first *jazāʾuhu* is the subject (*mubtadaʾ*), and *man* is a second subject. *Man* is either a conditional or has the meaning of *alladhī* (the one who). His saying: ﴿shall himself be its penalty﴾ is the predicate of *man*, and the clause is the predicate of the first *jazāʾuhu*. The pronoun in His saying: ﴿They said: its penalty﴾ refers to the thief. It is also possible that *man* is the predicate, on the meaning: "the penalty of the thief is whoever is found in his bag," with the pronoun in *raḥlihi* referring back to *man*, and his saying *fa-huwa* (himself) being an added clarification and emphasis. In my view this is not one of the places for making the pronoun explicit (*ibrāz al-ḍamīr*), as some of the exegetes held. It is also possible that the sense is: "its penalty is the enslavement of whoever is found in his bag," and then it is confirmed by His saying: ﴿shall himself be its penalty﴾. This statement of theirs is the statement of one who did not doubt himself, because they undertook to enslave whoever was found in his bag, and this is more than the requirement of their own law, since their law was that no one should be seized except one whose theft was established. The affair of Yāmīn with the drinking-cup was open to doubt, but they bound themselves to the rule that whoever is found in his bag is held to be a thief.

Their saying: ﴿Thus do We requite the wrongdoers﴾ means: this is our practice and our religion regarding the people of theft, that the thief is to be held in possession as he himself held the stolen thing.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

Some people have related that this ruling was in the early period of Islam and then was abrogated (*nusikha*, i.e. naskh, the abrogation of a ruling by a later ruling) by the hadd punishment of amputation. This is weak. As far as I know, it never existed. al-Zahrāwī related from al-Suddī that their ruling was only that the thief should be put to service in proportion to his theft. This is weakened by the return of the *ṣuwāʿ*, for then Yāmīn should not have been seized, since nothing remained for which he could serve.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 12, verse 76:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿So he began with their bags before the bag of his brother; then he brought it out from his brother's bag. Thus did We devise for Joseph. He could not have taken his brother under the king's law, unless God willed. We raise by degrees whom We will, and above every possessor of knowledge is One who knows.﴾

His beginning with their bags as well is an establishing of the scheme and a removing of the appearance that it is a scheme. The majority of people recited "wi‘ā’" (وِعاءِ) with a kasra on the waw. Al-Hasan recited "wu‘ā’" (وُعاءِ) with a damma on it. Ibn Jubayr recited "i‘ā’" (إعاءِ) with a hamza in place of the waw. This is common with a kasratted waw, and it is more frequent with a dammated one, and there has come from the fathah-vowelled one a single instance, in "wahad" (وحَدٍ).

God, exalted is He, attributed the scheming (al-kayd) to Himself when He brought out the decree by which He permitted for Joseph the taking of his brother in a manner which, in people's habitual usage, is a scheme. Al-Suddi and al-Dahhak said: "kidnā" (كِدْنا) means "we devised" (ṣana‘nā). As for ﴿the king's law (dīn al-malik)﴾, Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, explained it as "his authority (sultānihi)", and Qatadah explained it as "judgement and rule (al-qaḍā’ wa’l-ḥukm)". These are close in meaning. The exception in this verse is a narration of a state (ḥikāyat ḥāl); the implied sense is: "except that Allah willed what occurred of this scheme". It may also be estimated that it is a general principle (tasannun) after the negation was established.

The majority recited "narfa‘u" (نَرْفَعُ) in the form of the honoured speaker's pronoun, and "nashā’u" (نَشاءُ) likewise. Al-Hasan, ‘Isa and Ya‘qub recited with the yā’ (بِالياءِ), meaning Allah, exalted is He. Abu ‘Amr, Nafi‘ and the people of Madinah recited "darajāti man" (دَرَجاتِ مَن) with the "darajāt" construct-annexed to "man". ‘Asim and Ibn Muhaysin recited "darajātin man" (دَرَجاتٍ مَّنْ) with tanwin on "darajāt". The majority recited "wa-fawqa kulli dhī ‘ilm" (وَفَوْقَ كُلِّ ذِي عِلْمٍ). Ibn Mas‘ud recited "wa-fawqa kulli dhī ‘ālim" (وَفَوْقَ كُلِّ ذِي عالِمٍ). The meaning is that human beings have ranks in knowledge, so every scholar must have someone more knowledgeable than him, whether from among humans or Allah, Mighty and Majestic. As for the reading of Ibn Mas‘ud, it is said that "dhī" is extra, and it is said that "‘ālim" is a verbal noun like "al-bāṭil".

It is narrated that the inspector, whenever he finished with a man's baggage and found nothing in it, would seek forgiveness from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, repenting of that act of his. The apparent sense of the words of Qatadah and others is that the one seeking forgiveness was Joseph, because he was inspecting them and knew where the cup was, until he finished with them and reached the baggage of Binyamin, and said: "I do not think this youth agreed to this, nor took anything." His brothers said to him: "By Allah, we will not leave until you search him, for that is more pleasing to you and to us." So he searched at that time and brought out the cup. This searching by Joseph implies that the one who called out only made the theft by his own opinion. Or it may be said: all of that was by the command of Allah, the Exalted. What strengthens this is His saying: "kidnā" (كِدْنا). And how could it not be by Joseph's opinion, when he was compelled in his attempt to bind them to the ruling of theft so that his taking of his brother would be completed?

The pronoun in His saying "istakhrajahā" (اسْتَخْرَجَها) refers to the cup, and it may refer to the theft.

It is narrated that when the brothers of Joseph saw that, they said: "O Binyamin, son of Rachel! May Allah disgrace you! Your mother bore two thieving brothers. How did you steal this cup?" He raised his hands to the sky and said: "By Allah, I did not do it." They said to him: "Then who placed it in your baggage?" He said: "The One who placed the merchandise in your baggage."

What we have mentioned of the meaning in His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿and above every possessor of knowledge is One who knows﴾ is the saying of al-Hasan and Qatadah. It has also been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, and it was narrated from him, may Allah be pleased with him, that one day he related a wondrous story, and a man among those present marvelled at it and said: "Praise be to Allah, and above every possessor of knowledge is One who knows." Ibn 'Abbas said: "Evil is what you have said. Indeed, the Knower (al-‘Alīm) belongs to Allah, and He is above every possessor of knowledge."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Between this and the saying of al-Hasan there is a difference.

The Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 12, verse 77:

His Exalted and Majestic saying:

﴿They said: "If he steals, a brother of his has stolen before. But Joseph kept it hidden within himself and did not reveal it to them. He said: 'You are worse in position, and Allah knows best what you describe.'"﴾

The pronoun in "qalu" (they said) refers to Joseph's brothers, and the brother they pointed to is Joseph. They referred to him in indefinite form (nakkaruhu) to belittle the matter, since it was something the present company had no knowledge of. Then they attached it to Benjamin, since he was his full brother. Their saying: ﴿If he steals, a brother of his has stolen before﴾ may bear two interpretations:

The first: they established the theft on Benjamin's side, and on Joseph's side, according to the apparent ruling, peace be upon them both. So it is as if they said: "If he has stolen, it is no novelty from the two sons of Rachel, for his brother Joseph had stolen." Thus this is a disparagement by the brothers of the two sons of Rachel: Joseph and Benjamin.

The other interpretation that their wording allows implies that the theft on the side of Joseph and Benjamin is merely presumed, as if they said: "If what has been charged against this one, Benjamin, is true in itself, then what was charged against Joseph before is true too," and it seems that the story of Joseph and the suspicion about him was, in their view, stronger than what appeared regarding Benjamin.

Some commentators said: "The implied meaning is: it was said about Joseph that he stole," and similar to this is a statement whose meaning does not fit the wording of the verse.

(p-126) These statements from them, peace be upon them, were only according to the apparent sense and the requirement of the ruling against those who had come down, so they did not mean to slander Joseph in his absence, but intended only to report a matter that had occurred, so that some of the disgrace might be removed from them, and it concerns these two full brothers in particular.

As for what has been narrated about Joseph's theft, there are three versions. The majority hold that his paternal aunt was his nurse. When he grew up, Jacob wished to take him from her, so she became deeply attached to him and feared separation from him. She took the belt (mintaqa) of Isaac, which was an inherited heirloom among them, and fastened it on him under his clothes. Then she cried out and said: "I have lost the belt, and Joseph has taken it." He was searched and it was found with him, so she claimed him as a slave, according to their law, and he remained with her until she died, then he went to his father. Ibn Idris said, on the authority of his father: The sons of Jacob ate a meal, and Joseph took a bone (irq) and hid it, so they accused him of theft for that. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Qatada said: His mother had ordered him to steal an idol belonging to her father, so he stole it and broke it, and that act, on her part and his, was a changing of wrongdoing (taghyir al-munkar). In al-Zajjaj's book it is said that the idol was of gold.

The pronoun in His saying: ﴿fa-asarraha﴾ (but he kept it hidden) refers to the resentment (al-hazzaza) that arose in Joseph's soul from their saying, and the speech implies it. This is like how speech implies the pronoun in the verse of Hatim:

"By your life, wealth does not benefit a man when the death rattle comes upon him one day and the chest is constricted by it."

And this is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then indeed your Lord, for those who emigrated after they were tried, then struggled and were patient, indeed your Lord after that is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [an-Nahl: 110]. So by "it" is meant the state resulting from these mentioned actions in the verse.

Some said: he concealed the reward (al-mujazah). Others said: he concealed the argument (al-hujjah). What we have mentioned before is more fitting. Ibn Abi 'Abla read: "fa-asarrahu Yusufu" with a masculine pronoun.

(p-127) His saying: ﴿You are worse in position﴾ and the rest of the verse. Apparently he said it openly, as if he had kept his dislike of their statement hidden, then rebuked them with his saying: ﴿You are worse in position﴾, meaning, because of the badness of your deeds, and Allah knows whether what you have described is true. The wording contains an indication of their lying. What strengthens this in my view is that they abandoned pleading for themselves and turned to pleading through the elderly man, peace be upon him. A group said—and this is the apparent sense of the words of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both—: Joseph did not say this statement except within himself, and it is only an explanation of what he kept hidden in himself; that is, this statement is what he kept hidden, so it is as if the meaning is: he said within himself, "You."

Al-Tabari mentioned here a narrative, the summary of which is that when the drinking-cup was brought out from Benjamin's baggage, his brothers said: "O sons of Rachel, will misfortune not continue to befall us from your side?" Benjamin said: "Rather, the sons of Rachel are afflicted by you: you took my brother and destroyed him, and this one placed the cup in my baggage just as he placed the silver coins in your baggage." They said: "Do not mention the silver coins, or we will be seized for them." Then they entered upon Joseph, and he took the cup and struck it, and it hummed. He said: "It informs that you took a brother of yours and sold him." Benjamin prostrated and said: "O Mighty one, ask this cup of yours; it will inform you of the truth."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Similar to these narratives are those whose summary we preferred to shorten. It is also related that Rubil became angry, and his hair stood up until it came out of his clothes. Joseph ordered a young boy of his to touch him, and his anger subsided. Then Rubil said: "Someone from the sons of Jacob has touched me." Then they consulted together about fighting Joseph—and they were people of strength who had no equals in that—but when Joseph sensed this, he rose to Rubil, seized him by his collar and threw him down. They saw from his strength what they regarded as great at that moment, and they said: "O Mighty one."

[p. 128] They addressed him by the title "al-ʿAzīz" (the Minister), since at that moment the former holder of the office had either been dismissed or died, as has been related on this point. Their saying, ﴿So take one of us in his place﴾, may be figurative, for they knew it was not valid to enslave a free man in exchange for someone whose enslavement the Sunna (the prophetic tradition) had made lawful. It is like saying to someone whose action you dislike: "Kill me and do not do such-and-such," when you do not actually want him to kill you, but are exaggerating in order to make him relent. On this reading, Yusuf's words, ﴿God forbid﴾, are apt, because it is seeking refuge from something that is not permissible. Alternatively, their saying, ﴿So take one of us in his place﴾, may be literal. It is unlikely of them, being prophets, that they would wish to enslave a free man. So the only remaining possibility is that they meant the arrangement of a surety (ḥamāla), that is: take one of us until your companion returns to you. Their aim in this was that Benjamin would reach his father and Jacob would learn the real state of affairs. Yusuf, peace be upon him, refused this, because a surety (ḥamāla, the guarantee of producing a person) in matters of the prescribed punishments (ḥudūd) and the like, meaning bringing forward the one guaranteed, is permissible by mutual agreement but is not binding if the claimant refuses. However, a surety in a case like this, under which the surety would bear the same punishment that the guaranteed person would bear, is not permissible, by consensus (ijmāʿ, the agreement of scholars). In al-Wāḍiḥa it is stated that a surety for the person alone, without bearing punishment, is permissible in all the ḥudūd except in cases involving life.

Their saying, ﴿For we see you to be among the good-doers﴾, may mean that they were describing him by what they had seen of his goodness in all his dealings with them and with others. It may also mean: "We see for you a kindness upon us in this matter, if you bestow it upon us." This is the interpretation of Ibn Isḥāq.

The word "maʿādh" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), and it is not permissible to state the verb along with it. The word "ẓulm" (wrongdoing) in his saying, ﴿Indeed we would then be wrongdoers﴾, is used in its literal sense, since it is placing a thing in other than its proper place. Al-Ṭabarī mentions that it is related that when Yusuf despaired them with this statement, he said to them: "When you come to your father, convey to him my greetings, and say to him: 'The king of Egypt prays for you that you do not die until you see your son Yusuf,' so that he may know that in the land of Egypt there are truthful people like him."

As for His, the Exalted's, saying, ﴿So when they despaired of him﴾, the verse continues. It is said: yaʾisa and istaʾsa (both forms of despair) have one meaning, just as it is said: sakhira and istaskhara (both forms of mock), and from this is His, the Exalted's, saying: "yastaskhirūn" (they mock). And just as it is said: ʿajiba and istaʿjaba (both forms of wonder). From this is the verse of Aws ibn Ḥajar: [p. 129]

*And one who marvels at what he sees of our forbearance,*
*Even if war had thrust him back, he would not have wavered.*

From this also: nawika and istanwaka (both forms of foolishness). On this basis, the verse of the poet in some interpretations comes:

"......................."
*And she grew foolish, though youth is foolishness.*

This is the reading of the majority. Ibn Kathīr read: "istāyasū" (they despaired), "lā tāyasū" (do not despair), "lā yāyas" (does not despair), and "ḥattā idhā istāyasa al-rusul" (until when the messengers despaired). Its origin is "istaʾyasū" in the pattern istafʿalū from "aʾisa," with the verb's root transposed from "yaʾisa" to "aʾisa." This is not like jadhaba and jabadha (both meaning to pull), for these are two original forms, while the first is a transposition. What shows this is that the verbal noun of "yaʾisa" and "aʾisa" is one and the same, namely "al-yaʾs," whereas jadhaba and jabadha have two verbal nouns.

His, the Exalted's, saying, ﴿they withdrew apart, conferring privately (najiyyan)﴾, means: they separated themselves from others, so that some of them were conferring privately with one another. The word "najiyy" is an adjective applied to someone who has a private conversation (najwā), whether one or many, masculine or feminine. It is like ʿadūw and ʿadl, and its plural is "anjiya." Labīd said:

*And I attended the secret councils of al-Afāqa, standing tall,*
*..........., my ankle, and the retinues of kings were witnesses.*

As for "their eldest" (kabīruhum), Mujāhid said: it is Shamʿūn, because he was their senior in opinion, management and knowledge, even though Ruʾbīl was the oldest of them in age. Qatāda said: it is Ruʾbīl, because he was the oldest of them. This is more apparent, and al-Ṭabarī preferred it. Al-Suddī said: the meaning of the verse is: "The eldest of them in knowledge said." Their brother reminded them of the covenant in Jacob's words: ﴿You shall surely bring him back to me, unless you are surrounded [by an overwhelming force]﴾ [Yūsuf: 66].

As for His saying, ﴿what you neglected﴾, the word "mā" may be a superfluous particle in the sentence with no place in its grammatical structure (iʿrāb). It may also be in the nominative position as the subject, with the predicate being His saying, ﴿concerning Yūsuf﴾. This is what Abū ʿAlī said. It is not permissible for His saying, ﴿from before﴾ [Yūsuf: 77] to be connected to ﴿what you neglected﴾. On this reading, it is verbal (maṣdariyya), and the implied meaning is: "From before your neglect concerning Yūsuf, [it] is established or fixed," and with this implied element the phrase ﴿from before﴾ [Yūsuf: 77] is connected. It may also be in the accusative position as a conjunction, on the basis that the implied meaning is: "and you know your neglect," or "and you know that which you neglected." On this latter reading it may mean "that which," and it may also be verbal.

As for His, the Exalted's, saying, ﴿then I will not leave the land﴾, he meant the territory and the place where the disliked matter befell him, which led to his father's anger. The intent behind this expression is to place a restriction upon himself and commit himself to confinement, as though he imprisoned himself in that region in order to establish an excuse.

As for his saying, ﴿or God judges for me﴾, it is a general expression covering everything that God might decree, such as death, or victory and attaining one's hope, and other things. Abū Ṣāliḥ said: "or God judges for me by the sword." "Yaḥkuma" is in the subjunctive by coordination with "yaʾdhana" (permits). "Aw" may also be in this position with the meaning of "illā an" (unless), as you say: "I will certainly hold you to it, or you pay me my right," so here "yaḥkuma" is in the subjunctive after "aw."
