On this reading, it is verbal (maṣdariyya), and the implied meaning is: "From before your neglect concerning Yūsuf, [it] is established or fixed," and with this implied element the phrase ﴿from before﴾ [Yūsuf: 77] is connected. It may also be in the accusative position as a conjunction, on the basis that the implied meaning is: "and you know your neglect," or "and you know that which you neglected." On this latter reading it may mean "that which," and it may also be verbal.

As for His, the Exalted's, saying, ﴿then I will not leave the land﴾, he meant the territory and the place where the disliked matter befell him, which led to his father's anger. The intent behind this expression is to place a restriction upon himself and commit himself to confinement, as though he imprisoned himself in that region in order to establish an excuse.

As for his saying, ﴿or God judges for me﴾, it is a general expression covering everything that God might decree, such as death, or victory and attaining one's hope, and other things. Abū Ṣāliḥ said: "or God judges for me by the sword." "Yaḥkuma" is in the subjunctive by coordination with "yaʾdhana" (permits). "Aw" may also be in this position with the meaning of "illā an" (unless), as you say: "I will certainly hold you to it, or you pay me my right," so here "yaḥkuma" is in the subjunctive after "aw."

It is related that when they reached Jacob, he wept and said: "My sons, every time you leave me, you lose something. You went and lost Yūsuf. Then you went and lost Shamʿūn when he was held as a pledge. Then you went and lost Benjamin and Ruʾbīl."

**Commentary of Ibn ʿAṭiyya (al-Muḥarrar al-Wajīz) on Sūrat Yūsuf, verses 81–83:**

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿Return to your father and say, "O our father, your son has stolen, and we bear witness only to what we know, and we were not guardians of the unseen."﴾ ﴿And ask the town in which we were, and the caravan in which we came, and indeed we are truthful.﴾ ﴿He said, "Rather, your souls have beautified for you a matter. So patience is beautiful. Perhaps Allah will bring them all to me. Indeed, He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise."﴾

The command to return: it is said that it came from the words of their eldest, and it is said that it was rather from the words of Yūsuf to them. The first is more apparent. Al-Jumhūr (the majority of reciters) read *sariqa* (سَرَقَ), affirming the theft as a fact regarding Yāmīn according to the apparent meaning of the matter. Ibn ʿAbbās and Abū Razīn read *suriqa* (سُرِّقَ), with a damma on the *sīn* and a kasra on the *rāʾ* and with shadda. It seems that this reading indicates conjecture on their part; they did not assert with certainty that he had committed theft, and they only meant: he was made a thief by what appeared of the circumstances. This reading is also narrated from al-Kisāʾī. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk read *inna ibnaka sāriqun* (إنَّ ابْنَكَ سارِقٌ), with an *alif* and tanwīn on the *qāf*. Then, according to both readings, they qualified their saying: ﴿and we bear witness only to what we know﴾, meaning: our saying to you, ﴿your son has stolen﴾, is only a testimony before you concerning what we know from the apparent course of events, while knowledge of the unseen belongs to Allah; we were not guardians of that. This is the saying of Ibn Isḥāq.

Ibn Zayd said: their saying ﴿and we bear witness only to what we know﴾ meant: we did not bear witness before Yūsuf that the thief is enslaved in your law except by what we knew of that, and ﴿we were not guardians of the unseen﴾ means that we did not know that theft would be taken from the baggage of one of us; rather we thought that this would never happen at all. So we bore witness before him, when we were asked, by our knowledge. Al-Ḥasan read *wa-mā shahidnā ʿalayhi illā bi-mā ʿalimnā* (وَما شَهِدْنا عَلَيْهِ إلّا بِما عَلِمْنا), with the addition of *ʿalayhi* (عَلَيْهِ).

His saying ﴿and we were not guardians of the unseen﴾ may mean: at the time we made a covenant with you, we only intended that nothing from us, from our side, would befall him that he disliked; we did not know the unseen, that he would come with what makes him a slave. It has also been narrated that *lil-ghayb* (لِلْغَيْبِ) means *lil-layl* (لِلَّيْلِ), i.e., "at night," and *al-ghayb* in the dialect of Ḥimyar means "the night." It is as if they said: we did not bear witness before you except by what we knew from the apparent state of his affairs, and we were not guardians at night of what might occur of his theft or of deception concerning him.

Then they called upon the people of the town in which they had been, which is Egypt. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and others. This is *majāz* (مَجاز, figurative usage), and what is meant is its people. Likewise His saying ﴿and the caravan﴾. This is the saying of the majority and it is the correct view. Abū al-Maʿālī, in *al-Talkhīṣ*, related from some of the theologians that he said: this is from *ḥadhf* (حَذْف, ellipsis) and not from *majāz*; *majāz* is rather a word borrowed for other than what it was meant for.

The judge Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The omission of the modifier (*ḥadhf al-muḍāf*) is itself the essence and substance of *majāz*. This is the view of Sībawayh and others among the people of reflection. Not every omission is *majāz*. Abū al-Maʿālī preferred in this verse that it is *majāz*, and he related that this is the saying of the majority, or something close to it. A group said: rather, they referred it to asking the inanimate objects and animals literally, and since he is a prophet, it is not far-fetched that they could inform him of the truth.

The judge Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Although this is permissible, it is far-fetched, and the first view is stronger.

Here there is an implied statement required by the apparent meaning, whose estimate is: when they said this statement to their father, he said: ﴿Rather, your souls have beautified﴾. This is on the basis that the speech of their eldest continues up to here. Whoever holds that the speech of their eldest ended at His saying ﴿your son has stolen﴾ makes the estimate there to be: when they returned, they said ﴿your son has stolen﴾, and so on to the end of the verse. The apparent meaning is that His saying ﴿Rather, your souls have beautified for you a matter﴾ is only a bad assumption about them, as was the case in the story of Yūsuf before. It so happened that his assumption was true there, but it was not confirmed here.

*Sawwalat* (سَوَّلَتْ) means: it adorned, it made appealing, and it made it a *sūl*. The *sūl* is what a person wishes for and is eager for.

His saying ﴿So patience is beautiful﴾ (فَصَبْرٌ جَمِيلٌ) is either an inceptive (*mubtadaʾ*) whose predicate is *amthal* (أمْثَلُ, "better") or *awlā* ("more fitting"). The inception with an indefinite noun is permissible since it is qualified. Or it is the predicate of an implied inceptive, whose estimate is: "so my affair is, or my matter is, or my patience is beautiful patience." This is more suitable for the indefinite noun to be a predicate. The meaning of describing it as *jamīl* (beautiful) is that there is no complaint in it to any human being and no impatience with the decree of Allah, the Exalted.

Then, peace be upon him, hoped from Allah that He would reunite them with him, and they were: Yūsuf, Yāmīn, and Rūbīl, who had not left the land. His hope had several aspects:

The first: the dream that Yūsuf had seen, for Yaʿqūb had been awaiting its fulfilment. The second: his good assumption of Allah, the Exalted, in every state. The third: what they had told him about the king of Egypt, that he would pray for him to see his son. Thus a sense of seeking and hope arose in him from here. The description with knowledge and wisdom is fitting for what he hoped for, namely meeting his sons. In it there is also submission to the wisdom of Allah, the Exalted, in everything that befell him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 12, verses 84–86:

God Almighty says:

﴿He turned away from them and said, "Alas for Joseph!" and his eyes turned white from grief, and he was suppressing it.﴾ ﴿They said, "By God, you will not stop remembering Joseph until you are wasted away or become among the dead."﴾ ﴿He said, "I only complain of my anguish and my grief to God, and I know from God what you do not know."﴾

The meaning: when his suspicion of them grew, and he did not believe their words but doubted them, ﴿He turned away from them﴾, that is, he turned his face away from them, and he began to lament and grieve. Al-Hasan said: "This nation was singled out for istirja' (saying "Surely we belong to God and to Him we return"). Do you not see the words of Ya'qub: ﴿Alas for Joseph!﴾?"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

What is meant is "Ya asafi" (O my grief), but this is the dialect of those who turn the ya' of the possessive pronoun into an alif, as in "ya abata" (O my father) and "ya ghulaman" (O boy). He called upon grief as if to mean: "Be present, for this is one of your times." It was also said: his words "Ya asafa" are in the manner of nudba (a lament for the dead, in which the speaker calls out to someone or something as though mourning it), and the omission of the ha' that belongs to the nudba is a sign of intensifying the grief, while showing self-control on his part, peace be upon him, since he had bound himself to patient perseverance (sabr jamil). It was also said: his words "Ya asafa" are a call containing an appeal for help.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

It is not far-fetched that both istirja' and "Ya asafa" may be combined for this nation and for Ya'qub, peace be upon him.

﴿And his eyes turned white from grief﴾: that is, from constant weeping, which is the fruit of grief. It is narrated that "Ya'qub, peace be upon him, grieved the grief of seventy bereaved mothers, and was given the reward of one hundred martyrs, and his suspicion of God never wavered," narrated by al-Hasan from the Prophet (ﷺ). Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid read "al-hazan" with a fatha on the ha' and the zay. Qatada read it with a damma on both. The majority read it with a damma on the ha' and a sukun on the zay.

﴿and he was suppressing it﴾ means kazim (one who suppresses), as He said: ﴿those who suppress their anger﴾ [Al 'Imran: 134]. He described Ya'qub with this because he did not complain to anyone; rather he would grieve inwardly and hold his distress in his chest. He would suppress it, meaning he would return it to his heart and not let it out in complaint, anger or distress. Some said: "kazim" means "makzum" (one who is suppressed). God Almighty described Yunus, peace be upon him, as makzum in His words: ﴿when he called out while he was makzum﴾ [al-Qalam: 48]. This only holds if one understands that he was filled with his grief, so it is as if he suppressed his anguish in his chest. The form "kazim" in the pattern of "kazim" is clearer. Some explained "al-kazim" as "distressed" and "troubled," and all of these are close in meaning. Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: asaf, when it comes from one who is less than a human being, is anger, and from this is God Almighty's saying: ﴿So when they angered Us, We took revenge on them﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 55]. From it is also the saying of the man whose sheep was taken from his servant: "I was angered (fa-asift) and slapped it." When it comes from something one cannot bear, it is distress and sorrow.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

The clarification of this point is that asaf is used for anger and is used for grief, and each of these two indicates the state in which it is said.

God Almighty's words ﴿They said, "By God, you will not stop"﴾, etc. The meaning: "By God, you will not stop," so the (la, "not") is omitted in this place of the oath, because the sense indicates it. Among this is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"I said, 'By God's oath, I will not cease sitting here, even if they cut off my head and my limbs before you.'"

From it is also the saying of another:

"By God, there remains through the days one with a horn, on a high rocky ledge where the mint and myrtle grow."

He intended: "he will not cease" and "he will not remain." Al-Zajjaji said: (ma) may also be omitted in this place, and some grammarians considered this an error. Among the places where (la) is omitted and the sense indicates it is the saying of a poet:

"So no, by the father of Dahma, her honour did not depart from her people as long as the striker strikes the tinder."

His saying "as long as the striker strikes the tinder" requires that what is omitted is (la), not (ma).

(Fati'a) has the same meaning and function as (zala) and (barih), meaning "to cease." You say: "By God, I will not cease sitting," just as you say: "I have not ceased and I have not stopped." From this is the saying of Aws ibn Hajar:

"It did not cease until its dust was like a pavilion on a windy day, raised high."

Al-Haras (ḥaraḍ) is one whom old age, love or grief has worn down to a state of decay in his limbs, body and senses. According to this meaning is the reading of the majority: "ḥarađan" with a fatha on the ra' and the ha'. al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan read it with damma on both. A group read it as "ḥurḍan" with a damma on the ha' and a sukun on the ra'. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 12, verse 87–88:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿O my sons, go and search for Joseph and his brother, and do not despair of relief from Allah. Indeed, none despairs of relief from Allah except the disbelieving people.﴾ ﴿So when they entered upon him, they said, "O Chieftain, adversity has touched us and our family, and we have come with goods of little value, so give us full measure and be charitable to us. Indeed, Allah rewards the charitable."﴾

The meaning: Go to the land from which you came and where you left your two brothers, Benjamin and Rubil. "Fa-tahassasu" means: seek out thoroughly and disperse. Tahassus is seeking a thing through the senses, and it is used for both good and evil. Its use for good is in this verse, and its use for evil is in the Prophet's ﷺ prohibition in his saying: "And do not spy (tahassasu)."

His saying: ﴿min Yusuf﴾ is connected to an omitted element that "tahassasu" governs. The estimate is: "so seek out news or the truth concerning the matter of Joseph," but what the apparent wording indicates is omitted for brevity.

One group read "tay'asu," another read "ta'ayasu" according to what preceded, and al-A'raj read "tiasu" with a kasra on the ta. Joseph and Benjamin were singled out for mention because Rubil remained as a chosen one, whereas these two had been prevented from returning.

Al-rawh means mercy. Then he made despair of Allah's mercy and relief from it a characteristic of the disbelievers, since it involves either denial of Lordship or ignorance of the attributes of Allah, blessed and exalted. Al-Hasan, Qatada and Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz read "min ruhi Allah" with a damma on the ra. The sense of this reading seems to be: "Do not despair of a living one in whom the spirit of Allah, which He bestowed, remains; for whoever's spirit remains, hope is kept for him." From this is the poet's saying:

"And in one other than the one the earth has covered, hope."

From this is also the saying of Ubayd:

"Every one absent returns, but the absence of death does not return."

It appears from the hadith of the man who said: "When I die, burn me, then grind me, then scatter me in the sea and on the land on a windy day. If Allah has power over me, let Him punish me with a punishment He has not inflicted on anyone among the worlds." that he despaired of Allah's relief. But this is not the case, because the Prophet's ﷺ saying at the end of the hadith, "So Allah forgave him," requires that he died a believer, since Allah does not forgive a disbeliever. So the hadith must be interpreted: either "qadara" means "constricted and scrutinized the reckoning," which is a clear meaning; or it is from "al-qudra" (power), and his error was in thinking that reassembly after being ground and scattered was impossible, not attributable to Allah's power, so he erred in making the possible impossible, and no disbelief follows from this for him.

Al-Naqqash said: Ibn Mas'ud read "min fadli," and Ubayy ibn Ka'b read "min rahmati Allah."

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿When they entered upon him﴾ and so on. In this place there is an ellipsis of omitted elements that the apparent text indicates: they passed from Syria to Egypt and reached it. The pronoun in "alayhi" refers to Joseph. By "al-durr" they meant the hunger they were in and the matter of their brother, which had worried their father and grieved them all. "Al-bidá'a" is a portion of wealth intended for buying something; it came to be used in the idiom of jurisprudence for what carries no profit for its bearer. "Al-muzjah" means: pushed, sought to be made acceptable. From it comes izjá' al-sahab (driving the clouds), and from it izjá' al-ibil (driving the camels), as the poet said:

"Over swift she-camels whose marrow is driven..."

And as al-Nabigha said:

"The wind blew from the direction of Dhi Urul, driving with the night from its cold a bitter gust..."

(p-141) And al-A'sha said:

"The giver of a hundred white camels and their slave, with young ones following their young..."

And another said:

"And a need not pushed away from the pilgrim..."

And Hatim said:

"Let there weep over Milhan a guest who is turned away, and a widow driving the night with a widow..."

The gist of this: whoever drives something and gently manages its movement has "azjahu." So when the dirhams given are of low value and need to be excused and interceded for, they are "muzjah." It was said: this was because they were counterfeit, said by Ibn Abbas; al-Hasan said: they were few; it was said: they were deficient, said by Ibn Jubayr; and it was said: their goods were merchandise, which is why they said this. There is disagreement about those goods: what were they? It was said: they were ghee and wool, said by Abdullah ibn al-Harith; Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: they were dried game meat, reported by al-Naqqash; Abu Salih and Zayd ibn Aslam said: they were pine nuts and the green seed.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

"And that is pistachio." It was said: they were doum-palm fruit; it was said: they were cotton; it was said: they were ropes, packs and saddle-pads. Makki related that Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "al-muzjah" means "the gift."

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

I do not know a basis for this, and the meaning rejects it. It is possible that it was a misreading of Malik's words, with the word spelled with an unpointed ha' and a ra'. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, based his view that the measuring is the seller's obligation on this verse; that is apparent from it, though it is not an explicit text.

Their saying: ﴿and be charitable to us﴾ means: by the difference between the good dirhams and this inferior payment, said by al-Suddi and others. It was said: charity was not forbidden for those prophets, and it was forbidden only for Muhammad ﷺ, said by Sufyan ibn Uyayna.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is weak, refuted by the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "We, the company of prophets, charity is not lawful for us."

A group said: charity was forbidden for them, but they said this as a figure of speech and a plea in the bargaining, as you say to one you are haggling with over goods: "Give me a discount of such-and-such and take such-and-such." You do not intend that he gift you, but you make his moving toward you appealing so that he returns with you to his offer. Ibn Jurayj said: they specified with their saying ﴿and be charitable to us﴾ the matter of their brother Yamin, that is: give us full measure in the sale, and be charitable to us by releasing our brother to his father.

Their saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah rewards the charitable.﴾ Al-Naqqash said: it is said that this is among the ambiguous expressions (ma'arid) that provide an alternative to lying. They used to think him a disbelieving king not of their religion; had they said, "Indeed, Allah will reward you for your charity in the Hereafter," they would have lied, so they said to him words that suggested he was their intended meaning, while they could validly exclude it through interpretation.

One group read "tay'asu," another read "ta'ayasu" according to what preceded, and al-A'raj read "tiasu" with a kasra on the ta. Joseph and Benjamin were singled out for mention because Rubil remained as a chosen one, whereas these two had been prevented from returning.

Al-rawh means mercy. Then he made despair of Allah's mercy and relief from it a characteristic of the disbelievers, since it involves either denial of Lordship or ignorance of the attributes of Allah, blessed and exalted. Al-Hasan, Qatada and Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz read "min ruhi Allah" with a damma on the ra. The sense of this reading seems to be: "Do not despair of a living one in whom the spirit of Allah, which He bestowed, remains; for whoever's spirit remains, hope is kept for him." From this is the poet's saying:

"And in one other than the one the earth has covered, hope."

From this is also the saying of Ubayd:

"Every one absent returns, but the absence of death does not return."

It appears from the hadith of the man who said: "When I die, burn me, then grind me, then scatter me in the sea and on the land on a windy day. If Allah has power over me, let Him punish me with a punishment He has not inflicted on anyone among the worlds." that he despaired of Allah's relief. But this is not the case, because the Prophet's ﷺ saying at the end of the hadith, "So Allah forgave him," requires that he died a believer, since Allah does not forgive a disbeliever. So the hadith must be interpreted: either "qadara" means "constricted and scrutinized the reckoning," which is a clear meaning; or it is from "al-qudra" (power), and his error was in thinking that reassembly after being ground and scattered was impossible, not attributable to Allah's power, so he erred in making the possible impossible, and no disbelief follows from this for him.

Al-Naqqash said: Ibn Mas'ud read "min fadli," and Ubayy ibn Ka'b read "min rahmati Allah."

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿When they entered upon him﴾ and so on. In this place there is an ellipsis of omitted elements that the apparent text indicates: they passed from Syria to Egypt and reached it. The pronoun in "alayhi" refers to Joseph. By "al-durr" they meant the hunger they were in and the matter of their brother, which had worried their father and grieved them all. "Al-bidá'a" is a portion of wealth intended for buying something; it came to be used in the idiom of jurisprudence for what carries no profit for its bearer. "Al-muzjah" means: pushed, sought to be made acceptable. From it comes izjá' al-sahab (driving the clouds), and from it izjá' al-ibil (driving the camels), as the poet said:

"Over swift she-camels whose marrow is driven..."

And as al-Nabigha said:

"The wind blew from the direction of Dhi Urul, driving with the night from its cold a bitter gust..."

(p-141) And al-A'sha said:

"The giver of a hundred white camels and their slave, with young ones following their young..."

And another said:

"And a need not pushed away from the pilgrim..."

And Hatim said:

"Let there weep over Milhan a guest who is turned away, and a widow driving the night with a widow..."

The gist of this: whoever drives something and gently manages its movement has "azjahu." So when the dirhams given are of low value and need to be excused and interceded for, they are "muzjah." It was said: this was because they were counterfeit, said by Ibn Abbas; al-Hasan said: they were few; it was said: they were deficient, said by Ibn Jubayr; and it was said: their goods were merchandise, which is why they said this. There is disagreement about those goods: what were they? It was said: they were ghee and wool, said by Abdullah ibn al-Harith; Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: they were dried game meat, reported by al-Naqqash; Abu Salih and Zayd ibn Aslam said: they were pine nuts and the green seed.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

"And that is pistachio." It was said: they were doum-palm fruit; it was said: they were cotton; it was said: they were ropes, packs and saddle-pads. Makki related that Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "al-muzjah" means "the gift."

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

I do not know a basis for this, and the meaning rejects it. It is possible that it was a misreading of Malik's words, with the word spelled with an unpointed ha' and a ra'. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, based his view that the measuring is the seller's obligation on this verse; that is apparent from it, though it is not an explicit text.

Their saying: ﴿and be charitable to us﴾ means: by the difference between the good dirhams and this inferior payment, said by al-Suddi and others. It was said: charity was not forbidden for those prophets, and it was forbidden only for Muhammad ﷺ, said by Sufyan ibn Uyayna.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is weak, refuted by the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "We, the company of prophets, charity is not lawful for us."

A group said: charity was forbidden for them, but they said this as a figure of speech and a plea in the bargaining, as you say to one you are haggling with over goods: "Give me a discount of such-and-such and take such-and-such." You do not intend that he gift you, but you make his moving toward you appealing so that he returns with you to his offer. Ibn Jurayj said: they specified with their saying ﴿and be charitable to us﴾ the matter of their brother Yamin, that is: give us full measure in the sale, and be charitable to us by releasing our brother to his father.

Their saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah rewards the charitable.﴾ Al-Naqqash said: it is said that this is among the ambiguous expressions (ma'arid) that provide an alternative to lying. They used to think him a disbelieving king not of their religion; had they said, "Indeed, Allah will reward you for your charity in the Hereafter," they would have lied, so they said to him words that suggested he was their intended meaning, while they could validly exclude it through interpretation.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 12, verses 89–92:

The words of the Exalted:

﴿He said, "Do you know what you did with Joseph and his brother when you were ignorant?"﴾ ﴿They said, "Are you indeed Joseph?" He said, "I am Joseph, and this is my brother. Allah has truly been gracious to us. Indeed, whoever fears Allah and is patient, then indeed Allah does not allow the reward of the good-doers to be lost."﴾ ﴿They said, "By Allah, Allah has certainly preferred you over us, and we were indeed sinners."﴾ ﴿He said, "No reproach will be upon you today. Allah will forgive you, and He is the Most Merciful of the merciful."﴾

It is narrated that when Joseph, peace be upon him, was told by his brothers, ﴿Adversity has touched us and our family﴾ [Yusuf: 88], and they sought his pity, he was moved and had mercy on them. Ibn Ishaq said: His tears welled up and he began weeping, and then he set about revealing his matter to them. It is narrated that he uncovered his face and said to them, ﴿Do you know...﴾, the verse.

His words ﴿what you did with Joseph and his brother﴾ mean: [the acts of] separating the two of them in childhood, causing them harm, and mistreating Yamin after Joseph's disappearance, for they used to humiliate him and revile him. He did not refer to the later affair of Yamin, because they had done nothing to him in it. He attributed their deed either to ignorance of sin, or to the ignorance of youth and lack of experience (ḥinka). When he addressed them with this address, and it is likely that accompanying it were his bearing, his countenance and his smile, which indicated to them [who he was], they came to their senses, and a strong conviction arose in them that he was Joseph. So they addressed him with a question of confirmation (istifhām taqrīr), i.e., a question intended to establish a fact.

A group read ﴿Are you indeed Joseph﴾ (Arabic: أإنَّكَ لأنْتَ يُوسُفُ) with the two hamzas pronounced fully (taḥqīq). Another group read with an alif inserted between two hamzas and both pronounced fully: "āinnaka". Another group read with the second hamza eased (tashīl): "ainnaka". Ibn Muḥaysin, Qatada and Ibn Kathir read "innaka" as a declarative statement with emphasis. Ubayy ibn Ka'b read "a-innaka aw anta Yūsuf" (أئِنَّكَ أو أنْتَ يُوسُفُ). Abu al-Fath said: This should be understood as the omission of the predicate of "inna", as if he had said: "Are you indeed other than Joseph, or are you Joseph?"

Abu 'Amr al-Dani relates that in the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b it is: "aw anta Yūsuf". A group among those who read "innaka" interpreted it as an interrogative with the interrogative particle dropped, and Joseph answered them, disclosing his matter, saying, ﴿I am Joseph, and this is my brother﴾. Mujahid said: He meant: whoever fears [Allah] by abandoning sin and is patient in prison. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: whoever fears fornication and is patient in celibacy.

The author, Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The intended meaning of the wording is in fact generality concerning great matters. These two (Mujahid and al-Nakha'i) only specified because these were among the calamities that befell him. Had we supposed that other calamities had befallen him, he would have feared [Allah] and been patient.

The majority read "yattaqi" without a yā' (يَتَّقِ). Ibn Kathir alone read "yattaqī" with the yā' affirmed (يَتَّقِي). Its explanation has been disputed. It is said: he treated the yā' as vowelled and made the jussive (jazm) by dropping the vowel, as the poet said:

Did it not come to you, while news spreads, of what the she-camel of the Banu Ziyad suffered?

Abu 'Ali said: This is something we do not attribute to it, because it occurs in poetry, not in ordinary speech. It has also been said: "man" (مَن) is in the sense of "alladhī" (the one who), and "yattaqi" is a nominative verb, and "yaṣbir" is conjoined to the meaning, because "man", although in the sense of "alladhī", contains the meaning of a condition, and similar to it is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿so I would give charity and be among the righteous﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 10]. It has also been said that he intended "yaṣbiru" in the nominative, but he made the rā' quiescent for lightness, just as Abu 'Amr read "wa-yamrukum" (وَيَأْمُرْكُمْ) with a quiescent rā'.

His words, the Exalted: ﴿They said, "By Allah, Allah has certainly preferred you over us"﴾, the verse. This is from them a means of gaining his favour, and within it is an acknowledgement of sin, and in it is an implicit plea for forgiveness from him. The word "āthara" (آثَرَ) encompasses all preference and kinds of gifts. Its origin contains two hamzas, and the second is eased; it is not permissible to pronounce it fully. The verbal noun is "īthār" (إيثار).

"Khāṭi'īn" (خاطِئِينَ) comes from "khaṭi'a yakhṭa'u", and it denotes one who deliberately errs. The "mukhṭi'" (مُخْطِئ) is from "akhṭa'a", and it denotes one who intended the correct thing but was not granted success in it. From this is the saying of the poet, who is Umayya ibn al-Askar:

And two emigrants who surrounded him, on the morning of the morrow, indeed they erred and failed.

His words, ﴿No reproach will be upon you﴾, are a gracious pardon. Ikrima said: Allah revealed to Joseph: "By your pardoning your brothers, I have raised your remembrance."

It is related in a hadith that when Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith and Abdullah ibn Abi Umayya came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) as emigrants, he turned away from them because of the ugliness of their earlier conduct towards him. This grieved them, and they went to Abu Bakr and asked him to intercede, but he refused. They went to Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, and he did likewise. So Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith went to his cousin Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, and Abdullah went to his sister Umm Salama. Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "The opinion is that you should meet the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at the gathering and cry out to him: 'By Allah, Allah has certainly preferred you over us, and we were indeed sinners.' For he will not be pleased to be [treated] below any of the prophets, so he is bound to say: 'No reproach will be upon you both.'" So they did that, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to them: ﴿No reproach will be upon you﴾, the verse.

Al-tathrīb (التثريب) means blame, punishment, and what accompanied them of bad belief or the like. Some people have rendered "tathrīb" as "ta'yīr" (reproach). From it is the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "If the slave-girl of one of you commits fornication, let him flog her and not reproach her (yuthrib)," meaning: let him not reproach her. It was recorded by the two Shaykhs in the chapter on the ḥudūd (legal punishments).

Some reciters paused at ﴿upon you﴾ (عَلَيْكُمْ) and began with ﴿today Allah will forgive you﴾, while most of them paused at ﴿today﴾ (الْيَوْمَ) and began with ﴿Allah will forgive you﴾ as a supplication. This is the interpretation of Ibn Ishaq and al-Tabari, and it is the correct one. "Al-yawm" (today) is an adverb of time (ẓarf), and according to this, the governing element for it is what is attached to "'alaykum", its estimation being: "No reproach is established or settled upon you today." This pause is more preferable in meaning, because the other reading contains a judgement on the forgiveness of Allah, except if that were by revelation.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 12, verses 89–92:

The words of the Exalted:

﴿He said, "Do you know what you did with Joseph and his brother when you were ignorant?"﴾ ﴿They said, "Are you indeed Joseph?" He said, "I am Joseph, and this is my brother. Allah has truly been gracious to us. Indeed, whoever fears Allah and is patient, then indeed Allah does not allow the reward of the good-doers to be lost."﴾ ﴿They said, "By Allah, Allah has certainly preferred you over us, and we were indeed sinners."﴾ ﴿He said, "No reproach will be upon you today. Allah will forgive you, and He is the Most Merciful of the merciful."﴾

It is narrated that when Joseph, peace be upon him, was told by his brothers, ﴿Adversity has touched us and our family﴾ [Yusuf: 88], and they sought his pity, he was moved and had mercy on them. Ibn Ishaq said: His tears welled up and he began weeping, and then he set about revealing his matter to them. It is narrated that he uncovered his face and said to them, ﴿Do you know...﴾, the verse.

His words ﴿what you did with Joseph and his brother﴾ mean: [the acts of] separating the two of them in childhood, causing them harm, and mistreating Yamin after Joseph's disappearance, for they used to humiliate him and revile him. He did not refer to the later affair of Yamin, because they had done nothing to him in it. He attributed their deed either to ignorance of sin, or to the ignorance of youth and lack of experience (ḥinka). When he addressed them with this address, and it is likely that accompanying it were his bearing, his countenance and his smile, which indicated to them [who he was], they came to their senses, and a strong conviction arose in them that he was Joseph. So they addressed him with a question of confirmation (istifhām taqrīr), i.e., a question intended to establish a fact.

A group read ﴿Are you indeed Joseph﴾ (Arabic: أإنَّكَ لأنْتَ يُوسُفُ) with the two hamzas pronounced fully (taḥqīq). Another group read with an alif inserted between two hamzas and both pronounced fully: "āinnaka". Another group read with the second hamza eased (tashīl): "ainnaka". Ibn Muḥaysin, Qatada and Ibn Kathir read "innaka" as a declarative statement with emphasis. Ubayy ibn Ka'b read "a-innaka aw anta Yūsuf" (أئِنَّكَ أو أنْتَ يُوسُفُ). Abu al-Fath said: This should be understood as the omission of the predicate of "inna", as if he had said: "Are you indeed other than Joseph, or are you Joseph?"

Abu 'Amr al-Dani relates that in the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b it is: "aw anta Yūsuf". A group among those who read "innaka" interpreted it as an interrogative with the interrogative particle dropped, and Joseph answered them, disclosing his matter, saying, ﴿I am Joseph, and this is my brother﴾. Mujahid said: He meant: whoever fears [Allah] by abandoning sin and is patient in prison. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: whoever fears fornication and is patient in celibacy.

The author, Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The intended meaning of the wording is in fact generality concerning great matters. These two (Mujahid and al-Nakha'i) only specified because these were among the calamities that befell him. Had we supposed that other calamities had befallen him, he would have feared [Allah] and been patient.

The majority read "yattaqi" without a yā' (يَتَّقِ). Ibn Kathir alone read "yattaqī" with the yā' affirmed (يَتَّقِي). Its explanation has been disputed. It is said: he treated the yā' as vowelled and made the jussive (jazm) by dropping the vowel, as the poet said:

Did it not come to you, while news spreads, of what the she-camel of the Banu Ziyad suffered?

Abu 'Ali said: This is something we do not attribute to it, because it occurs in poetry, not in ordinary speech. It has also been said: "man" (مَن) is in the sense of "alladhī" (the one who), and "yattaqi" is a nominative verb, and "yaṣbir" is conjoined to the meaning, because "man", although in the sense of "alladhī", contains the meaning of a condition, and similar to it is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿so I would give charity and be among the righteous﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 10]. It has also been said that he intended "yaṣbiru" in the nominative, but he made the rā' quiescent for lightness, just as Abu 'Amr read "wa-yamrukum" (وَيَأْمُرْكُمْ) with a quiescent rā'.

His words, the Exalted: ﴿They said, "By Allah, Allah has certainly preferred you over us"﴾, the verse. This is from them a means of gaining his favour, and within it is an acknowledgement of sin, and in it is an implicit plea for forgiveness from him. The word "āthara" (آثَرَ) encompasses all preference and kinds of gifts. Its origin contains two hamzas, and the second is eased; it is not permissible to pronounce it fully. The verbal noun is "īthār" (إيثار).

"Khāṭi'īn" (خاطِئِينَ) comes from "khaṭi'a yakhṭa'u", and it denotes one who deliberately errs. The "mukhṭi'" (مُخْطِئ) is from "akhṭa'a", and it denotes one who intended the correct thing but was not granted success in it. From this is the saying of the poet, who is Umayya ibn al-Askar:

And two emigrants who surrounded him, on the morning of the morrow, indeed they erred and failed.

His words, ﴿No reproach will be upon you﴾, are a gracious pardon. Ikrima said: Allah revealed to Joseph: "By your pardoning your brothers, I have raised your remembrance."

It is related in a hadith that when Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith and Abdullah ibn Abi Umayya came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) as emigrants, he turned away from them because of the ugliness of their earlier conduct towards him. This grieved them, and they went to Abu Bakr and asked him to intercede, but he refused. They went to Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, and he did likewise. So Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith went to his cousin Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, and Abdullah went to his sister Umm Salama. **Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 12, verses 96–100:**

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Then when the bearer of good tidings came, he cast it over his face, and he regained his sight. He said: "Did I not tell you that I know from Allah what you do not know?"﴾ ﴿They said: "O our father, ask forgiveness for us for our sins. Indeed, we have been sinners."﴾ ﴿He said: "I will ask my Lord to forgive you. Indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful."﴾ ﴿Then when they entered upon Yusuf, he took his parents to himself and said: "Enter Egypt, if Allah wills, in security."﴾ ﴿And he raised his parents upon the throne, and they fell down before him in prostration.﴾

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that the bearer of good tidings was Yahudha (Judah), because he had been the one who brought the shirt stained with blood.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

My father, may Allah be pleased with him, related to me, saying: I heard the preacher Abu al-Fadl ibn al-Jawhari, from the pulpit in Egypt, saying: When Yusuf, peace be upon him, said: ﴿Take this shirt of mine and cast it over the face of my father﴾ [Yusuf: 93], Yahudha said: "You know that I went to him with the shirt of grief, so let me go to him with the shirt of joy." So they left him to that. Al-Suddi also said this meaning.

"Irtadda" means: he returned himself; it is said "irtadda al-rajul" and "raddahu ghayruhu" (another returned him). "Basiran" means: seeing. Then he made them stand upon his statement to them: ﴿Indeed, I know from Allah what you do not know﴾. This, Allah knows best, is his awaiting the interpretation (ta'wil) of the dream, and it is possible that he was indicating only his good opinion of Allah, the Exalted. It is also narrated that he said to the bearer of good tidings: "On what religion did you leave Yusuf?" He said: "On Islam." He said: "Praise be to Allah, now the blessing is complete." In the Mushaf of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, it reads: "Then when the bearer of good tidings came from between the hands of the caravan." Al-Tabari related from some grammarians that he said: the "an" in His saying ﴿Then when the bearer of good tidings came﴾ is superfluous (za'ida), and the Arabs sometimes add it in speech after "lamma" (when) and after "hatta" (until) only. Here there are omitted elements that the apparent text indicates, which are: so Ya'qub set out with his entire family, and they traveled until they reached Yusuf, then when they entered upon him. "Awa" means: he gathered them to himself and showed honor and welcome to them both. In the hadith: "As for one of them, he took refuge with Allah, and Allah sheltered him." It was said: by the two parents he meant his father and his mother, as Ibn Ishaq and al-Hasan said. Some of them said: his father and his grandmother, the mother of his mother; this was related by al-Zahrawi. It was also said: his father and his maternal aunt, because his mother had already died; this was said by al-Suddi.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The first is more apparent according to the wording, unless it is established by a sound chain that his mother had died. In the Mushaf of Ibn Mas'ud it reads: "He took to himself his two parents and his brothers."

And His saying: ﴿Enter Egypt﴾ means: settle, dwell, and remain. For they had already entered upon him. It was also said: rather, he said that to them on the road when he met them; this was said by al-Suddi. This exception (istithna', "if Allah wills") is what the Qur'an urges a person to say about everything he will do in the future by his saying. Ibn Jurayj said: this is postponed in wording but connected in meaning to His saying: ﴿I will ask my Lord to forgive you﴾.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In this interpretation there is weakness.

"Al-'arsh" is the throne of a king, and everything that is roofed is called "arish" and "'arsh," but the language has specified "'arsh" for the throne of a king. "Kharru" means: they inclined toward the ground. Scholars differed about this prostration: it was said that it was like the familiar placing of the face on the ground among us; and it was said: rather it was less than that, like a deep bow and the like, which was the manner of greeting kings in that time. The exegetes agreed that this prostration, in whatever form it took, was a greeting and not worship. Qatada said: this was the greeting of kings among them, and Allah gave this nation the salam (peace) as the greeting of the people of Paradise. Al-Hasan said: the pronoun in "lahu" refers to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. This view was rejected.

Al-Tabari related that when Ya'qub reached Egypt in his company, Yusuf, peace be upon him, asked Pharaoh to receive him; so he went out to him, and the kings went out with him. When Yusuf drew near to Ya'qub – and Ya'qub was walking leaning on Yahudha – Ya'qub looked at the horses and the people and said: "O Yahudha, is this the Pharaoh of Egypt?" He said: "No, it is your son." When each of them drew near the other, Yusuf went to begin with the greeting, but Ya'qub prevented him from that, and Ya'qub had more right to it and was superior to him. He said: "Peace be upon you, O remover of sorrows."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

And similar to this are some of the stories.

At this time Yusuf said to Ya'qub: "Indeed Pharaoh has been good to us, so enter upon him thankfully." He entered upon him, and Pharaoh said: "O shaykh, what has changed you to what I see?" He said: "The successive afflictions upon me." He said: Then his foot did not move until revelation descended: "O Ya'qub, do you complain to one who neither harms you nor benefits you?" He said: "O Lord, it is a sin, so forgive it." Abu 'Amr al-Shaybani said: Yusuf went ahead of Ya'qub in walking in some of those places, and Jibril descended and said to him: "Do you go ahead of your father? Your punishment for that is that no prophet will emerge from your offspring."

**

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And he said: "O my father, this is the interpretation of my dream from before. My Lord has made it true, and He was kind to me when He brought me out of the prison and brought you from the desert after Satan had stirred discord between me and my brothers. Indeed, my Lord is Subtle in what He wills. Indeed, He is the Knowing, the Wise."﴾

The meaning: Yusuf said to Ya'qub: this prostration that you performed is what my dream from long ago has come to, regarding the eleven stars and the sun and the moon.

And His saying: ﴿My Lord has made it true﴾ is the beginning of enumerating the blessings of Allah, the Exalted, upon him. And His saying: ﴿and He was kind to me (wa qad ahsana bi)﴾ means: He caused His kindness to befall me and attached it to me. This is one way of expressing the arrival of kindness with "bi" (in/to me). It may also be said "ahsana ilayya" and "ahsana fiyya," and from this is the saying of Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul: "O Muhammad, be kind to my clients (mawali)." These ways differ in meaning, and the most fitting of them for Yusuf is his saying "bi" (to me), because it is a kindness that came to him without his intending the end it reached.

Yusuf mentioned his being brought out of the prison and left out his being brought out of the well, for two reasons:

The first: mentioning his being brought out of the well would renew the deed of his brothers and their shame by it, and stir up their rancor, rouse those mischiefs, and corrupt their souls.

The second: he went out of the well into slavery, and out of the prison into kingship, so the blessing here is clearer.

His saying: ﴿and brought you from the desert﴾ encompasses the gathering of the family and the transition from wretchedness to blessing by settling in a town. Ya'qub's dwelling was on the outskirts of al-Sham, in the desert of Palestine, and he was the owner of camels, sheep, and desert life.

"Nazagha" means: he did an act by which he caused corruption, and from it is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Let none of you point at his brother with a weapon, for Satan may stir (yanzagh) in his hand." Yusuf mentioned only this much of his brothers' affair in order to clarify the excellent placement of blessings, because when a blessing comes after hardship and trial, its place is more beautiful.

His saying: ﴿Subtle in what He wills﴾ means: among the matters, what He wills to do.

People differed about: how long was between Yusuf's dream and its manifestation? One group said: forty years; this is the saying of Salman al-Farisi and Abdullah ibn Shaddad, and Abdullah ibn Shaddad said: that is the longest a dream has been delayed. Another group, among them al-Hasan, Hasan ibn Faraqad, and Fudayl ibn 'Iyad, said: eighty years. Ibn Ishaq said: eighteen. It was said: twenty-two; this was said by al-Naqqash. It was said: thirty. It was said: thirty-five; this was said by Qatada. al-Suddi and Ibn Jubayr said: thirty-six years. It was also said that Yusuf, peace be upon him, lived one hundred and twenty years, and it was said that Ya'qub remained with Yusuf more than twenty years, then he died ﷺ.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

There is no reason for leaving Yusuf's informing his father of his condition from the time he left the prison to the position of honor, except the revelation from Allah, the Exalted, when He wished to test Ya'qub and his sons, and wished the form of their gathering. There is no god but He. Al-Naqqash said: that revelation was in the well, and it is His saying, Exalted: ﴿And We revealed to him: you will surely inform them of this affair of theirs while they do not perceive﴾ [Yusuf: 15], and this is possible.

Among what is related in the reports about Ya'qub, peace be upon him: al-Hasan said: When the bearer of good tidings reached him, he found nothing with which to reward him, so he said to him: "By Allah, we have found nothing with us, and we have not baked bread for seven nights; but may Allah ease for you the agonies of death." Among his reports is that when his trial grew severe, he said: "O Lord, You have blinded my sight and kept Yusuf away from me; will You not have mercy on me?" Allah revealed to him: "I will have mercy on you and return to you your son and your sight. I did not punish you with this except that you cooked a lamb in your house, and a neighbor of yours smelled it, and you did not give him a share of it." He said: So after that Ya'qub would invite him to his lunch and dinner. Al-Tabari related that when his household was reunited, his sons asked him to pray to Allah for them until revelation came that Allah had forgiven them. He said: So Ya'qub would pray while Yusuf was behind him and they were behind Yusuf, and he would supplicate for them. He remained so for twenty years, then revelation came to him: "Indeed I have forgiven them, and I have given them the covenants of prophethood after you."

Among his reports is that when death came to him, he bequeathed to Yusuf that he should bury him in al-Sham. When he died, Yusuf embalmed him with myrrh and carried him to al-Sham. Then Yusuf died and was buried in Egypt. When Musa, peace be upon him, afterward left the land of Egypt, he carried the bones of Yusuf until he buried them in al-Sham with his forefathers.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 12, verses 101–102:**

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿My Lord, You have given me of the kingdom and taught me of the interpretation of events (ta'wil al-ahadith), Originator of the heavens and the earth. You are my Guardian in this world and the Hereafter. Cause me to die in submission (Muslim), and join me with the righteous.﴾ ﴿That is from the news of the unseen which We reveal to you. You were not with them when they agreed upon their plan while they were scheming.﴾

Ibn Mas'ud read "آتَيْتَنِ" and "عَلَّمْتَنِ" with the ya' omitted, for lightening (al-takhfif). Ibn Dharr alone read "رَبِّ آتَيْتَنِي" without "قَدْ".

Many of the commentators (mufassirun) mentioned that when Yusuf (peace be upon him) enumerated in this verse the blessings of God upon him, he longed to meet his Lord, and to meet the eminent among the righteous of his predecessors and others among the believers. He saw that the whole of this world was [p. 156] scant, so he wished for death in his saying: ﴿Cause me to die in submission, and join me with the righteous.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: "No prophet wished for death except Yusuf."

Al-Mahdawi mentioned another interpretation, which in my view is the strongest: that there is no wish for death in the verse. Rather, Yusuf (peace be upon him) enumerated the blessings of God upon him, then prayed that God complete these blessings upon him for the rest of his life. That is: "Cause me to die upon Islam when my appointed time arrives, and make my joining be with the righteous." He only wished for being brought to die upon Islam, not for death itself.

It has been related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Let none of you wish for death because of a harm that has befallen him..." – the hadith in its entirety. And it is related from him (ﷺ), in some of his supplications: "And if You intend a trial for the people, then take me to You without being tried." It is also related from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab that he said: "O God, my bones have grown weak, and my desire has spread; so cause me to die without being negligent or incapable."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

It seems that the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ), "because of a harm that has befallen him," refers only to the harms of this world, such as poverty, sickness, and the like. The wish for death out of fear of the corruption of religion remains permissible. What indicates this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "There will come a time upon the people when a man will pass by the grave of another man and say: 'Would that I were in his place,' not because of religion, but because of the afflictions and trials he sees." His saying "not because of religion" implies the permissibility of that wish if it were on account of religion. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was only describing how the condition of people will be.

As for His saying: ﴿You have given me of the kingdom﴾, it has been said that "min" here is partitive (lil-tab'id), and it has been said that it is for specifying the kind (li-bayan al-jins). The same applies to His saying: ﴿of the interpretation of events﴾. What is meant by "al-ahadith" [events] is dreams, and it has been said: the stories of the prophets and nations.

As for "Fatir" (Originator), it is a vocative (munada). His saying ﴿You are my Guardian﴾ means: the one who manages my affairs, the one who undertakes to support me and show me mercy.

As for the saying of the Exalted: ﴿That is from the news of the unseen﴾ and the verse that follows: "That" refers to what preceded of the story of Yusuf. This verse is an allusion to the Quraysh and a reminder of the sign of the truthfulness of Muhammad (ﷺ), and within this is a rebuke to his deniers. The pronoun in "ladayhim" refers to the brothers of Yusuf, and likewise the pronouns up to the end of the verse. "Ajma'u" means: they resolved and determined. "Al-amr" here is the casting of Yusuf into the well. "Al-makr" (scheming) is to plot against a person a plan that harms and injures him. "Al-khada'ah" (deception) is to do something to a person and say to him what makes him do an action that is harmful to himself.

Al-Tabari related from Abu 'Imran al-Jawni that he said: "By God, God did not relate their story in order to shame them. They were prophets from among the people of Paradise. Rather, God related their story to us so that His servants would not despair."

(p. 158) These two verses indicate that the verse preceding them contains an allusion to the Quraysh and to Muhammad's contemporaries. It is as if He said: your reporting of the unseen is a clear proof of your prophethood, but most people do not believe, even though you are eager for their faith. That is, only those whom Allah wills believe. His saying ﴿and however eager you are﴾ is a fluent interjection (i'tiraḍ, a parenthetical clause inserted between parts of a sentence).

His saying ﴿And you do not ask them for any wage﴾ up to the end of the verse is a rebuke of the disbelievers and an establishment of proof against them. That is, how foolish they are, in that you call them to Allah without seeking any wage from them, so that someone might say: you call them because of a wage. Mubashshir ibn 'Ubayd read ﴿وَما نَسْألُهُمْ﴾ ("and We do not ask them") with the letter nun.

Then Allah, blessed and exalted, began to inform that His Mighty Book is a reminder and an admonition for all the worlds. May Allah benefit us by it and enlarge our share of it through His might.

The majority read ﴿وَكَأيِّنْ﴾ (wa-ka'ayyin) with a hamza on the alif and a shadda on the ya'. Sibawayh said: it is the kaf of comparison joined to ʾayy, and its meaning is the same as "kam" (how many) in expressing abundance. Ibn Kathir read ﴿وَكائِنْ﴾ (wa-ka'in) with a long alif and a hamza on the ya', which is from the active participle of "kāna" (to be), so it is kā'in; yet its meaning is also "kam". The full range of recitations of this word has already been discussed under His saying ﴿وَكَأيِّنْ مِن نَبِيٍّ قاتَلَ﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 146].

The word "āya" (sign) here means the created things set up as lessons, and the events that point to Allah, glorified is He, in His creations. The meaning of ﴿يَمُرُّونَ عَلَيْها﴾ ("they pass by it") is: when something of them comes that is perceived or known in general, the disbeliever is not admonished by it, does not reflect upon it, and does not take lesson from it, according to his desires and his blindness. Therefore he is, in this respect, like one who turns away. A similar meaning is in the words of the poet:

"The breeze passes gently by the dweller of Dhi al-Ghada,
and my heart is split by its blowing."

al-Suddi read ﴿وَالأرْضَ﴾ ("and the earth") in the accusative, by supposing a verb, and in this reading the pause is at "al-samawāt". ʿIkrima and ʿAmr ibn Fā'id read ﴿وَالأرْضُ﴾ in the nominative as a beginning (mubtada'), with the predicate being His saying ﴿يَمُرُّونَ﴾. In the reading with the genitive ﴿الأرْضِ﴾, then ﴿يَمُرُّونَ﴾ is a qualifier of ﴿آيَةٍ﴾. In the Mushaf of ʿAbdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) it is: ﴿والأرْضِ يَمْشُونَ عَلَيْها﴾ ("and the earth, they walk upon it").

His saying ﴿وَما يُؤْمِنُ أكْثَرُهُمْ﴾ ("and most of them do not believe") up to the end of the verse. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it concerns the People of the Book, who believe in Allah and then associate partners with Him in that they disbelieve in His Prophet, or in that they say: ʿUzayr is the son of Allah, and the Messiah is the son of Allah. ʿIkrima, Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Zayd said: it concerns the disbelieving Arabs, and their belief is their acknowledgment of the Creator, the Provider, and the One who causes death; He named it belief even though it was followed by their associating idols and images with Him. Thus this belief is merely linguistic, in the sense that it is a certain kind of assent. It was also said: this verse was revealed because of the words of the Quraysh in the circumambulation and the talbiya (the invocation): "Here I am, O Allah, there is no partner for You, except a partner who is Yours, You own him and what he owns." And it is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ), whenever he heard one of them say "There is no partner for You," would say to him: "Qat, qat" (Enough, enough), meaning: stop here and do not add "except a partner who is Yours."

Al-ghāshiya is that which covers, overspreads and overwhelms. Abu Hafs and Bishr ibn ʿUbayd read ﴿أو يَأْتِيَهُمُ الساعَةُ بَغْتَةً﴾ with the letter ya' (so the verb is "yaʾtiyahum", with the subject being the Hour). Baghta means suddenly, unexpectedly, and that is harder.

Although this verse, beginning with His saying ﴿وَكَأيِّنْ﴾, concerns the disbelievers by the ruling of what precedes it, sinners also take a share of its wording. Belief is in reality (haqīqa), while associating partners is linguistic, like ostentation (riyā'). The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Ostentation is the lesser association (shirk al-asghar)."

His exalted saying ﴿قُلْ هَذِهِ سَبِيلِي﴾ ("Say: This is my way") up to the end of the verse is an indication of the call of Islam and the entire Sharia. Ibn Zayd said: the meaning is: this is my command, my sunna and my method. Ibn Mas'ud read ﴿قُلْ هَذا سَبِيلِي﴾. The sabīl is the path, and it may be feminine or masculine, and likewise al-ṭarīq (the road).

(p. 160) Al-baṣīra is a name for a person's belief regarding a matter, of truth and certainty. Al-baṣīra also, in the language of the Arabs, means the line of blood on a blade. In the well-known hadith: "You look at the blade and see no trace (baṣīra)." Some people interpreted with this meaning the verse of al-Ashʿar al-Ju'fi:

"They went with their traces (baṣā'irahum) upon their shoulders,
and my trace (baṣīrati) runs upon it, a swift and sure horse."

He describes a people who sold the blood of their protector, so it is as if his blood left lines upon their shoulders, since they were marked among people by the selling of that blood.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is also permissible that al-baṣīra in the verse of the poet refers to the correct belief, meaning: they made their belief the seeking of the fire, and their insight regarding that they put behind their backs, just as you say: so-and-so cast my affair behind his back.

His saying ﴿أنا ومَنِ اتَّبَعَنِي﴾ ("I and whoever follows me") may be an emphasis of the pronoun in "adʿū" (I call), and it may be that the whole verse is an enjoiner of good and a caller to Allah, to the disbelievers in Him and to the sinners. ﴿سُبْحانَ اللهِ﴾ ("Glory be to Allah") is a declaration of Allah's transcendence, that is: and say "Glory be to Allah," and say it disassociating yourself from polytheism.

It is narrated that this verse, ﴿قُلْ هَذِهِ سَبِيلِي﴾ up to its end, was inscribed on the banners of Yusuf, peace be upon him.
