That is, how foolish they are, in that you call them to Allah without seeking any wage from them, so that someone might say: you call them because of a wage. Mubashshir ibn 'Ubayd read ﴿وَما نَسْألُهُمْ﴾ ("and We do not ask them") with the letter nun.

Then Allah, blessed and exalted, began to inform that His Mighty Book is a reminder and an admonition for all the worlds. May Allah benefit us by it and enlarge our share of it through His might.

The majority read ﴿وَكَأيِّنْ﴾ (wa-ka'ayyin) with a hamza on the alif and a shadda on the ya'. Sibawayh said: it is the kaf of comparison joined to ʾayy, and its meaning is the same as "kam" (how many) in expressing abundance. Ibn Kathir read ﴿وَكائِنْ﴾ (wa-ka'in) with a long alif and a hamza on the ya', which is from the active participle of "kāna" (to be), so it is kā'in; yet its meaning is also "kam". The full range of recitations of this word has already been discussed under His saying ﴿وَكَأيِّنْ مِن نَبِيٍّ قاتَلَ﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 146].

The word "āya" (sign) here means the created things set up as lessons, and the events that point to Allah, glorified is He, in His creations. The meaning of ﴿يَمُرُّونَ عَلَيْها﴾ ("they pass by it") is: when something of them comes that is perceived or known in general, the disbeliever is not admonished by it, does not reflect upon it, and does not take lesson from it, according to his desires and his blindness. Therefore he is, in this respect, like one who turns away. A similar meaning is in the words of the poet:

"The breeze passes gently by the dweller of Dhi al-Ghada,
and my heart is split by its blowing."

al-Suddi read ﴿وَالأرْضَ﴾ ("and the earth") in the accusative, by supposing a verb, and in this reading the pause is at "al-samawāt". ʿIkrima and ʿAmr ibn Fā'id read ﴿وَالأرْضُ﴾ in the nominative as a beginning (mubtada'), with the predicate being His saying ﴿يَمُرُّونَ﴾. In the reading with the genitive ﴿الأرْضِ﴾, then ﴿يَمُرُّونَ﴾ is a qualifier of ﴿آيَةٍ﴾. In the Mushaf of ʿAbdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) it is: ﴿والأرْضِ يَمْشُونَ عَلَيْها﴾ ("and the earth, they walk upon it").

His saying ﴿وَما يُؤْمِنُ أكْثَرُهُمْ﴾ ("and most of them do not believe") up to the end of the verse. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it concerns the People of the Book, who believe in Allah and then associate partners with Him in that they disbelieve in His Prophet, or in that they say: ʿUzayr is the son of Allah, and the Messiah is the son of Allah. ʿIkrima, Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Zayd said: it concerns the disbelieving Arabs, and their belief is their acknowledgment of the Creator, the Provider, and the One who causes death; He named it belief even though it was followed by their associating idols and images with Him. Thus this belief is merely linguistic, in the sense that it is a certain kind of assent. It was also said: this verse was revealed because of the words of the Quraysh in the circumambulation and the talbiya (the invocation): "Here I am, O Allah, there is no partner for You, except a partner who is Yours, You own him and what he owns." And it is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ), whenever he heard one of them say "There is no partner for You," would say to him: "Qat, qat" (Enough, enough), meaning: stop here and do not add "except a partner who is Yours."

Al-ghāshiya is that which covers, overspreads and overwhelms. Abu Hafs and Bishr ibn ʿUbayd read ﴿أو يَأْتِيَهُمُ الساعَةُ بَغْتَةً﴾ with the letter ya' (so the verb is "yaʾtiyahum", with the subject being the Hour). Baghta means suddenly, unexpectedly, and that is harder.

Although this verse, beginning with His saying ﴿وَكَأيِّنْ﴾, concerns the disbelievers by the ruling of what precedes it, sinners also take a share of its wording. Belief is in reality (haqīqa), while associating partners is linguistic, like ostentation (riyā'). The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Ostentation is the lesser association (shirk al-asghar)."

His exalted saying ﴿قُلْ هَذِهِ سَبِيلِي﴾ ("Say: This is my way") up to the end of the verse is an indication of the call of Islam and the entire Sharia. Ibn Zayd said: the meaning is: this is my command, my sunna and my method. Ibn Mas'ud read ﴿قُلْ هَذا سَبِيلِي﴾. The sabīl is the path, and it may be feminine or masculine, and likewise al-ṭarīq (the road).

(p. 160) Al-baṣīra is a name for a person's belief regarding a matter, of truth and certainty. Al-baṣīra also, in the language of the Arabs, means the line of blood on a blade. In the well-known hadith: "You look at the blade and see no trace (baṣīra)." Some people interpreted with this meaning the verse of al-Ashʿar al-Ju'fi:

"They went with their traces (baṣā'irahum) upon their shoulders,
and my trace (baṣīrati) runs upon it, a swift and sure horse."

He describes a people who sold the blood of their protector, so it is as if his blood left lines upon their shoulders, since they were marked among people by the selling of that blood.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is also permissible that al-baṣīra in the verse of the poet refers to the correct belief, meaning: they made their belief the seeking of the fire, and their insight regarding that they put behind their backs, just as you say: so-and-so cast my affair behind his back.

His saying ﴿أنا ومَنِ اتَّبَعَنِي﴾ ("I and whoever follows me") may be an emphasis of the pronoun in "adʿū" (I call), and it may be that the whole verse is an enjoiner of good and a caller to Allah, to the disbelievers in Him and to the sinners. ﴿سُبْحانَ اللهِ﴾ ("Glory be to Allah") is a declaration of Allah's transcendence, that is: and say "Glory be to Allah," and say it disassociating yourself from polytheism.

It is narrated that this verse, ﴿قُلْ هَذِهِ سَبِيلِي﴾ up to its end, was inscribed on the banners of Yusuf, peace be upon him.

(p-161) The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿We sent none before you except men to whom We revealed, from the people of the towns. Have they not travelled through the earth and seen what was the end of those before them? And the Abode of the Hereafter is better for those who are God-conscious. Will you not then use your reason?﴾ ﴿Until, when the messengers despaired and thought they had been denied, Our help came to them, and whomever We willed was delivered. And Our punishment is not averted from the criminal people.﴾

This verse contains a refutation of those who found it strange that messengers should be sent from among humans, such as the group who said: ﴿Has God sent a human as a messenger?﴾ [al-Isra' 17:94], and like the group who asked for an angel-king, and others.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "yūḥā ilayhim" with a *yāʾ* and a *fatḥa* on the *ḥāʾ*. This is the reading of ʿĀṣim in the transmission of Abū Bakr. In the transmission of Ḥafṣ he read "nūḥī" with a *nūn* and a *kasra* on the *ḥāʾ*, which is the reading of Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān and Ṭalḥa.

"Al-qurā" means the cities. He specified them, to the exclusion of the people of the *ʿamūd* (the nomads who lived in tents held up by pillars, *ahl al-ʿamūd*), because they, in every nation, are people of coarseness and extreme ignorance. Ibn Zayd said: "The people of the towns are more knowledgeable and more forbearing than the people of the *ʿamūd*."

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Their nobility is scant, and Allah has never sent a prophet from among them. Al-Ḥasan said: "Allah has never sent a messenger from the people of the desert (*al-badiya*, nomadic life), nor from women, nor from the jinn."

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Living a nomadic life (*al-tabaddī*) is disliked, except in times of turmoil (*fitan*) and when one flees with his religion. Like his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "It is about to be that the best property of a Muslim will be sheep," the hadith (prophetic report) to its end. In this regard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) permitted Salama ibn al-Akwaʿ.

(p-162) The Prophet (ﷺ) also said: "There is no returning to the desert (*taʿarrub*) in Islam." And he said: "Whoever goes out to the desert becomes coarse." Muʿādh ibn Jabal, may Allah be pleased with him, related from him that he said: "Satan is the wolf of man, like the wolf of sheep: he takes the far-off sheep. So beware of the mountain paths, and keep to the mosques, the congregations and the common folk."

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is objected to with the case of the nomadic life (*badw*) of Yaʿqūb (Jacob), and the objection is answered in two ways:

The first: that nomadic life was not among the people of the *ʿamūd*, but rather it was a settled life, with dwellings and encampments.

The second: that he called it *badw* only in comparison to Egypt, just as the city-dwelling daughters are *badw* in comparison to the cities (*al-ḥawāḍir*).

Then He referred them to consider the earlier nations in the regions of the earth which denied their messengers, so the punishment of Allah befell them. Then He urged them towards the Hereafter, to prepare for it and to guard against its ruinous things. Then He stood them before Him, rebuking them, with His saying: ﴿Will you not then use your reason?﴾

His saying: ﴿And the Abode of the Hereafter﴾ is an addition describing His favour upon the believers, meaning: He punished the disbelievers and delivered the believers, and the Abode of the Hereafter is best for them.

As for the annexation of "the Abode" to "the Hereafter": al-Farrāʾ said: it is the annexation of a thing to itself, as the poet said:

*If you were to dwell in the abodes of ʿAbs,*
*you would know humiliation with the certainty of knowledge.*

(p-163) In another version: "If the abodes of ʿAbs had become desolate to you..." This is like the saying "masjid al-jāmiʿ" (the congregational mosque) and the like. The Basrans said: this is by omission of an annexed noun, its estimated form being: "and the Abode of the life to come" or "the final period".

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

These nouns which are generic, like *masjid* (mosque), *thawb* (garment), *ḥaqq* (truth), *jabal* (mountain) and the like, when a speaker utters them, one does not know what he intends by them, so they are annexed to a defining specifier for the intended meaning. Sometimes they are annexed to another genus, as in your saying "thawb khazz" (a garment of silk) and "jabal turāb" (a mound of earth). Sometimes they are annexed to a descriptive, as in your saying "masjid al-jāmiʿ" and "ḥaqq al-yaqīn" (the truth of certainty). Sometimes they are annexed to a proper noun, as in your saying "jabal Uḥud" and the like.

Al-Ḥasan, al-Aʿmash, al-Aʿraj, Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, ʿĀṣim and ʿAlqama read "yaʿqilūn" with a *yāʾ*, and it is reported differently from al-Aʿmash. Abū Ḥātim said: the reading of the common people is "a-fa-lā taʿqilūn" with a *tāʾ* from above.

His saying: ﴿Have they not travelled through the earth and seen what was the end of those before them﴾ implies that the messengers whom Allah sent from among the people of the towns called their nations, and they did not believe in them until the exemplary punishments (*mathulāt*, calamities that serve as examples) came upon them. They then became among those who are taken as a lesson by their end. For this implication it is fitting that "ḥattā" (until) enters into His saying: ﴿Until, when the messengers despaired﴾.

(p-164) Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir, al-Ḥasan, ʿĀʾisha (in one report), ʿĪsā, Qatāda, Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb, al-Aʿraj, Abū Rajāʾ and Ibn Abī Mulayka read "kudhdhibū" with a doubled *dhāl* and a *ḍamma* on the *kāf*. The rest read "kudhibū" with a *ḍamma* on the *kāf*, a *kasra* on the *dhāl*, and without doubling. This is the reading of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Ṭalḥa, al-Aʿmash, Ibn Jubayr, Masrūq, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Ibrāhīm and Abū Jaʿfar. Shayba ibn Niṣāḥ related it from al-Qāsim from ʿĀʾisha. Mujāhid, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Ḥārith read "kadhabū" with a *fatḥa* on the *kāf* and the *dhāl* (reports differ from them).

As for the first reading: "ẓannū" may mean certainty (*yaqīn*), and the pronoun in "ẓannū" and in "kudhdhibū" refers to the messengers, and the deniers are the polytheists of those to whom they were sent. The meaning is: the messengers were certain that the polytheists had denied them and were resolute in this, and that there was no turning away from it. It is also possible that "ẓann" retains its own meaning, and the two pronouns refer to the messengers, and the deniers are the believers among those to whom they were sent. That is: when the promises were long delayed, the messengers supposed that the believers at first had denied them and doubted by their saying.

As for the second reading, "kudhibū" with a *ḍamma* on the *kāf*, a *kasra* on the *dhāl* and without doubling, it may mean: until the messengers despaired of victory, or of the faith of their people (according to the differing interpretations of the exegetes on this), and the addressees thought the messengers had lied regarding what they claimed of prophethood, or regarding what they threatened them with of punishment, since the respite had lengthened and well-being had continued. Since, on this interpretation, the addressees were the deniers, the verb in His saying "kudhibū" was put in the passive form. This is the well-known opinion of Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Jubayr. Al-Ṭabarī transmitted that Muslim ibn Yasār said to Saʿīd ibn Jubayr: "O Abū ʿAbd Allah, a verse has reached me in every way: ﴿Until, when the messengers despaired and thought they had been denied﴾. This means that the messengers thought they had been lied to (in the light form)." Ibn Jubayr said to him: "O Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, the messengers only despaired of their people answering them, and their people thought the messengers had lied to them. Then the help came." Muslim stood up to Saʿīd, embraced him and said: "You have relieved me; may Allah relieve you."

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

May Allah be pleased with them, how great was their character in knowledge! This interpretation, in this reading, was held by Ibn Masʿūd and Mujāhid. Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī preferred this interpretation and said: returning the pronoun in "ẓannū" and "kudhibū" to the addressees is permissible, even though no explicit mention preceded them, for two reasons:

The first: that the mention of the messengers requires the mention of those to whom they were sent.

The second: that they have been alluded to in His saying: ﴿the end of those before them﴾.

(p-165) This reading may also allow that the pronoun in "ẓannū" and "kudhibū" refers to the messengers, and the meaning is: "the one who informed them from Allah lied to them," and "ẓann" keeps its own meaning. A group of the people of knowledge related this interpretation. The messengers were human, so they weakened and their opinion became bad. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbās, and also by Ibn Masʿūd, and Ibn Jubayr said: "Were they not human?" Ibn Masʿūd, when someone asked him about this, said: "It is that which we dislike." ʿĀʾisha, the Mother of the Believers, may Allah be pleased with her, and a group of the people of knowledge rejected this interpretation, and considered it too great to describe the messengers with this. Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: "This is impermissible for the messengers."

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is the correct view. Where are infallibility and knowledge?

As for the third reading, with a *fatḥa* on the *kāf* and the *dhāl*: the pronoun in "ẓannū" refers to the addressees, and the pronoun in "kadhabū" refers to the messengers. It is also possible that both pronouns refer to the messengers, meaning: the messengers supposed that they had lied, in that they transmitted a falsehood, even though they did not intend it. This interpretation then returns to the rejected meaning mentioned earlier.

His saying: ﴿Our help came to them﴾ means: by the punishment of their disbelieving nations.

Then He described the state of the coming of the punishment, that it delivers the messengers and their followers, who are those whose mercy He willed, and that it sends down His might upon the criminal disbelievers. Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr, Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read "fa-nunjī" with two *nūn*s, from *anjā* (the causative of "to deliver"). Al-Ḥasan read "fa-nunajjī," with the second *nūn* vowelled with a *fatḥa* and the *jīm* doubled, from *najjā yunajjī*. Abū ʿAmr also, and Qatāda, read "fa-nujjī" with one *nūn*, a doubled *jīm* and a *sukūn* on the *yāʾ*. One group said that it is like the first, the second *nūn* being assimilated into the *jīm*. Some objected that this is not a place for assimilation, because the *nūn* and the *jīm* are dissimilar in their qualities, though not in their points of articulation, and said: "The *nūn* was only omitted in the written text, not in pronunciation." This reading has been reported from al-Kisāʾī and Nāfiʿ. ʿĀṣim and Ibn ʿĀmir read "fa-nujjiya" with a *fatḥa* on the *yāʾ*, on the pattern *fuʿʿila*. A group read "fa-nunjiya" with two *nūn*s and a *fatḥa* on the *yāʾ*, transmitted by Hubayra from Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim, and this is an error by Hubayra. Ibn Muḥayṣin and Mujāhid read "fa-najā," a past verb with a light *jīm*. This is the reading of Naṣr ibn ʿĀṣim, al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan, Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ and Abū Ḥaywa. Abū ʿAmr al-Dānī said: "I read for Ibn Muḥayṣin: 'fa-najjā' with a doubled *jīm*, meaning: the help delivered."

The *ba's* (*al-baʾs*, the punishment) means the torment. Abū Ḥaywa read "man yashāʾ" with a *yāʾ*. The report of the destruction of the disbelievers came with His saying: ﴿and Our punishment is not averted﴾, to the end of the verse, for in these words there is a clear threat and a warning to the contemporaries of Muḥammad, peace and blessings be upon him. Al-Ḥasan read "baʾsuhu" with a *hāʾ*.

This is the reading of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Ṭalḥa, al-Aʿmash, Ibn Jubayr, Masrūq, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Ibrāhīm and Abū Jaʿfar. Shayba ibn Niṣāḥ related it from al-Qāsim from ʿĀʾisha. Mujāhid, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Ḥārith read "kadhabū" with a *fatḥa* on the *kāf* and the *dhāl* (reports differ from them).

As for the first reading: "ẓannū" may mean certainty (*yaqīn*), and the pronoun in "ẓannū" and in "kudhdhibū" refers to the messengers, and the deniers are the polytheists of those to whom they were sent. The meaning is: the messengers were certain that the polytheists had denied them and were resolute in this, and that there was no turning away from it. It is also possible that "ẓann" retains its own meaning, and the two pronouns refer to the messengers, and the deniers are the believers among those to whom they were sent. That is: when the promises were long delayed, the messengers supposed that the believers at first had denied them and doubted by their saying.

As for the second reading, "kudhibū" with a *ḍamma* on the *kāf*, a *kasra* on the *dhāl* and without doubling, it may mean: until the messengers despaired of victory, or of the faith of their people (according to the differing interpretations of the exegetes on this), and the addressees thought the messengers had lied regarding what they claimed of prophethood, or regarding what they threatened them with of punishment, since the respite had lengthened and well-being had continued. Since, on this interpretation, the addressees were the deniers, the verb in His saying "kudhibū" was put in the passive form. This is the well-known opinion of Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Jubayr. Al-Ṭabarī transmitted that Muslim ibn Yasār said to Saʿīd ibn Jubayr: "O Abū ʿAbd Allah, a verse has reached me in every way: ﴿Until, when the messengers despaired and thought they had been denied﴾. This means that the messengers thought they had been lied to (in the light form)." Ibn Jubayr said to him: "O Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, the messengers only despaired of their people answering them, and their people thought the messengers had lied to them. Then the help came." Muslim stood up to Saʿīd, embraced him and said: "You have relieved me; may Allah relieve you."

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

May Allah be pleased with them, how great was their character in knowledge! This interpretation, in this reading, was held by Ibn Masʿūd and Mujāhid. Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī preferred this interpretation and said: returning the pronoun in "ẓannū" and "kudhibū" to the addressees is permissible, even though no explicit mention preceded them, for two reasons:

The first: that the mention of the messengers requires the mention of those to whom they were sent.

The second: that they have been alluded to in His saying: ﴿the end of those before them﴾.

(p-165) This reading may also allow that the pronoun in "ẓannū" and "kudhibū" refers to the messengers, and the meaning is: "the one who informed them from Allah lied to them," and "ẓann" keeps its own meaning. A group of the people of knowledge related this interpretation. The messengers were human, so they weakened and their opinion became bad. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbās, and also by Ibn Masʿūd, and Ibn Jubayr said: "Were they not human?" Ibn Masʿūd, when someone asked him about this, said: "It is that which we dislike." ʿĀʾisha, the Mother of the Believers, may Allah be pleased with her, and a group of the people of knowledge rejected this interpretation, and considered it too great to describe the messengers with this. Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: "This is impermissible for the messengers."

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is the correct view. Where are infallibility and knowledge?

As for the third reading, with a *fatḥa* on the *kāf* and the *dhāl*: the pronoun in "ẓannū" refers to the addressees, and the pronoun in "kadhabū" refers to the messengers. It is also possible that both pronouns refer to the messengers, meaning: the messengers supposed that they had lied, in that they transmitted a falsehood, even though they did not intend it. This interpretation then returns to the rejected meaning mentioned earlier.

His saying: ﴿Our help came to them﴾ means: by the punishment of their disbelieving nations.

Then He described the state of the coming of the punishment, that it delivers the messengers and their followers, who are those whose mercy He willed, and that it sends down His might upon the criminal disbelievers. Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr, Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read "fa-nunjī" with two *nūn*s, from *anjā* (the causative of "to deliver"). Al-Ḥasan read "fa-nunajjī," with the second *nūn* vowelled with a *fatḥa* and the *jīm* doubled, from *najjā yunajjī*. Abū ʿAmr also, and Qatāda, read "fa-nujjī" with one *nūn*, a doubled *jīm* and a *sukūn* on the *yāʾ*. One group said that it is like the first, the second *nūn* being assimilated into the *jīm*. Some objected that this is not a place for assimilation, because the *nūn* and the *jīm* are dissimilar in their qualities, though not in their points of articulation, and said: "The *nūn* was only omitted in the written text, not in pronunciation." This reading has been reported from al-Kisāʾī and Nāfiʿ. ʿĀṣim and Ibn ʿĀmir read "fa-nujjiya" with a *fatḥa* on the *yāʾ*, on the pattern *fuʿʿila*. A group read "fa-nunjiya" with two *nūn*s and a *fatḥa* on the *yāʾ*, transmitted by Hubayra from Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim, and this is an error by Hubayra. Ibn Muḥayṣin and Mujāhid read "fa-najā," a past verb with a light *jīm*. This is the reading of Naṣr ibn ʿĀṣim, al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan, Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ and Abū Ḥaywa. Abū ʿAmr al-Dānī said: "I read for Ibn Muḥayṣin: 'fa-najjā' with a doubled *jīm*, meaning: the help delivered."

The *ba's* (*al-baʾs*, the punishment) means the torment. Abū Ḥaywa read "man yashāʾ" with a *yāʾ*. The report of the destruction of the disbelievers came with His saying: ﴿and Our punishment is not averted﴾, to the end of the verse, for in these words there is a clear threat and a warning to the contemporaries of Muḥammad, peace and blessings be upon him. Al-Ḥasan read "baʾsuhu" with a *hāʾ*.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 12, verse 111:

The saying of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿Indeed, in their stories there is a lesson for those of understanding. It is not a narration that could be invented, but a confirmation of what was before it, and a detailed explanation of all things, and a guidance and a mercy for a people who believe.﴾

The pronoun in "qasasihim" (their stories) is general, referring to Yusuf, his parents, his brothers, and the rest of the messengers who were mentioned in general terms. Since all of that is in the Qur'an, He said of it: ﴿It is not a narration that could be invented﴾. When the story of Yusuf is contemplated, it becomes clear that in its wonders, and in Allah's testing of some people in some situations, His kindness to some people in some situations, and His beneficence to some people in some situations, there is a lesson for whoever has intellect and reflects well, until he knows that every matter is from Allah, the Blessed and Exalted, and to Him it returns.

His saying "ma kana" (it was not) is a form of negation, and the context of the situation requires that the proof establishes that it is not something invented, and that is through the evidences of prophethood and the evidences of inimitability (i'jaz).

"Al-hadith" here is the singular of "ahadith" (narrations/accounts), and the meaning of it as the opposite of "qadim" (old/eternal) has no place here.

"Tasdiq" is in the accusative either by supposing a meaning of "kana" (it was), or by taking "lakin" to mean the emphatic "lakinna" (but indeed). 'Isa al-Thaqafi read "tasdiqu" in the nominative, and likewise everything coordinated with it; this is by omitting the subject, the estimation being: "huwa tasdiqu" (it is a confirmation). Abu Hatim said: the accusative is on the estimation "wa lakin kana" (but it was), and the nominative on the estimation "wa lakinna huwa" (but indeed it is). The verse of Dhu al-Rummah is recited in both ways:

؎ "Nor was my wealth an inheritance I had inherited, nor was it blood-money, nor gain from a sinful deed."

؎ "But the gift of Allah from every journey, to every one whose tent is veiled, a tireless traveller."

He put "'ata'u Allah" in the nominative, and the accusative is better.

"Alladhi bayna yadayhi" (that which is before it) is the Torah and the Gospel. The pronoun in "yadayhi" refers to the Qur'an, and it is the subject of "kana". His saying "kulli shay'" (every thing) means of the beliefs, the rulings, and what is lawful and unlawful.

The rest of the verse is clear.

Completed, by the help and success of Allah, is the tafsir of Surat Yusuf. Upon him and upon our Prophet be prayers and peace, and praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
